div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

SowrrifiNG new in cigarettes, runs the advertise- inernt. Let us hope it is tobacco. "'I'LL join you in a minute" is what the minister Bahl to the couple who were waiting to be married. "SHE had star-like eyes and raven hair, her lips were like ripe re-1 cherries, and her neck like that of a, swan."—Puck. Iv there was but one potato in the world, a careful cultivator might produce 10,000,000,000 from it in 10 years, and that would supply the

world with seed again. _ FRIEND : "Trouble with your wife, eh? What 'rock did your domestic ship split on ? " Spinks : •"None at all. Hadn't rocks enough; that was the difficulty." "I PITY you, old man, when I see your creditors worrying you as they do. That is a trouble I never had myself." "No; you probably never had any credit." I SAID a conscientious auctioneer: "Ladies and .gentlemen, there is no sham a.boet these carpets. ,They are genuine tapestry carpets. I bought them horn old Tapestry himself." STRANGER. : "What do you have the wires on ..that barbed-wire fence so close together for?" Mississippi Farmer: "So that when the river rises we can use it for a fish net."

_ I OFFSPRING —" what makes pa so cross to- day ?" Ma—" He's writing a poem, dear, on the beauties of parental love." You can please any milkman by telling him that his milk is pure; but you may annoy him if you say it is of the first water. Milk is not diamonds,

yon know. MAMMA: "Will you have some more pudding, pet?" Little Pet : "No, ma'am. I'm full." Mamma: " Horrors ! Yon mus'nt say you're fell. It bent nice." Little Pet: "I mean my tomach'e lull." TRUE GuArrrunE.—Grateful farmer (who, after various losses, has been started again by the squire) —Ah ! your honour, I said to Bridget: "As long as the squire and his sons are about we shall never want for a few pigs and oxen." THERE are two occasions when a man is greatly interested in his personal appearance—the one is when he sees hair coming on his upper lip, and the other is when the hair is growing off the top of his head. "So your wife has left you?" "She has." "What were her last words on leaving you!" "'ls my hat on straight ?' " r THERE is nothing more calculated to take the conceit out of a fellow than seeing a crayon por- trait of himself by an amateur artist.

A mks said that porter taken in large quantities made him fat. His friend answered—" I once saw it make you lean—against a lamp-post." " 'IILLo Bill. 'Ow did yer get down? What sort of a journey ?" " Rippin my boy. Second- class carriage, third-class ticket, and first-class company." Quottiz : "Going to be married in a month? Well, old fellah, you mustn't fret about it, though I know what it is. Doosed depwessing idea." AT LAST. —Doctor : Your wife has dislocated her jaw, sir. Mr. Wagtung (rubbing his hands cheerfully): Ah, I thought that curtain-lecture last night would do it! UNSELFISII —Waiter (to farmer visiting London who has been dining in a restaurant): Ahem! Anything, air, for the waiter, sir? Farmer (looking at his plate) ; yes. Take all there's left; I'm stuffed ! WADOS (to young matron with the perambula- tor) : "Good morning, Mrs. Fullbloom. Are you taking the son out for an airing, or the heir out for a sunning?" Mrs. Fullbloom : "Neither, Mr. Waggs. Baby is a girl." PARSON : Don't you think my argument on the teetotal question thoroughly sand. Taper: Yes, air. All sound I EDITOR : "Sending poetry to this magazine, Mr. Scribbler, is a good deal like 'casting bread upon the waters.'" Scribbler : "Yes, air, I sup- pose it is. I notice that it generally returns after many days." MEYERSTEIN : "You vos a grew' feller to put OD air, aind it? I remembers your granlader vos nodding but der vilache hangman in Poland?" Blumenroth : " Yaw ! I remembers dot, too; and your gran'fader vos der lasd von he hangt ! ' "You are most entertaining," remarked the gallant old gentleman to his fair partner at dinner. "1 assure you that I envy your future husband." The maid turned. an appealing face toward him. "Would—would you mind introducing him?" she asked. _ _

-- OVERUEARD AT BlM:MON.—Johnnie : Did you :notice that lovely girl? What glorious eyes, with an expression like that of a startled fawn. Old hand (calmly): If she has that look she's froml London. Johnnie: Wey ? Old Hand: You see all the girls there are that way. Dodging 'buses and cabs, you know! JoHs : " A'm sayin', Jean, when ye gang tae the I market the morn, dinna buy ony mair barrels 0. apples free Tamson." Jean: " Whit's th' maitter I we Tarneon, John? Dis he nae pit the big apples at the top an' the wee anes at the bottom? John: "Ou, ay; but he disna mark the tap, an' I've opened three o' his barrels at the bottom tae show the customers." IT DISCOURAGED CONVERSATION.—BIoobumper " Well, I suppose the sewing-society went over a great lot of gossip this afternoon ?" Mrs. Moo- bumper: "No : we didn't talk a bit of gossip." Bloobumper : " How that that?' Mrs. Bloobumper "Every member was present." • A footman learned from his master that mat apropos meant "Oct of place." Meeting a brother footman who had been discharged, "Ah, my dear fellow, lam sorry for you. You are mat apropos." HE was a poor, half starved looking baggage man. "Doing anything ?" we asked him. "Oh, yes," he replied, with a grim smile, "the great aquarium trick." "What's that?" "Fasting." THAT BOY AGAIN.—Miss Flipflap (Who has just been asked to play something on the piano) : Oh I really I assure you I can't pay anything, really I— Tommy Flipflap : Say, Madge, why don't: you play that piece you spoke to me a,out? bliss I Flipfiap : What piece, Tommy? Tommy F. : Why that one you told me to ask you to play when I we had company 'cause you knew it better'n any of the others. I forgot the name ! Sin G. BsauxoNx once met Quin at a very small dinner party. There was a delicious pudding, which the master of the house, pusning the dish towards Quin, begged him to taste. A gentleman had just before helped himself to an immense piece of it. "Pray," said Quin, looking first at the gentleman s plate and then at the diah, "what is the pudding ?" NEVER VARIED. —A story is told to the effect that a young woman who, giving evidence in a court, on being asked her age and replying that she was 30, was asked if she had not given the same age when before the nutglstrate a couple of years previously. "I think it very likely," she answered coolly; "I'm nut one of those women who say one thing to-day and quite another to. morrow!" Tramping Jabs: "It's getting to be too hard work to pick up a livia' in this country. El it wuzn't to fur away I'd go to Central Ameriky. A man don't hay to do nothin' there. Whole country's covered with baaanas. Nothin' to do but lay under a tree all day an' «at bananas." Rusty rufe : "Got to pick 'em off u the trees, hain't ye ?'' "Course," "1 knowed thee wuz some drawback." ABOUT the time when Murphy so successfully attacked the stage-struck heroes in the pleasant face of "The Apprentice," an eminent poulterer went to a spouting-club in search of his aervant who, he understood, was that evening to make his debut in Lear, and entered t .e room at the moment he was exclaiming, "I am the King; you cannot touch me for coining." "No, you dog," cried the enraged master, catching the mad mon- arch by his collar, "but I can for not picking the ducks." He HARDLY KNEW HER. —A Yorkshire miner recently celled on a well-known local artist, with a view to getting his dead wife's portrait painted. "But, my good man," said the astonished knight of the brush, " I never saw your wife." " Weel, that duana matter," said Bill. " Yo've a picter of Moases, 'at liven three thahsatm yeor sin' ; surely y can manage wun o' my wife, 'ats nobbut been deead a munai !" This of course was irresistible, and the picture was duly finished, and when Bill went to fetch it away, he wiped his eyes and mur- mured gently : "SOS that's my wife? Ha charged aka iz l'•

div.p: CHRISTMAS CRACKERSg CHARADES. •
My first is a little bird. My second is a large bird. My whole combines the two. Sparrow-hawk.
My first is dark, My second is a proposition, My third is a storm, My whole is a bird famous for its vocal power.

'Tis as a name for a thief that our first will occur, Or a pickpocket sly, if you should prefer; Next 's congenial, of the same nature or kind, While the whole's a small cup for you to find. Nipper-kin

My first she wss a serving maid— She went to fetch some tea; How much she brought my second tells As plainly as can be. Now when the answer you have found, Name it to others too; My whole is just the very thing, In telling them, you'll do. Ann•ounes.

ru tell you—no, it cannot be That you should guess my first so pat; I've said it, tho', and so will you, When you havo puzzled long—that's fiat. My second is a thing—like a hat; Like anything you please—depotid on it. I've said it twice, so, in a thrice, Resolve my whole and make an end of it. No-thing.

My first denotes a brilliant place, Where belles and jewels shine; My next transports the merchant's stores, Or produce of the mine; Sweet pleasures in my whole abound, Apart from worldly strife; By nymphs and swains its always found, The happiest part of life. Court-ship.

My first ascends on soaring wing To heaven's gate. And bails the coming of the Spring In notes elate. My second shines on knightly heel, In battle won, A token that its wearer's steel Has prowess done. My whole beside ha lady's bower, In varied hue, In stately pride, unfolds its flower, Pink, white or blue. Tstrkspiir. winter's time nt A-retie seen. --- Nhen the weather is very cold Lid is formed into my second By children young and old. And if my whole you wish to find, V My first and second must be combined, 4nd then by looking you will see, AL winter favourite in me. Bnotolull.

When the stutshine and the shadows, In the prime time of the year, Are flitting o'er the meadows, My first you always hear. When man is softly sleeping, _...„,_•••44::77 And every care seems sped, • My second, darkly creeping, Oft fills his soul with dread. My whole's what we despise or shun, Or a delusion sprung from hate or fun. Hum-bug.

div.head: -GAMES.
div.p: -GAMES.

UISTORICAL Pfurnnrs" is a game requiring a little artistic touch, and is very popular. Each member of the company is supplied with a sheet of paper and pencil. He is called upon to try and re- present some well-known historical incident. Very bad specimens of draughtsmanship are sure to be offered, and even the very worst example, will sometimes provide lots of fun and laughter. Most people fancy they can do something in the way of sketching. This game will soon find out their
ficiencies:

--------- A VXRY popular game with little folks is called "Blowing the Boll."' The players sit or stand (they generally become too excited to sit after a few moments) round an uncovered table. A tiny bailie made by rolling up some wool, and placed in the middle of the table. Everybody then begins to blow upon it, each blowing it away from his own vicinity, and the object of all being to blow it over the edge of the table, in order that the one by whose right side it falls may pay a forfeit. Buff WITH THE WAND.—This is a variation of Blind Man's Buff. The blind man stands with a cane or walking-stick in hand, in the centre .of the room, and the rest of the company join hands in a ring and dance round to some lively tune. At a pause in the music, the Blind Man lets the "wand" fall gently on the head or shoulders of one, of the circle, that person is bound to take hold of the end, and to imitate, disguising his voice as best he can, any three cries (of birds, beasts, chimney-sweep, milkman, &c.), the Blind Man may choose to utter. The Blind Man then makes a guess at the person i holding the wand, and if he guesses rightly, such person becomes Blind Man in tuna. If the guess is wrong the circle moves on again as before, and the Blind Man makes a fresh attempt. A CAPITAL GAME, often appreciated by the child- ren of a larger growth, is "Shadow Guessing." A white sheet is put up at one end of the room, and some one sits upon a stool a little in front of it. The table, containing a lighted lamp or candle, is placed at the end of the room, all other lights being extinguished. Each member of the party passes in turn between the table and the person who is look- ing at the sheet, his or her shadow being thus thrown out in strong relief. If the guesser can tell whose shadow it is on the sheet the "owner" of the shadow must take his place. Of course, in the ordi- n.ry way it would be easy enough to recognise one's friends, but when gentlemen drape their heads in antimacassars and ladies CIVBB the room on all-fours, holding a cushion so as to obscure the view, it 18 obvious that the poor guesser has a difficult task. SzuP•SxAv•Sxonirrm. —Any number may play, but six or seven make the best game. The whole pack of cards is used, and dealt completely out, face downwards. Each player looks at his cards. The elder hand leads off, turning up any card he pleases, at the same time saying "Snip. Any playershold- ing the next highest card of the same suit forthwith turns it up, and says "Snap.' The player holding the next highest plays in like manner, saying "Snorurn." The player holding the next card says, "Hi Cockalornm, " and if any player holds yet an- other in sequence, he plays it and says "Jig." The sequence is not continued any further, the playing of a card as "Jig" constituting it -a " stop," as a matter of course. Where the sequence is not com- pleted, but comes to an untimely end, the person playing the last card leads again. Kings, of course, are "stops, the ace ranking as the lowest card. The object of each player is to play out one's cards, as the player who is " first out" wins, and receives from each of the others a counter for each card he holds. At first sight this game looks simple, but there is a good deal of judgment required to play it to the best advantage. Thus, suppose the leader has the six, seven, nine, and knave of a given suit, . the card to lead is the seven. If, as is probable, the intermediate cards are played by others, you still come in again at each stop, and the knave will be the "Jig," thus keeping the lead in'yonr own hand, while the six is now a stop, and may again give you the lead, should the same snit be led from a lower card. Had you, on the other hand, led your six, the ten, which you do not hold, would have been the "Jig," and you would have lost both these advantage& Aces, and cards which cannot be led to, by reason of their immediate predeces- sors having been already played, should be led out early. Kings and other known stops, on the other \hand, should be retained to recover the lead, until an opportunity occurs for getting rid of two or three together, when it may be well to take advantage of it.

LADIES'
LETTER

MY DEAREST NELLIE, The superior persons may talk as they like about wasting time and thought on one's clothes; very likely we should be happier if we were arrayed In garments that grew on us at the proper times, and never changed in fashion. It is true, the anxiety of choosing frocks and hate is very wearing, par- ticularly at a time like the present, when all gam rules we have gone by for years are suddenly changed, and a quite new and alarming set put in their places. For if we get a new set of dresses with extensive skirts, who will assure us that the fashion will not change again, and as abruptly, before many weeks, and all our pretty purchases be made useless? Children's dresses have lately received con- siderable attentions, and even fashions in respeot to theni zre very changeable. At present thick woollen materials woven in a plain colour are being more used than any other fabrics for making smart walking dreases for little girls. The favourite colours in cloths of this description are a rich shade of golden brown, prune, bottle green, and sealing-wax red. Either of these colours trim well with black, be it in the form of velvet, satin' or a fancy braid. For afternoon or better frocks the skirts are generally trimmed with flounces, and the bodices are then completed to correspond, with flounce tqaulettes or braces. Smaller children lock best dressed in frocks which are made en princess or in a smock shape. The same thick woollen materials ere used to fashion these little frocks, provided they be in a soft texture.

A dainty little maid in a frock of Venetian bine velvet was quite the best dressed of a party recently. The yoke of 'sae was outlined by a breastplate of velvet, from which fell a frill of lace to the waist, pointed epalettes of velvet beiag over the shoulders, and the sleeves frilled with the lace. Tea gowns arp still much worn; nor shall we ever, I fincy, be able to exist without its many and varied charms. It is always difacult to get As well-shaped garment of this kind made of use:span- sive material. All the beat styles are kept for the velvets and brocades, which are beyond the reach of many. An ideal garment, however, coda he arranged at home with perfeet ease sad economy.

A very pretty tea gown is made of petunia cloth with a pointed cape of velvet to match, outlined with sable, deep rands of point de Venice falling from the full puffed sleeves, with similar lace forming a bib, which hung from the neck to the waist, disappearing beneath a girdle of cut jet. The very latest hats are covered with black moire, but this seems a very chilly-looking material, and velvet, felt, or beaver look infinitely more seasonable and cosy. Broadly speaking, two shapes, with but slight variations, are universally worn; that with a very wide fiat brim, almost cireular in plan, just slightly bent up over the left temple, and a somewhat smaller shape, the brim of which is more oval than round, and is caught up closely to the crown at the side. A pretty hat of the former type is covered with rather pale chest. lent brown velvet put on quite plainly; two sable tails starting from a big bow of the velvet in front surround the crown, and a very narrow band of the same fur edges the under aide of the brim, which is bent up over the temple to show two full rosettes of turquoise blue velvet, A hat of the second shape described is of black velvet, edged with a very narrow line of cat jet. The crown is encircled by a wider band of jet, and the brim is caught to the cro'wn with a high tuff of black ostrich feathers starting from behind two pale green wings connected by a jet ornamlnt.

Fur seems getting daily more expensive, so much so that many of us must eschew such costly etceteras ; and it behoves us t.) turn our attention to some inexpensive substitute. So far as muffs are concerned this is easily managed, but the matter Is a more difficult ono when we consider fur trim. Icings and linings. A dainty muff may be made of almost any material, such as velvet, plush, fancy or plain cloth. It is lined with quilted satin or silk, and may be of a contrasting colour. It is gathered on each side under a band of fur, and meets at the top with a frill. 2of a yard of velvet 22 inohes wide and 1 yard of fur will be required. Yours as ever, Jionviis.

_ It is suggested that women would find a field for em- ployment by qualifying themselves as hairdressers. They could go hem house to house, and for a small lee ar- range their clients' hair for the day. There are many busy women, especially in London, who would gladly pay, say; sixpence or a shilling a day, for the luxury of having their hair dressed becomingly and in the latest fashion at no cost of time or trouble to themselves. Professor Lombroso, the eminent Italian scientist, who holds such very strong adverse opinions as to the ability of women to feel pain as acutely as men do, has lately been pursuing his investigations in another direction, and he has now delivered himself of the unqualified opinion that women of the criminal and immoral type are invariably larger of hands and feet and smaller in the head than average women.

Going to Neep. Many plans have been recommended to procure the blessing of repose for those who cannot' lay them down in peace and sleep." Exercise late is good. " After supper run a mile," and it is certainly not advisable to go direct from a hot sitting-room to a warm bed-room for the night. A turn out into the cool air is much more healthy, aid often succeeds in procuring a quiet night. The bed should be firm and elastic—not feathers. - In India, Europeans use a pillow for their knees to keep the bed cooler. To procure sleep we have been advised to get up and walk about, and use the flesh brush, and this will be found highly useful where a dry state of skin gives that restless feeling called " the fidgets." We have found total instantaneous immersion in a cold bath highly useful. The Chinese advise to wash the mouth with cold water ; in India they tickle the soles .of the feet. Boerhave recommends to listen to dropping water, also Spenser. Others advise the olean harp, whi!e lEsetapiades used to be rocked asleep, and this certainlv succeeds with infants, and seems to act on the circula- tion in the brain. Franklin advises a cold air bath, taken by walking about the room in one's night-dress, and this is very successful. Others put the feet in very warm water. Electricity has been recommended for this as for everthing else. Kant comes very near the mark when ho advises to direct the thoughts to indifferent sub- jects—which means to take them from the grief oi anxiety which keeps us awake. Artifices succeed either by exhausting attention, or by carrying the mini. rapidly from one subject to another, but they eltei. counteract sleep by promoting activity of mind. A desultory state without emotion is.the most favourable to sleep, and if we have achieved that we are on th, very edge of insensibility. By gently ringing the 'change., on our senses, touching the strings lightly, and flying nft to another before the first is aroused to complete atten- tion, we attain that very gentle play of the nerve:- which quickly subsides into insensitiveness. We have not spoken of the treatment of sleeplessness which be longs especially to the province of the physician. W advise that no one should treat himself by drugs for thi condition. Let him try first, if he will, all the mean, which we have indicated ; let him stUdy the cause: which prevent sleep, and reduce his hours of brain work while increasing bodily exercise. Let him try regulateu meals, great moderation in stimulants and in smoking ; let him use the cold bath and exercise at night; and it _ .- .

.these fail, have recourse to his "doctor." lisre ari drugs which quiet nervous irritability without narcotis- ing, mid in certain cases they may be used with advant- age. But to be cast into a deep sleep by opium or choral, or analogous drugs, should be left to the judg- ment and management of skilled hands.—" Cassell' Book of Health."

A rushing, blinding, bewildering shock, as two trains met at the sharp curve with deadly force, and both went whirling through space, down, down the steep embankment to the valley below. A collision. One train was five minutes_ too_ early, another three minutes late There was some carelessness over signals, and for that carelessness helpless human beings paid with

their lives. There wai dire confusion and dismay, then those who had escaped began to collect themselves. Lanterns were brought from an adjacent village, and the dead, the dying and wounded were extricated from the wreck, and were laid side by side in the pale moonlight on the cool, green, daisy-studded grass. Tien there came a cry that some one was lying, face downward, in the brook that ran through the valley. Strong men hurried there. They saw a mass of dark, curling hair, a long silk cloak wrapped aronnd the body, and a travelling-bag held in stiff, white hand. They raised the slim figure ; it was that of a woman, young and fair; but a cry of horror rose to their lips as they held their lanterns dawn to her face; it was crushed beyond all semblance to humanity— crushed beyond all hope of recognition. Someone suggested that the travelling-bag be opened • perhaps it contained something that might lead to the poor soul's identification.
It did contain something—an address, printed in gold lettering upon the silken pocket of the Russian leather bag—the address in full of Uldene Chester. _ _
A few pocket-handkerchiefe were daintily em- broidered in silk floss with the name—Uldene. _

"This is Rutledge Chester's young bride," said someone in the crowd. "I met her once. It is certainly she. He must be telegraphed for at once.'' A dark-browed man, muffled to the chin, stood staring down on the mutilated figure in horror too great for words. "Dead I" he muttered, under his breath. "It is better so; she is out of my wi.y for ever I" No remorse came to him that she lay dead in all her youth and her fair young beauty; his con- science, and his heart—harder than marble—did not suffer one pang that should have come to him, knowing, as he did, that he had snared her in his cruel meshes, dragging her down to her doom. "What satisfactory news to take back across the ocean with me— The girl is dead! She will never cross our path again—never again—unless the dead have power to rise from the grave I '"

" Are—you mad 7 What, in Heaven's naiiie, wo-ffd my wife be doing on the train? There is some mistake 1" Then suddenly be began to tremble with a strange dread. His heart began to be with awful throbs. A cry came from his white lips. He was beginning to understand that Uldene's letter was no jest. She hid left him. Yes, this young bride, on whose love for himself he would have staked his hopes of heaven, he had believed and trusted her so implicitly, had left him. Yes, she nad left him. He was beginning to comprehend the import of the telegram. Some- thing had happened to the train on which she was gone. What bad happened? What WAS it? What was the worst? Was she living, or (lead I

In less than ten minutes Rutledge was at the station. _ James, his faithful valet, went with him, for Mr. Chester seemed quite unfit to travel alone. With a white, drawn face he entered the car. The train was an express that went at almost frightful speed. Yet it seemed to the agonised young husband that it only crawled along. How was he- to live until Allendale was reac.hed? How was he to bear the cruel suspense, the agony of waiting? His strong hands were clenched, his teeth set. The breath came in hot gasps from his pale lips. Over and over again the words of the telegram rang in his ears. It was well for him the journey was not long. Suspense would have killed him had it continued.

In the gray, early dawn the train reached Allen- dale Station. Confusion seemed to reign everywhere. As Rut- ledge Chester stepped from the car, a strange, hushed silence fell upon the csowd on the plat- form.
Two gentlemen came forward hastily. One was one of the officials of the road, a Mr. Dean, and the other the gentleman who had cent him the telegram to come on.
They both looked with great compassion at the handsome, haggard young husband. "You are Mr. Chester, I believe," said one of the gentlemen, advancing and touching him on the arm.
" Yes, yes," cried Rutledge, hoarsely. "How is she—my wife l Let me see her at once." "Not this moment, you must wait a little," was the reply. "It was a terrible accident, re- member."

"If I wait I shall die," said Rutledge Chester, with forced calmness, more terrible to bear than the wildest outbreak of grief. "Tell me at least how she is." The two gentlemen looked at each other, neither daring to speak. "For Heaven sake, take. me to her "he cried. "I have borne all I can bear—take me to her, I cannot bear another moment of this suspense." He saw the look they exchanged, and a terrible terror seized him. "You see suspense is driving me mad I" he groaned. "Is she alive—or—dead?" -
" You will need all your courage, air," said the official, pityingly—" all the bravery that a man can show. You must not fail. There are many here whose sorrow is equal to yours." _
" I will not fail," slid Rutledge Chester. "Tell me the worst, and in Heaven's name I will bear it. Tell me the worst; is my darling living—or dead?"

"It is the worst, sir," replied the official. "You mean—" he gasped. Then he stopped abruptly. "1 mean," said the official, pityingly, "that your young wife is dead I Remember, Heaven gives and Heaven takes away," he added, solemnly. "Dead I" he muttered—" dead l" and he looked at the gentlemen with dazed, despairing eyes. Then with a violent effort he controlled himself, and asked to be taken to her. They went with him to the long, narrow wait- ing-room where the dead lay side by side, their faces reverently covered from the garish morning light. He passed them in awed silence. When they brought him lo the spot where the slender figure lay, covered by the long silk cloak, a low moan broke from his lips. He had recog- nised the cloak—one he had purchased for her himself not long before.

"Let me see her face!" he cried. "Oh, my beautiful Uldene ! my lost love, my beautiful young wife!" They drew back his outstretched hand with gentle force. "You have loved her too well to look upon the havoc death has made," they whispered. " The beantiful face—ah, how shall I find words to say it ?—is beyond all recogni,iun. We recognised, or identified her, rather, by the satchel she still clasps in her death-cold hand. The address was inside. Do not attempt to lift the handkerchief we have placed over the mutilated face; the, horror of the sight you would see would drive yon mad." In grief pitiful to behold, Rutledge Chester knelt down by the body which he believed was hat of Indent), his youn., wife, and what he suffered only Heaven knew. But the fiercest storm must wear away, the most violent grief must, in time, sob itself out. We must part from those we love better than life itself, and bear it. But grief could not bring life back to that still form, breath to those ice cold lips' and warmth to the cold, white hands, so like the frozen petals of to, lily. He leturned home on the next train, bearing with him what he supposed were the remains of his darling, lost Uldette, and a few days later their were placed in the marble vault of the Uheatere, and on the cold, white tablet were the ohlialodi worda
SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF ULDENE, Beloved wife of RUTLEDGE _CHESTER.
Aged 17 Years and 11 Months. Rest in Peace. (To be continued.)

div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

There is a good deal of uncertainty as to what form the tactics of the Government will ultimately take with regard towards accelerating the progress of the Parish Councils Bill. It is not by any means decided as yet that the guillotine will be applied— although undoubtedly there is a strong movement of opinion in that direction,and,for my part,l think it the wisest of all possible policies. We have to let the labourer feel the difficulties we had to con- front in order to give him self-government, and he will understand that beat when he sees that in or- der to get the Bill through we had to throttle its Jimmies.

But, unfortunately, opinion is somewhat divided on the question among Liberals themselves. In the influential and resolute little party below the gang- way, led by Mr. Labouchere and Sir Charles Dilke, there is a strong feeling against the guillotine— not from any objection to the accelerated methods of doing busine,s, but because it is regarded as a precedent, dangerous in case a strong Tory Govern- ment should be returned to office. It is said that there is also some difference of opinion on the Trea- sury Bench. Mr. Fowler is believed to favour pro- ceeding a certain length with the Bill, and then Carrying it over; but both Mr. Gladstone and Sir William Harcourt are deeply pledged against such a method of procedure.

I regret to state that the condition of the Speaker shows a greater amount of physical prostration than has been generally known. lie is unable to leave his bed, and requires the most careful and constant nursing. There has been some idea of re- moving him from London in the course of the pre- sent week. But he has suffered so much from weakness that probably this will be impossible. The strain upon Mr. Mellor has so far produced no bad results. If his health were to break down the busi- ness of the House would most certainly have.to be inapended.

As I was driving along Whitehall from my office Un Saturday evening, I suddenly caught sight of a sight open victoria passing rapidly and unobserved lii the deepening darkness. In it, in spite of the mpid pace, I recognised the figure of the G.0.M., sitting alone, and erect, and passing thus through the darkness, there was something strangely im- pressive in his appearance, and in the sense that the foremost man of the Empire was thus sweeping Unnoticed past all those teeming crowds. It may have been imagination, but it seemed to me that the face looked unusually pale and singularly stern. Alone, absorbed, separated in the reverie of his lonely.soul from all those multitudes, the Old Man Seemed to reveal more of his inner self than if he had his faithful companion by his side, or some- body to bring by conversation all that strange 11451 varied play of feature which conversation brings out. I thought I could see in the set Mid stern look a momentary revelation of that iron Will and exhaustless purpose, which has so often Moved mountains of buttressed wrong and hoary tyranny.

The nervous anxiety as to the future policy of the Povernment when is being displayed by the Tories Is rather significant. Mr. St. John Broderick proves to hi 8 own satisfaction in Monday's " Times " that Mr. Gladstone is preparing fora speedy dissolution; but the wise politicians who control Printing House- square politics devote a column and a half to set- forth their opinion that the exact contrary is the ape.

Putting aside the incidental characteristics of the Times" article—its indecent reference to Mr. Gladstone's age in an insinuation that he will cling °lnce solely because he has entered his eighty- afth year. its amusing denunciations of the Govern- ent for the " shabby trick " of giving Tory squires a little of the trouble they richly earned during the Session, and its sneers at the Irish mem- bers who covered the "Times " with a disgrace that can only be wiped out with its own existence —there is food for thought in the fact that our bitter enemies are so anxious. They are beginning tO realise the mischief done by their friends, the lords. Mr. Gladstone will see that the voters realise it Ids° before an appeal to the country will be made.

There are some good stories in two big volumes Of the " Life and Letters of Dean Stanley," which taa just been published by Mr. John Murray. The meap, though a Liberal, was opposed to the dises- tablishment of the Irish Church ; but his appear- ance on plattosms devoted to the defence of the Church was generally the signal for an outburst of execration. Once at St. James's Hall the audience allowed themselves so disinclined to hear him that the promoters of the meeting requested him to retire. However, he held his ground until he had Managed to say t bat all Liberal statesmen up to that date had favoured concurrent endowment. Having said so much, the Dean was advised by the Arch- blehoo of York to sit down, as he had said all be could say of importance on the question. "It was Perfectly true," said the Liberal clergyman," and I did so..

"Re is a traitor! " "He is a Liberal ! "were !Tarte ,of the cries levelled at. the distinguished divine by his opponents at St. James's Hall. As reurastances proved, the Dean's policy in 1868-9 Mistaken. When the Irish Church was dis- established , society did not go to pieces in Ireland, or did the defenders of the Church shoiilder rifles :Lkick Her Majesty's Crown into a certain famous a"eri as they seriously threatened to do. They 2ted far more sensibly. They set themselves to ‘.:..te task of reconstructing their Church system,and eY did so with wonderful success. People have ?ever fully realised how close is the analogy be- Lween the positions of those who fought against Giadstonws great measure in 1869 and the con- ct of the Uniooists of the present day.

div.head: SOCIAL, POLITICAL AND LLTERARY NOTES.
div.p: SOCIAL, POLITICAL AND LLTERARY NOTES.

In one of the London journals there has again been raised the oft repeated question: Is Christian- ity played out? But for the assurance that it is asked sincerely, We might feel inclined to ignore it altogether, and leave everybody to answer it for themselves, but it is supported by such a searching examination of what to-day passes for Christianity, that it is rendered difficult to restrain ourselves from interposing an expression of opinion on a very important matter. To begin with, it is impossible for Christianity to be played out, inasmuch as it has not been accorded a fair trial. To many it has been no different than any other Erystera which has been affected by changing governments and successive lungs and queens, and it has generally been judged according to the expressed religious conviction of the reigning ' sovereign. To-day there are people mad enough to sup- pose that if the church was disestablished Christianity I would instantly lose its power and crumble in the dust, 1 and so convinced are they of this purely imaginary idea that their only thought is of the safety of the church. I Beplorable fact that we should find such notions so gen- erally accepted, and Christianity it is certain has lost largely by their adoption. To be rightly understood we must preclude the idea of Christianity being either a system or institution, in any sense. It is not the exclu- sive possession or any particular denomination I It is not embodied either in heterodox or orthodox theology, and it makes no earthly difference or heavenly either, for the matter of that, whether you believe in the doc- trines of any sect, so long as we obey the voice of God, which speaks to us in our own souls. Are we only just beginning to realise that Christianity is a life ? If it has been fairly tried and we are socially and spiritually in our present sad plight after the trial, then we unhesitat- ingly pronounce Christianity to have been a dismal fail- ure. If church connections have a regenerating power then the great majority are in the way of salvation, hut, alas, we have been deceiving ourselves, and thought we could hoodwink the Almighty. Man ! you cannot play a double part in this great question,and though you may act deceitfully in the ordinary business of life with satis- faction to yourself, attendance at church and pious I recognition of its services will not explain away any defects in the life. We have paid our pew rent, and though it would be unchristian not to do so, we are not Christians because we do so. Our names on charitable subscription lists is not a guarantee of oui adoption of Christianity. Money may be a power but it cannot pur- chase this for us, much to the great regret, I doubt not, of many poor self-deceived souls.

' The fact is, as Mr. LeGallienno points out in his " Re- ligion of a Literary man," that if we want to know what Christianity, is, we must go to its founder as the only true authority. By this method alone may we dis- sect the real from the pretentious, and see the true light which will undoubtedly prove to be the light of the worldC Its sincere acceptance will not allow the exist- ence of poverty and distress, of suffering and woe, of sweating and extortion, of Insanitary dwellings, and of the great social differences of to-day. When we rightly conceive the nature of Christianity, we may then en- deavour to attain the ideal it presents, but until then we are beating in the air, and it is perfectly useless to keep on reiterating the question : Is Christianity a failare 2 without our having first tried it.

We are now well used to hearing systems advocated and philos)phies explained, which are put forth as in- fallible remedies of our great social evils, and Socialism is certainly not one ot 6the latest. Mr. T. A. Picton, M.P., does not, however, share the idea that its recog- nition will be productive of the benefits which Socialists claim for their pet scheme, and in which they so in- nocently believe. In a remarkably able address on the sublect he emphasised the opinion that the individual must be personally dealt pith, before any change can be effected in the community. He regards it as a kind of personal slavery ; and there will certainly have to be more elaborate arguments in its favour than those hitherto advanced, or the chances of its adoption will continue extremely remote. The senseless pamphlets which are courted about by your rank Socialist is a sad confession of intellectual weakness, and hew any man can lead himself into accepting statements which bear upon their surface an indifference •to established prin- ciples of political economy it is difficult to compre- hend.

The debate on the Navy on Tuesday last ended in a victory for the Government by a majority of 36. If no other object was gained, it is satisfactory to note that there is a general agreement in the House, as to main- taining our Naval supremacy. Lord George Hamilton. as Mr. Gladstone remarked,may not have been well advised in speaking sarcastically of the legislative work of the present session in moving this motion. It detracted somewhat from the effect of his speech, and brought upon him the reproof of the Grand Old Man. As the amendment to the motion stated, the Government re- cognise that it is necessary to make adequate provision for the naval defence of the empire,and protection of its interests, and:this they will endeavour to carry out. It is obvious to every true-hearted Englishman that weak- noes in our navy must be avoided, it we are to maintain our trade and commerce, and to retain our position at the head rf the nations. Any honest attempt in this direction on the part of governments of every colon% will be supported by the loyal inhabitants of Gres. Britain.

-- The Autobiography of Mrs. Annie Besant,at present an apostle of Theosophy, has just been published by T. Fisher Unwin and has on the whole received a recogni- tion from the 'Press. It was an utter impossibility in re- viewing a book of this character, to avoid noticing the frequent changes in Mrs_ Besant's spiritual career, and this has perhaps been called attention to, more than any other particular incident in her life. There may be very little incident to relate which is not in some way or other identified with her conflicts on spiritual matters. From the orthodox religion to atticism from atticism to Social- ism, and from Socialism to Theosophy, indicate the more important changes in an eventful career, and one that has been full of hard fighting and continuous struggles. If in her latest change she fiv.ds or realises the ambition of her life, then she may rest content, but her wander- ings have been so frequent, that it is hard to believe that she will remain long in her new home. Anyhow we must wait and see. talk.

div.head: CHRISTMAS ODE.
div.p: A CHRISTMAS ODE.

Backward, through the ages hoary, Scan we now the Sacred morn, When the Lord of life and glory, In Ephratah's town was born. Men knew not the heavenly Stranger. With no pageant marked His way : Rude and cheerless was the manger Where the Kingly Infant lay. To the poor and needy only Was the Son beloved sent: And His days, and nights so lonely Were in works of mercy spent. If, by cords of love all tender, Unto Him men's hearts are bound, Fitting service they will render, 4 In His lowly path be found. Surely not in pagan fashion Will disciples keep His birth : Could they shame His cross and passion With the revellings of earth ! Nor in temples deck'd with holly Will they with the thoughtless bow ; All displays of pomp and folly , Mock " The Man of svrows " now. Where the poor in want are sighing, Low in hovels dark and dim ; There, beside the famisli'd, dying„ Should their alms be seen of Him. From the highway, and the city, Where the naked outcasts roam ; Sharing in their Master's pity, They should bring the wand'rers home. Deeds like these to Him are precious, True devotion surely prove; And the Lord himself most gracious, Meets them with benignest love. Earth without thee, Lord, is dreary, Full of sorrow, toil, and pain; • And thy watchers, few and weary, Scan the Orient again. Men are groaning for salvation, • Looking unto Thee alone : Great Desire of every nation, Come, 0 come, and take thy throne. Then shall Life's eternal river • Every trace of sin destroy : And Thy presence, Lord, for ever, Fill the ransom'd world with joy. JAS. H. W. CLINDINNING. AN UNNATURAL SON.

div.p: HE VI; AMMER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1893.

WARRINGTON SAVINGS BANK. ANNUAL MEETING. The 76th annual meeting of the trustees and managers of the Warrington Savings Bank was held at the Bank, • But termarket-street, on Tuesday morning, Major Pickmere in the Chair. There were also present—the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) ; the Revs. F. W. Willis (rector), and Join Yorige ; Aldermen Francomb. Harrison, Blackh unit, and Holmes ; Councillors LI. Roberts, and F. W. Monks ; and Messrs. Joseph Davies, Robert Davies, John Ged4es, George Dakin, John Peers, J. H. Flem- ing, William Derbyshire, F. Monks, T. B. Carter. John Harrison, T. Whittle, J. Rymer Young, and J. E. Davies (actuary). Tho Actuary read the general statement of accounts for the year ended 20th November, 1893, as well as the auditor's report, a printed copy being supplied to each ' gentleman present. The Chairman moved "That the statement of accounts prepared by the actuary, and examined by the auditor, is approved, and copies are directed to be transmitted to the National Debt Commissioners, and to the Committee of Inspection, and that he duplicate statement be pub- licly affixed in the Savings Bank."—Alderman Harrison seconded the adopticn of the report, which was adopted. The Committee of Management presented the follow- ing report which was adopted :—" The Committee of Management in preseni ing the general statement of the Bank for the year ending 20th November, 1893. have to report that the total funds a mount to £296,409 9s. 3d.,as under : With the National Debt Commissioners--en gen- eral account, £293,448 7s. 41., on separate surplus fund account, carrying interest £1,400; on separate surplus fund account, not cam, ins., interest, £7OO ; £295.548 7s. 41. With Joseph Charlton Parr, treasurer, £B6l Is. 11d. ; total, £296,409 9s. 3d. Tne total amount due to depositors is £293,262 Os. 7d. ; leaving a surplus of £3,147 Bs. Bd. It is plainly seen and vouched that the Government have to our credit a much larger amount than would pay the amount due to our depositors, and beyond the above stated surplus of £3,147 Bs. Bd., there is the value of the bank premises and office furniture, &c., which for the purpose of com- pleting the statements of assets and liabilities are put at the low estimate of £1,300, increasing the surplus to £4,447 Bs. Bd. The Government also hold on account of depositors in this Bank £10,885 2/ per cent. consolidated stock. Although the past year nas been an exception- ally bad one for everybody, and must have been no easy matter for anyone to save during such hard times, it is gratifying to us to state that the total amount due to depositors has only been reduced during the year £526 103 s. id., and the number of accounts has increased 59, the total number of depositors now being 10,793. The inspector appointed by the Government Inspection Committee has attended at the Bank during the year, and that committee's report to us of his inspection is satisfactory in every way, and we are able to state that the Bask is properly worked under the provisions of the Act of Parliament. By the Act of 1891, depesitors are now allowed to re-deposit any sum previously with- drawn in the same year beyond the £3O deposit limit, and may also deposit in the whole up to £2OO. The extracted list of depositors' balanses certified by the auditor is placed on the Bank counter during the hours of business, and any depositor may personally satisfy himself that the same amount as is in his pass book is certified to the Government as being to his credit. A copy of the Government certificate is printed with this report, and the original may be seen at the Bank by any depositor desiring to see it. The committee are pleased to present so favourable a report, and hope that the Bank will continue to be useful to the large number of provident people who are now depositors, and that others may be prevailed upon to join the Bank and make a beginning to save and so prepare for times of need. For the Committee of Management, Jour; R. PICEMERE, chairman, WILLIAM LONG. vice-chairman. December sth, 1893." Councillor F. W. MONKS proposed, "That the report of the Committee of Management is approved, and that this meeting acknowledges the valuable services rendered to the institution by the gentlemen acting on the com- mittee during the past year, and tenders its best thanks ,to them." He thought they would feel satisfied, as he did, that the very best had been done for the institution , that was possible. (Hear, hear.) It was matter for I congratulation that the funds of the Bank had not been I drawn upon to a greater extent than £5OO considering the great distress that was prevalent in the town. He thought they might offer facilities for penny banks in connection with Sunday and day schools. He was con- nected with one penny bank in the town, and he should be quite willing to do what he could to assist in the matter. (Hear, hear.) Mr. T. B. CARTER seconded the resolution, which was carried. MT. ROBERT DAVIES moved that Major Pickmere be re- elected cnairman arid Mr. W. Long vice-chairman of the Bank.—Mr. GEDDES seconded, arid the motion was agreed to.—The CHAIRMAN returned thanks, and said the committee took great interest in the business of the Bank. He considered that this was an institution which was second to none in England with regard to the manner in which its business was conducted. (Hear, hear and applause) On the motion of the HECTOR, seconded by Alderman Houle's, It was decided that the following managers be elected to join the trustees on the Committee of Manage- ment for the ensuing year, namely :—The Rev. John Yonge, and Messrs. William Derbyshire, J. 11. Pleming, William Owen, John Peers, Henry Roberts, Thomas Whittle, and J. R. Young. The list of trustees and managers was read. Some dis- cussion took place with reference to the list of managers. It was pointed out that some of the managers never at- tended the meetings connected with the Bank, and that some lived considerable distances from Warrington. A hope was expressed that the list would be amended, and it was ultimately decided that certain gentlemen be written to asking them to resign their positions. The following were added to the list of managers t—Messre. C. J. Holmes, Arthur Edelsten, William Tinsley, A. H. Crosfield, J. Crosfield, E. L. Fleming, Alfred Woods, and the Rev. W. H. Drummond. A vote of thanks having been accorded to Major Pick- mere and to Mr. Long the _feting ended.

SUICIDE OF AN EARLESTOWN TRADES- MAN. On Friday morning last, much excitement was occasioned in Earlestown, on the circumstances of a rumour that Mr. W. Hemmons, pork butcher, of Cross-lane, Earlestown, had committed suicide by poisoning himself. Inquiry showed that the rum- our was only too true. It appears Mr. Hemmons, who was well known in the town, had for some few months past been in rather low spirits, from some cause which has not transpired. Formerly he oc- cupied an old established pork butchers' shop, in Market-Bt., the busiest thoroughfare in the town, but for some reason he had to quit there, and was forced to take a new shop lately erected in Cross- lane, which is quite out of the way of the majority of the purchasers. Whtther this has had anything to do with the depression of spirits, we cannot say. On Thursday, he intended attending Warrington County Court, where he was plaintiff in one or two cases. He at ant t catch his train, but was unfortunate in miss- ing it, and he then drove over in his trap. When he reached the Court, he found the eases had been struck out, and he returned home under the impression that he had lost the cases altogether. During the day he pur- chases sixpenny-worth of laudanum from Mr. Peak's ' chemist, and soon after nine o'clock at night, he sent a , girl named Elizabeth Clarke,for another sixpenny-worth. It is said that when he returned from Warrington, he quarrelled with his wife, but this she denies. At any rate she left home and went to her sister's at Newton, and Mr. Hemmons followed. He reached home abait midnight, and about two o'clock in the morning,the ser- vant, Emma Vernon,found him lying unconscious at the bottom of the stairs. She sent for Dr. Patterson, who applied the usual remedies, and restored the deceased to consciousness, and left instructions with those in the house how to deal with him. About nine o'clock on Friday morning he was sent for again, and he found Hemmons again unconscious, and all efforts at restora- tion were fruitless, and he died about 11.30. It is a curious coincidence that the man who ozcupied the shop in Market-st., before Mr. Hemmons, was also a pork butcher, and he after leaving it, committed suicide by hanging himself.

div.head: – THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL.
div.p: - THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL.

-- At a mass meeting of railway men in connection with the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants held at West Hartlepool on Sunday, at which representatives were present from Newcastle, Gateshead, Tynemouth, &c., a resolution was unanimously passed condemning the action of the House of Lords in regard to the Em- ployers' Liability Bill, and expressing the opinion that the insertion of the contracting-out clause practically destroyed the most useful portion of the measure. The Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation has passed a resolution condemning the action of the depu- tation from the Miners' Permanent Relief Society which waited upon Lord Salisbury and expressed views in , favour of contracting out" of the Rrnpinyers' Liability Bill, and asking Lord Salisbury and Mr. Asquith to receive a deputation which would represent the actual views of the miners on the question.

The Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress on Tuesday night issued to the trades societies and trades councils a further circular against the " con- tracting out" clause which the Peers introduced into the Employers' Liability Bill. It points out that in most cases, if not in all, where insurance funds exist member- ship is insisted upon as a condition of employment, and that heuce the Lords' amendment would give the power to two-thirds of the workmen in any industry to compel the remaining third to contract themselves out of the Act or to leave the service ef their employer. The com- mittee add that under these circumstances they fail to discover any appreciable difference between tho course adopted by the House of Lords and that of trades unions compel:ing non-unionists to join their society.

, On Thursday night the Home Secretary (Mr. Asquith) received a deputation from the LAneashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation in support of the resistance of ,he Government to the proposed contracting-out clause of ' the Employers' Liability Bill. In reply he said that the House of Commons had already expressed its opinion of the Lords' amendments, and ho asked the question— does the bill, if carried into law with absolute prohibi- tion of contracting out, have the effect of putting an end to relief and accident funds ? He said emphatically that it did not. No misrepresentation could be more complete than to say that the bill prohibited the exist- ence of these funds. All it did was to say that it should not be in the power of the employer or workman by private arrangement to deprive the servant of his rights or the employer of his legal obligations. He had the greatest confidence that when the employers considered the question dispassionately they would, in their own interests of the workmen and in the performance of a social duty,continue to make contributions to the funds.

div.head: ACC RINGTON ELECTION.
div.p: THE ACC RINGTON ELECTION.

A LIBERAL VICTORY. The polling in the Accrington division election took' place on Thursday. The contest has been fought under conditions of unusual excitement, and a heavy vote was recorded. Thef result was declared at eleven o'clock as follows :—Mr. J. F. Leese, Q.C. (L), 5,822 ; Mr. Hermon-flodge (C), 5,564 •, majority for Mr. Lees,. 258. At the last election Mr. Leese's majority was 547. A section of the Independent Labour party, under advice from BOllle of their leaders, refrained trom voting and matters were further complicated by the fact that the register contained about 3,000 removals.

Si. MARY'S BAND or Ilors.—On Monday evening a goodly number of people assembled at the Infants'school- room, the monthly entertainment of the above society being the attraction. These meetings are very attrac- tive ones, and speak well for the energy of the officers, in sustaining the interest so well. The programme consisted of songs, recitations, by the junior members, and also by several adults, who kindly gave their assis- tance. Mr. W. Aitken occupied the chair, and Mrs. Aitken presided at the pianoforte. TEA Msermo.—On Monday evening the class under the leadership of Mrs. R. Cook and Mrs. Wigfield were entertained to tea by them. Thera were about 90 mem- bers present and a pleasant evening was spent by all. After tea a meeting was held and Mrs. Cook, Mrs. Gun- nell, and Mrs. Wigfield addressed the members. Several members testified to the good derived from the class. Mesdames Wigfield, Gunnell, Owen, and Snoddy pre- sided over the tea arrangements. SlClNESS.—lnfluenza has been rather prevalent in the neighbourhood for a short time past and many of the villagers have had a touch of it. The Rev. J. R. Jones, curate of St. Mary's,has been laid up with this complaint for some days,but we are pleased to hear of his improve- ment.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—On Wedßeßday night the weekly meeting of the shove association was held in the Wesleyan School, Mr. Wigfield in the chair. The subject for the evening was Mr. J. Peers' paper on " Rest." The paper was a very able one. At the close several members discussed the paper and questioned Mr. Peers. A lively discussion between Mr. Peers and Mrs. Garnett caused much amusement, other members join- ing in. A very pleasant evening was spent. INFANTS' CONCERT.—On Thurday evening a juvenile concert was held in the Infanta' school. Mr. J.B.Aitken was in the chair, and the room was crowded. The pro- ceedings opened with an allegory, entitled " The Fairy Ring,' the story being of some children while at play, finding a ring of evergreens which is charmed, and Walter Wagtail (Dan Matthews) enters the ring and is unable to come out. Minnie Maxwell (L. Acomb) also enters the ring to share his trouble, and the Fairy King Oberon (Jesse Pownell) and his Queen (M. Isherwood) with their attendant elves appear and set the children free. There were various other characters. The children I performed the various parts with great tact and with a degree of accuracy seldom attained at such concerts. The lovely dresses worn by the children added not a little to the brightness of the scene. A Japanese parasol song, with action, was also very well executed, and much ap- plauded. The performance of "Ten Little Nigger Boys" was very laughable, and received a hearty encore. Nursery Rhyme Quadrilles by the " Babies " were also skilfully performed, and with great accuracy, taking into consideration the size of the children. To procure such a state of perfection must have taken much hard work on the parts of Miss Byrnes and Miss Marion Fos- ter, but the success of the evening will doubtless re- compense them. The performance concluded with a "Good Night" song by the children. Mrs. Aitken ac- companied the songs on the pianaforte. Recitations, Ex., were also given.

SANKEY SCIZOOL BOARD.,—Tho monthly meeting of the above Board was held in the Board-room, Great Sankey, on Tuesday afternoon, Major Ridgway in the chair. The other members present were—The Rev. E. S. Jackson, Mr. Henry Bate, Mr. Joseph Wright, with Mr. Samuel Sutton (clerk), and Mr. George Clarke (head master).— The Clerk reported that there was a balance in the hands of the treasurer in favour of the Board of £240 ss. 7d. A letter from the Local Government Board was received informing the Board that an application had been made by Mrs. E. Skidmore, 5. Worrall's-row, Great Sankey, requiring tree public school accommodation for her two children, and inquiring whether they were pre- pared to provide free places in accordance with the Education Act, 1891—The Clerk said that he had asked Mr. Shearer to inquire into the case, and let him know the facts. He had done so, and had reported that he visited Mrs. Skidmore's house. He explained to her that she did not live in the district of Great Sankey, and con- sequently she had no claim upon the Board for free places for her children, but if she would apply to hint he had no doubt but the Guardians would pay the fees while her husband was out of work. With this both she and her husband seemed perfectly satisfied. The Chairman: I don't think we can do better than forward Mr. Shearer's report to the Education Department. The suggestion of the Chairman was agreed to.—The next meeting of the Board was fixed for the last Monday in January, at 2.30, at the Board Schools.—Mr. Clarkeeiire- sented the following return for the month :—December 2nd, on the books 291 ; present, 266 ; average, 2471 ; money received, 14s. Bd. December 9th, on books 291 ; present, 263 ; average, 240 6 ; money received, 13s. 10d. December 16th, on books 291 ; present, 267 ; -average, 2360 money received, 14s. 4d.—This was all the busi- ness PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT SANKEY BOARD SCHOOL.—On Monday the Rev. E. S. Jackson and the Chairman of th, Board (Major Ridgway) awarded the prizes offered to the elder girls of the Sankey Board Schools, by Mr. George Bolton, distributed the annual prizes for attendance and good conduct. Mrs. and Miss Ridgway and the Clerk to the Board were also present. The competition between the girls in the different tests was very cloae, and at last resulted in the prizes being awarded to the following children :—Minnie Hatton, £1; Agnes Wilkinson, £1 ; Edith Bingham, 1.03. ; May Davies, 10s. ; Ruth Matthews ss, ; May Woods, ss. Mrs. Ridgway now presented the books to the successful children as follows :—lnfants, J. Molyneux, H. Taylor, F. Woodward, T. Rigby, Sarah •Peever. Standard I. : A. Schofield, W. Whitfield, A. Gould, Hannah Wilkinson, Mary Harrison. Standard If. : J. Carrington, R. Rodgers, W. Hatton, J. Moss, W. Hewitt, Elizabeth Cooper, May Warburton, Stella load. Standard 111. V. Gould, F. Rigby, Elizabeth Hatton, Annie Corwell. Standard IV. : Elizabeth Cottrell, ali” Woods, Edith Bingham, Ivy Longshaw, Alice Carring- ton, Dinah Harrison. Standard V. : G. Hatton, H Rigby, T. Kirby, N. Griffiths, A. Woods, H. Bracegirdle, J Hall, Margaret Hayes. Standard VI. : J. Rcdeers, W. Whitfield, May Davies, Elizabeth Carrington. Standard VII. : F. Dumbell, Emily Matthews.—After two songs had been rendered, a hearty vote of thanks was given by the children, to Mrs. and Miss Ridgway,. and to the gentlemen of the Board, and the proceedings ter- minated. Pain DAY AT FRIENDS' SCHOOL.--OR Monday evening there was a large attendance of parents and friends of the children at the Friends' Schools, Penketh, to witnesi. the annual distributibn of prizes. Among these present were Alderman and Mrs. Holmes, Mr. W. Brett, Wand Mrs. A. Rathbone, Mrs. W. Pierpoint (Latchford), Mr S. W. Davies (Birkenhead), Mr. C. Jackson Holmes,Mrs.M. E. Davies, Mrs. W. Darbyshire,Miss Priestman, Mr. Geo. Clarke (Sankey), Mr. J. Peers, Mr. C. B. Aylward, Mr. and Mrs. Wm. Houghton, Mr. and Mrs. E. B. Harlock. Miss Garnett, Miss Moses, Mr. S. Sutton, and Mr. Chas. Sudlow. The staff of the school included Mr.A.Polla.d, superintendent ; Mrs. Pollard, Mr. G. F. Linney, Mr. Percy S. Reynalds, Mr. John E. Smith, Miss Willmott, and Miss Chapman. Letters of apology for inability to be present were received from Mr. W. D. Jeans and the they. 8.5.-Jackson. The room had been tastefully de- corated far the occasion by the teachers, and presented a bright and attractive appearance. Mr. A. Pollard occupied the chair. Alderman Holmes distributed the prizes to the scholars, whose names were as follow ; Charles Holland, Fred. Sargent, W. Charnock, J. VI Darhyshire, C. Sutton, Leigh Spencer, D. Hall, J. Wareing, G. Cooke, W. El. Johnston, Fred Lloyd, John Darbyshire, R. Andrew, H. Wharton, H. Rhodes, D Nixon, R. Davies, P. Pollitt, E. Sutton, S. Walmsley. R. Spencer, H. Ward, W. Holland, K. Longoroff, F. Walms lay, A. Darbvshire, G. Worth, J. Ashworth, F. Leicester, E. Curtis, I.; Youde,E.Handley,A.Adair, H. Darbsshire, M. Lowe, and J. Percival. An encoui aging re- port was afterwards read, and a most enjoyable. enter- tainment occupied the rest of the evening, in which the school choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Edward Moore, took a prominent part. The following was the programme :—Duet by F. Walmsley and Edith Curtis ; song "Round the World," by the choir ; recitation "Wil- low the King," F. J. Sargent; violin solo "The Fairy 13arque," H. Campbell ; recitation "The Echo and the Ferry," Grace Wentworth ; recitation "The Romance of a Friend's Bonnet," Amelia Darbyshire ; song by the choir ; violin duet by Mr. Woolman and Mr. Mbore ; an instrumental waltz "Queen of my Love," by the school orchestra. After an interval of tee minutes the amus- ing scene from the " Pickwick Papers" of the trial Barden v. Pickwick was cleverly performed by a party ,of boys, and brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: "STACKING" OF COAL
div.p: THE "STACKING" OF COAL

'The Lancashire and Cheshire Minors' Federation has considered the question of stacking coal, and has re- qu(sted that information of the quantity of coal in stor,k at each colliery shall be sent by the officials of the union ; to tho general secretary, so that the whole question, with the information gathered, may be considered at tho annual conference in Leicester in January. There are still about 1,000 members of the Federation in the twe counties who are unemployed.

div.head: JUVENILE TRAGEDIANS.
div.p: JUVENILE TRAGEDIANS.

STABBING A BOY. Two young lads where charged at Northwich,on Tues- day with stabbing a boy whom they had enticed into a " cave" which they had excavated. No Malice was shown, an the magistrates allowed the boys to escape an payment of the surgeon's fees. It was believed that :the youngsters desired to "reproduce" a drama which they had seen acted at Northwich, but they had, natur- ally much to learn with reference to the nse of the knife in the way of " make believe." It is to be hoped that their misfortunes will cure them of their passion for a profession which is already overcrowded with failures.

div.head: INIEUEST.
div.p: THE INIEUEST.

An inquest en the body of Mr. Hemmons was held at the Railway Hotel, Earlestown, on fuesday morning lor Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner. Louisa Hemmons was the first witness called, and she said the deceased William Hemmons, was her husband. He was a pork butcher and 34 yeats of age. On Decem- ber 14th, her husband went to Warrington to attend the County Court. He went out at 10.15 to catch the train, but missed it, and he afterwards went in the trap. He seemed rather excited. She saw him again between 12 and 1 'o'clock, and about 2.30 she went to lie down. Ile came upstairs and spoke to her about the business, and she told him not to trouble himself, and he turned round and said " Well, never mind, Louie." He did not seem very well, and had been low spirited all week. She had no quarrel whatever with him. She afterwards went to Newton to see her sister Mrs. Knox, About 1130 on Thursday night her husband came to Knox's at Newton, and went back again home, but she did not go, as she was too unwell. He did not ask her to go with him. It was about four o'clock in the morning when she left her sister's trmse to go home, word having been brought her that her husband had been taken ill, and Dr. Patterson had just been. She never left him a minute after that until he died. She knew nothing about any poison he was supposed to have taken. He died about 11.30 on Friday morning.—The Coroner Did not a small bottle fall out of his pocket, and the servant put it in the closet ?—They said so.—Do you mean to say you did not know that a bottle fell out of your husband's pocket ? She really did not see the bottle. Her husband had been low spirited for the last four months. His business had not been as prosperous during the. strike, as it otherwise would have been.—ln reply to Inspector Kelly, witness said she went to Newton on business for fur husband. It was note fact that they had a quarrel. She could prove that her husband did not strike her on the face. When she asked him the result of his cases at the Court, he said he was too late, and did not tell her anything further. They had not quarrelled and were most comfortable that day. Mr. A. Peake, chemist, said on the 14th inst. he sold isome laudanum to Mr. Hemmons, which he understood was for a sprain. About half the quantity he sold him would have been fatal to a man not used to taking it. He afterwards sold sixpennyworth more to a servant between 9 and 10 o'clock the same night. He did not ask what it was for. They brought him the same bottle, with the label on, as though it had been emptied in tho ordinary way.—ln reply to Inspector Kelly, he said he could not remember having supplied Mr. Hemmons with any poison before, although he had sold other things to the family generally. . . . _

EinmaVe'rnon,servant in the employ of Mrs.flemmons, stated that she remembered Mr.liemmons going away to Warrington. He went in the trap. So far as she knew, he had not quarrelled with his wife during the day. He told her in the presence of his wife, that he had lost his cases. Mr.flemmons was man excitable state on Thurs- day night, wandering about the kitchen. He told wit- ness to go to bed, and she left a little girl named Hilda, and a girl named Elizabeth Clarke up. She saw him give the latter some money, aud she afterwards heard him drinking in the back kitchen. Ho afterwards draok some compo for his cough. The little girl Hilda,who was about four years of age' cime to witness early on Friday morning, and said, "Emma, what have you put my daddie on the floor for, his legs are stiff IP The girl Clarke had gone home before this. When Hilda came to her she jumped out of bed and went to the stairs, and found Mr. Heminons lying on the floor at the bottom of the stairs, and he was unconscious. She called in Mrs. Pilling. It would then be about two o'clock. She found a bottle in his pocket, about ten o'clock in the morning, and she gave it to Mrs. Pilling. She did not know who washed the label off it. It was not a fact that she washed the bottle so that nobody should know. The girl Hilda sat up with her father.—ln reply to Inspector Kelly she said she saw a fiat bottle in deceased's pocket on Thursday morning before he went to the County Court. It was labelled " Laudanum."—The Coroner : Do you mean to say there was a laudanum bottle in his pocket before be went to the County Court ?—Yes. Mrs. Pilling got it out of his pocket. She was sure it was Thursday morning she noticed it, because he kept handling it in his pocket. She said, "Oh, Mrs. Pilling, Mr. Hemmons is up to something to-day, with that bottle in his pocket.' The Coroner here remarked that he might say to the jury that the police informed him that they had the greatest difficulty in getting any information from the widow or the servant. They were informed that the bottle was discovered in the afternoon by Mrs. Pilling, and that Mrs. Hemmons had seen it. Ann Pilling said she went at 9 o'clock on Thursday morning to work at Mr. Hemrnons. She was there until sor 6 o'clock, and went back about 6.30, and stayed 1 until 8 o'clock. She knew the servant found a bottle in his coat pocket. Witness took it, and hid it in the bread mug. She afterwards went to look for the bottle, but could not find it. She did not think that it was !audit- num,as she could not read. She never told anybody about finding it. Mr. Hemmons had seemed very strange that week, and walked about the kitchen, as he had not done before. Mr. Hemmons told her he had lest his case,and he did not dire to tell his wife. He was under the idea that because the cases had been dismissed, he had lost them for good.—lnspector Kelly : What about the rum bottle? I took it out of his pocket, when he was laid out. _

Dr. Patterson said he was called about 2 o'clock on Friday morning, and found diseased in an unconscious state, and two women were present. He did not know about the poiaen at first. When he had been there about a quarter of an hour, Mrs. Pilling told him something about laudanum. He left about 3.15. Deceased was not altogether unconscious. Witness left instructions as to what they should do. Ile was there again about 9 o'clock, and deceased was then unconscious. He tried electricity, and then sent for Dr. Mouncey's assistant, and they together did all they could to revive him. He did not know what they were doing with him between 3.30 and 9 o'clock. He told them to keep him awake If possille.—lnspector Kelly: Did you hear anything about a quarrul between Hemmons and his wife ? Mrs. Pilling told me they had had a row. . . .

Robert Knox deposed to Mrs. flemmons visiting his house, and said she was unwell, and could not return to Earlestown. Word came afterwards that her husband had been taken ill. Ile knew nothingof any quarrel that had taken place, but Mr. Ilemmons had been very strange all week, and for two or three weeks previously. He did not attach any importance to that until the climax came. Witness went to Etrlestown, and when he got there, Dr. Patterson had been. He was shown a bottle, by the servant, labelled poison, and he threw it down the closet. Ile did rwt know whether it had a laudanum label on it or not. Ile had an idea that the deceased had committed suicide, and he wanted to des- troy the trace of it. The coroner said if some of the other witnesses had adopted the same frank course, as this one, it would have shortened the inquiry. After a short consultttion, the jury returned a veroict of " Suicide, whilst labour- ing under temporary insanity.

div.head: MYSTERY OF THE NORTH SEA.
div.p: A MYSTERY OF THE NORTH SEA.

A SELF-CONDEMNED VILLIAN. Henry Rumbald, the " skipper "of a fishing boat, was hanged at Lincoln on Tuesday for the murder of a woman. The rude bravado which the prisoner displayed at his trial disappeared after his conviction under the beneficent influence of the Bishop of Lincoln and another clergyman, and a few days ago, after exhibiting sym- ptoms of mental distress, he maele, it is said, a confes- sion of anther and unsuspected crime which he had committed—namely, the wilful running down of a fish- ing boat and her crew in the Nwth Sea. The confession will, it is said, prove to be of a starting nature.
