div.p: DEATH OF MR. T. C. EDWARDS-MOSS.

We announce with regret the death of Mr. Tom Cottingham Edwards-Moss, second son of the late Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss. The deceased recently took to bed will. an attack of typhoid fever, to which he succumbed in London at the early age of thirty-eight. He was well-known in this district, not only from the close connection of his family with it, but also from his having been the first Par- liamentary representative of the Widnes Division after the redistribution of seats. At the elect ion he defeated Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the Liberal candidate, and at the general election in the following year he also defeated Mr. Augustine Burrell, now Liberal member for the Western Division of Fifeshire. Prior to the general I election last year he announced his intention of retiring from Parliamentary life, owing to ill-health, and conse- quentiv he did not seek re-election, his successor in the 'representation of Widnes Division being Mr. J. S. CHIBA. When a student at Oxford, he was renowned tor his skill as an athlete, and in the University boat race between Oxford and Cambridge he pulled the stroke oar in the boat of the former on two occasions when the Dark Blues won. He was well-known is the North of Scotland, along with his brothers and his late father, where he spent some time, and where he was noted for his love of field sports. All oarsmen—especially Oxford oarsmen— will receive the news of the mournful death of Mr. Moss with a sense of personal loss. Affectionately known as " Cottie" Moss by his friends, he was one of the most brilliant oarsmen and scullers whom Eton and Oxford have ever produced, and the list of his triumphs and suc- cesses is a Ion.; one. He rowed against Cambridge in four successive years. being in the winning boat in 1875 and 1878, and in the losing one in 1876—when he rowed stroke on the bow side—and taking part in the cele- brated dead heat of March 24, 1887. Since these dates he has frequently been the coach of Oxford crews, being universally recognized as one of the best Mentors who have ever helped the Dark Blues to victery. He was equally successful in Brasenose Crlllee eights and fours, while in the Henley Regattas of 1877 and 1878 he won the Diamond Sculls twice, and the Silver Goblets, with W. A. Ellison once. As a memorial of his presidency on the Isis he gave to the Oxford University Boat Club some years ago a handsome silver tankard, which is annually held be the leading boat in the torpid races; and there is assuredly no one of her athletic sons whose loss Alma Hater will more sincerely and regretfully deplore.

TUE FUNERAL. The funeral took place on Tuesday morning. The body of the deceased arrived from the Metropolis by an early train and was conveyed from Otterspool station to St. Anne's Church, Aigburth, and was interred in a family vault. The service was performed by the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, vicar of Roby. The chief mourners present were Sir John Edwards-Moss (brother), Lady Zdwards-Moss, Miss Ethel Edwards-Moss (sister), Mrs. IMackenzie (sister), Mr. Tom Edwards-Moss (nephew), Mr. Gilbert Winter Moss (uncle), and Miss Davidson. Among others present at the interment were the Rev. Canon Diggle, the Rev. Dr. Oliver,Mr. J. H. Stock,M.P., his Honour Judge Shand, Colonel R. Ireland Bla.ckburne and Mrs. Ireland Blackburne, Mr. A. Mackenzie Smith (chairman of the Widnes Division Conservative Associa- tion), Mr. R. Madge (secretary), Alderman Alex. Gar- nett, and Messrs. Charles Langton, H. B. Gilmour, S. Sandbach Parker, Walter Gladstone, R. F. Gladstone, Alfred Fletcher, Danson Cunningham, Gordon Hough- ton, James Wood, E. W. Turner, W. T. Husband, G. fl. Pilkington, W. L. Pilkington, A. Gordon Brown, G. H. Dagleisb, R. B. Neilson H. C. Neilson, A. T. Neilson, R. W. Jones, j. Maddox, A. T. Parker, J. E. Tinue, G. Bradbury, N. T. Christopherson, R. Mackee' J. Brandwood, B. Storer, Joseph Matthews. and W. K. Hill. Closed carriages were sent by Mrs. Earl, Mrs. Edward Banner, Mr. Stanley Rogerson, Mr. Alfred Fletcher, and Mrs. Langton. The coffin which was of elm with silver mountings, was supplied by Messrs. Woolright and Co., undertakers, Bold-street, , Liverpool, bore the following inscription engraved on al silver plate :—" Tom Cottingham Edwards-Moss, born 7th April, 1855 ; died 16th December, 1893." Upon and about the coffin were placed a profusion of beautifui wreaths, sent by, among others,Sir John Edwards-Moss, Mrs. Mackenzie, Lady Maud Ramsden, Sir William and Lady Clarke, Canon and Mrs. Livingstone (cousins),Mrs. , Diggle (cousin), Sir Savile Crossley. Captain Beale Col- yin, Sir Charles and Lady Forbes, Mr. and Mrs. Gilbert Winter Moss, Miss G. E. Moss, Mr. Edward Tennyson d'Eyncourt, Miss Maxwell, Miss A. HIS WIFE. A PAINFUL CASE. Before Messrs. John Birchall, and M. M. Tate, presiding justices at the County Magistrates' Court on Wednesday, Peter J. King, of St. 'Wens, presi- dent of the Copper and Chemical Workers' Union, was summoned at the instance Of the West Derby Guardians to show cause why he should not pay for the maintenance of his wife, who was charge- able to the Union. —Mr. Arnold Cleaver, who ap- peared for the Guardians, said the summons alleged that £74 10s. was due from defendant, but he only asked for an order for 325., which represented eight weeks' pay- ment at 4s. from the date the magistrates' order was served on defendant on the 30th October.—Mr. Madden (instructed by Mr. G. J. Lygskey) appeared for the de- fendant. and at the outset took several technical objec- tions. He said this was an application for the mainten- ance of a lunatic wife, and the Legislature had provided under a special Act a proper method of procedure by which money can be recovered, or arrears for the main- tenance of a lunatic wife. The present proceedings had been taken under the Poor Law Amendment Act, 31 and 32 Victoria, chap. 122, section 33, which dealt with the maintenanoe of a wife who had been deserted by her husband. The summons, having been taken out under a wrong Act, was wrong,. The order itself was wrong, having been made under the Poor Law Amendment Act, although at the time the order was made the magistrates knew that Kitherine King was a lunatic in Prestwich Asylum--Mr. Eaton (magistrates clerk) : I shall advise the magistrates that they can amend or vary the order.—Mr. Madden then objected that the summons should have been taken out under the Lunacy Act, and not under the Poor Law Amendment Act. He also argued that the pro- ceedings were not in accordance with the Summary Jurisdiction Act, because there should have been a demand for the money served with the summons Mr. Eaton said that Mr. Cleaver simply asked for a dis- tress warrant, and not that the defendant should be sent to gaol.—Mr. Madden said that defendant would not pay a fraction if he could help it. Ills case was that he had chargeable to him a lunatic wife who had been guilty of adultery.—Mr. Cleaver (warmly) : I object Dr. corn- mine, who previously appeared for defendant, aban- doned that very charge.—Mr. Eaton : The magistrates are bound to act on the order.—Mr. Hudson, general re- lieving officer to the %Vest Derby Union. said that no money had been paid on the order since the 6:.h October last, but money had been paid previously—By Mr. Madden : Witness did not know that Mr. King had never paid anything towards his wife's support, nor did ' he know that the woman's father had paid the money. in question. He knew that Mr. King had repudiated the payment of a fraction. The order was lost in 1889. and although proceedings were afterwards taken the magis- trates dismissed the case because the order could not be , produced. The order was found last July in one of the drawers of the late relieving officer at the relief station in Kirkdale.—Mr. Madden said that the order should have been enforced each six months, but years had been allowed to lapse, and therefore the Guardians had no right to ask tor a distress warrant. The matter which affected thiscase he (Mr. Madden) had no right to deal with in that court, but that matter was the only reason why Mr. King refused to pay for the maintenance of his wife. The magistrates would know that from Mr. King's public character—he had distributed thousands , of pounds amongst the poor during the recent distress— that there must be some good reas,sn why Mr: King re- fused to pay for the maintenance of his wife.—The magistrates overruled Mr. aladden's objections,and made an order for the payment of the 321. demanded, and in , default distress to be levied.—Upon the applicatioil. of Mr. Madden, the magistrates stated a case for the High Court.

A MUSICAL SERVICE. In connection with the P.S.A. society in Wycliffe Church, the quarterly open service was held on Sunday afternoon. The servioe was a musical one, and consisted of selections from " The Messiah" rendered by an augmented choir, and an instrumental band under the conductorship of Mr. R. 11. Pearson. The church was filled in every part, chairs having to be placed in the aisles. The following were the instrumentalists :-Ist violins: Mr. J. Roberts, Mr. A. Knowles ; 2nd violins: Mr. R. Foster. Mr. W. Brown ; 'cello; Mr. H. Bond; bassi ; Mr. R. Whitfield, Mr Charnock ; organist: Mr. W. H. Payton. The soloists were Mrs. R. H. Pearsen, Mica N. Roberts. Miss Payton ; Messrs. A. Griffiths, W. H. Wallingten,and A. Scattergood. The whole of the selections were ex- ceedingly well rendered, and the audience frequently evinced their appreciation by applause. The chair was taken by the Rev. J. Yonge, who, is a brief welcome ad- dress referred to the success of the P.S.A. movement, • " and said he felt perfectly confident that the movement would be a permanent one. He hoped to hear of other P.S.A. societies being formed in the town, taken up by the different churches. A collection was taken at the close, in aid of the fonds of the society.—At the usual evening service the Rev. J• Yong° preached a special sermon to a large congregation on the subject of the " Hallelujah Chorus," its meaning, and its message.

div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

MONDAY. In the House of Commons on Monday evening the DEPUTY Speaker read a letter from the Presid€ nt of the French Chamber of Deputies in acknowledg.nent of the message of sympathy adopted last week by the House of , Comtnons.

_ Sir E. Gear, replying to a question. said the latest information received from the British senior naval officer at Rio de Janeird was to the effect that the Custom-house was closed and trade at a standstill.

The Indian Loan Bill, after a debate is which Mr. Courtney, Mr. Chaplin, ir W. Harcourt, Mr. Goschen, and others took part, was read a third time. Tho House again went into Committee on the Local Government (Parish Councils) Bill.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening Lord GEOROZ HAMILTON moved :—" That, in the opinion of this House, it is necessary, for the maintenance of the security of the country, and the continued protection of British interests and commerce, that a considerable ad- dition should at once he made to the navy ; this House. I therefore calls Ipon Her Majesty's Government to make before the Chris, au&S recess a statement of theirinten- tions, in order that immediate action may be taken thereon." The noble Lord went at length into the sub- ject of the shipbuilding programme of this country and of France and Russia, and argued that our operations were not cointnensurate with the progress of the other Powers. Mr. Gladstone moved as an amendment That, in she opinion of this House, it is a primary duty of the responsible Ministers of the Crown, to make adequate provision for the naval defence of the Empire and the protection of its interests, and this House relies on Her Majesty's adv.sers to submit to Parliament fit- ting proposals in duo time and measure to secure that end." The right hon. gentleman said Lord George 1 Hamilton's motion was a vote of want of confidence in Her MAjesty's Government, and after ridiculing this attempt, made for party purposes, to" break up the whole of our system of estimates," proceeded to show that the conclusions arrived at by his Lordship were fallacious, remarking amongst other things, that our means of construction were overwhelming compared with those of foreign countries. The motion brought the great question of Imperial defence within the com- mon lines of party action and thereby degraded that question from the elevation on which it stood. Be denied that there was any pretext for maintaining that we were in a state of present emergency and danger, And declared that in regard to our ships we were " be- fore the strength of any two countries." Mr. Balfour said the Prime Minister had shown his incapacity to un- derstand either his opponents or tke real gravity of the case. Sir C. Dilke contended that our superiority over Frauce and Russia combined should be in the proportion of live to three. Mr. Forwood, Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth, Mr. Chamberlain, and Sir W. Harcourt also took part in the debate. The motion was defeated by 240 to 204— majority for the Government, 36.

In the House of Lords, the standing orders having been suspended, the East India Loan Bill was passAl through all its stages. Earl SPENCER informed Lord Sidmeuth that the Govern. ment were fully alive to the imp. dance of GitTal ar, and that the question of constructing a (lock there was still under e-msideration by the Admiralty. The Marquis of SALISBURY Urged that this work should be pressed lorward. It was, io saii, iccessary to have Gibraltar in a safe position, especially now that " a moral junction had taken place between the fleets ef Cronstadt and Toulon."

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

The House of Commons considered on Wednesday the Lord's amendments to the Employers' Liability Bill. Mr. ASQUITH moved that the House should disagree with the amendment enabling workmen to contract out of the Act if an assurance fund had been established by the employers and the employed (the former contributi og not less than one-fourth), and if the workmen by a vote of two-thirds in a secret ballot still decided in favour of this contracting out. the right hon. gentleman said the Government would regard the adoption of this Arnenclinrnt NS fdtil to the bill. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN sup- ported the Lords' amendment. Mr. W. M'Lancx opposed it as not being es.kential in regard to future societies,and meationed as a fact which had largely influenced him in the present discussion the 'alleged harsh treatment of a servant of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany at Crewe on account of his opposition to the In- surance system. On a division the Lord's amendment on contracting out was rejected by 213 to 151. A minor amendment by the Lords was under discussion when the time for adjournment arrived.

THURSDAY In the House of Commons on Thursday evening, Mr. GLADSTONE, answering Mr. A. Morton. said every reason:- able facility was bairn given to private persons who were ready to undertake the reclamation of slob lands, but so far as the Government knew there WES no great disposition to embark capital in such enterprises, and he should be very much gratified indeed if there were more. The right hon. gentleman announced that an arrange- ment had been come to by which the Duke of Edinburgh was to surrender the annuity of £15.000 a year con- ferred upon him by Parliament in 1868, but to retain the £lO,OOO a year voted in 1873 on the occasion of his marriage. In view of the Duke's intention to spend a portion of each year in this country, Her Maj-sty's Government thought that this was a just and equitable arrangement. Ills Royal Highness had aiked that his name might be omitted from Lier Majesty's Privy Council. Mr. LABOUCHERE asked for leave to move the adjournment oi the House in order to discuss the proposed continuance of the £lO,OOO annuity, but on a division leave was refused by 177 to 59. Mr. BAIITLKY called attention to & speech in which Mr. KNOX (member for West Cavan), had referred to the allotmest of Smth African Chartered Company's shares in terms which he contended, reflected on members of the House. and moved that the speech was a breack ea privilege. Mr. KNOX, who disputed the accuracy of the report and apologised in respect of what he did actually say, wAs ordered to withdraw. After a long discussion a motion that " the question be not now put " was agreed to. The House resumed consideration of the Lords' amend- m-nts to the Employers Liability Bill. These amend- ments were disagreed with, and a committee was ap- pointed to draw up reasons for disagreement. • , Committee on the Local Government (Parisi] Coun- cils) Bill was then resumed.
The House of Lords sat for a few minutes in order that the Royal assent to the number of Acts might be signi— fied. Amongst those waft the Eaet Indian Loan (£10,000,000) Act.

div.head: "LADY OF QUALITY" AND HER LOVE LETTERS. •
div.p: A "LADY OF QUALITY" AND HER LOVE LETTERS. •

Mr. Justice Hawkins had before him on Wednesday an action brought by a " lady of quality "to recover letters which she had written to a young officer to whoi. she had been engaged." The plaintiff wits Lady Mabel sievier, sister of the Marquis of Aileshory, Ltnd the de- fendant a military officer named Crosbie. The parties were engaged, but in September last Lady Mabel wrote 'to Mr. Crosbie explaining that her " feelings" had changed, and that she could not marry him. Next day she marriel her present husband. The " presents." were, as usual, returned, but Mr. Cr/labia declined to re- turn L tdy Mabel's letters, and she brought an action to compel restitution. In her examination in chief Lady Mabel charged Mr. Crosbie with having sought to marry her for her money, but in cross-examination she ad- mitted that whilst the original settlement provided that. he should have an income of £5OO a sear, she herself proposed that the amount should be • £7OO. She per- sisted, however, in the imputation of mercenary motives. Tic action failed on a point of law, there be ing, in fact, no justification for it ; and Mr. Justice Hawkins, in recording judgement for Mr. Crosbie, said he could quite understand that that gentleman should desire to retain in his possession documents which showed, under the plaintiff's own hand, that the• charges made against him were a tissue of falsehoods. Ore of the most curious points in the case was the ad- mission by the plaintiff that there had been " communi- cations " with reference to an article in a " v,ciety " paper on the breaking off of this match.

What will the House of Lords do with the Liability Bill when it is again submitted to them for their ap- proval without the contracting-out clause ?If they persistin the line they have taken we may be quickly in the midst of that great constitutional Struggle which seems to be always impending When a Liberal Government is in office, but which has always hitherto been staved off. DURING the debate on the Em- fl Unfortunate Incident. ployers Liability Bill on Wednes- day evening, Mr. INFLAREN men- tioned an incident which—whether rightly or Wrongly depends upon the circumstances—tends tO discredit the result of the ballot that was taken some time ago of London and North- Railway employees as to contracting out. There was, said Mr. MIAREN, a workman at Frewe, named BRAID, who was a well known iitheral and Trades Unionist. Mr. BRAID was strongly against contracting out and advised his fellow workmen to vote against it. One morning, added Mr. M'LAREN, this out-spoken workman was cajled into the office and told that he must go to .warrington as a fitter, although he protested that a WaB not a fitter but a brass finisher. On reach- lag Warrington he informed the manager that he a. net a fitter, and' he was, therefore, sent back r Crewe. At Crewe he applied for reinstatement la his old place, hut was told that ho could not a. are it, and was " finished with." When stated la. this way it is not surprising that, as Mr. 4LAREN said, " there was not a man in Crewe who did not believe that this man was, in this Waderhand way, attempted to be got rid of, for the double reason that he was a prominent Liberal nd had voted against the employers in the ballot ,°4l the insuranc:fund." It is only fair to add, n°wever, that Mr. PLUNKET, one of the directors 15f the London and North-Western Railway Com- r,E.,ny, gave the affair a rather different complexion. :le said that this particular workman was trans- 'erred to Warrington because he was the fittest ll:lan—partly because he was a bachelor—and that _lle received an increase of wage when transferred. When sent back to Crewe he was re-engaged I..theilgh in another " shop "—but this, interposed. :x'r•I‘I'LaREN, was only after repeated protests eking all the circumstances of this case into ac- *rant, it is perhaps neither desiralak3 nor charit- able to eome to a conclusion adverse to the rnethods of the Railway Company or its o cials. The transference may have been merely coin- dent with the active part which BRAID was tak- lag against contracting out, but it is one of the an. fortunate class of coincidences which do not • wave a re-assuring effect upon workmen who are dltosed to take an independent line.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY. During the pat-ii month 1,830 vols. have been issued in the lending department and 44 in the reference depart- ment. being a decrease of 194 and 15 respectively,on the corresponding month last year. The library will be closed on Tuesday next, Bank Holiday. SISLEEDID NEW CURRANTS 2d. per lb, at COLLIER'S.— A drt. ELLBSIIRRE-ST. CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The anniversary sermons were preached on Sunday. by the Rev. S. Beaven, of Winsford, formerly of Run- corn Circuit. There were large congregations. The choir rendered in excellent style " In Jewry is God known." The collections were in aid of the Pruitt Fund. ROBBING DR. O'KEEYSE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, David Rush- ton, a tramp, pleaded guilty to stealing a coat and other articles of wearing apparel,altegether worth 30s. belong- ing to Dr. O'Keeffe, the medical officer. The prisoner had been previously convicted on 21 occasions and he was now sentenced to three months imprisonment. When In want of a CHASrIr and ELEGANT WEDDING Sr BIRTHDAY PRESENT go to PRITCHARD'S, 51. High-street.-- Advt.,

CLASSES. In connection with these classes, Mr. J. F. Moulton, the head teacher, held a spAline, eoaapetitiou on Tuesday evening. A large number of the students competed and Walter Caygill won the first pike and Charles Littler, the second prize. The prizes were two handsomely bound volumes on suitable subjects. FAILURE OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN. A petition has been filed in the Warrington County Court on behalf of William Cooper, Station-road, and 20, Waterloo-road, Runcorn, sailinaker. The statement of the debtor's affairs show that the liabilities of un- secured creditors amount to £lB7 6s. 6d. The assets are—stock-in-trade, £5 ; trade fixtures, utensils, &c., £lss. ; deposit in Peers' Economic Building Society : Jotal £ll Sc. From this has to be deducted for rent, ,tAtes, &c., C 6 55.; making a deficiency of £lB2 6s. 6 1.- The first meeting of creditors is fixed to be held on January 12th. DELICIOUS CRISP CRUST round COLLIER'S bread.—Ad. ASSAULT ON A WIDNES EVANGELIST. On Monday, at the Whines Police Court, before Mr H. Wade-Deacon and Councillor Gossage, a man named John Hooligan was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly, and also with assaulting an Evangelist name 4 Thomas J.Shelton on Saturday night.—lnspector Pattin- son stated that shortly before nine o'clock he saw the prisoner near the Market Hotel. He was drunk and went up to Shelton who was preaching at the time, and struck him deliberately in the mouth.—For the drunken- I ness the prisoner was fined ss. and costs, and for the assault 10s. and costs. Over 6,000 deliolous loaves sold every week at COLLIER'S. —Advt. _

IDEATE OF THE REV, G. H. RIGHT. Many Runcornians will learn with regret that the Rev. G. fl:Rigby, brother of the Solicitor-General, Sir John ' Rigby, took place on the night of the 15th inst., at Yard- ley Hastings Rectory, Northampton, after a short illness, from apoplexy. The deceased gentleman was well known in this district. He was the son of the late Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Runcorn, who carried on tho business of shipbroker for many years in this neighbourhood,and brother to Mr. William Rigby, who held the position of Commissioner, overseer, &c., in the t•,wn. The deceased had frequently occupied the pulpit in Runcorn Parish Church whilst the late Rev. Canon Barclay was vicar. PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test for fifty years, and quality and first class workm kinship are still guaranteed.— Advt. THE ALLEGED STABBING AFFRAY AT BOLD. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, and Councillor W. W. Gossage, the young woman Ellen Ellison, Bold, was again brought up on remand, charged with unlawfully wounding a woman named Margaret Rimmer, by stabbing her. Mr. Knowles appeared for piisoner.—Dr. Bate (Sutton Oak) stated that the woman was still in a weak state, but in no immediate danger, although she was not really altoge- ther out of danger.—Mr. Knowles said that prisoner had suffered from shock, and had tainted several times in tho cell. Her confinement was certainly injurious to her health, and he would therefore ask for bail.—After con- sulting with the clerk, the Bench allowed prisoner ball, herself in £4O and two sureties of £2O each. For sweet, white, home made breast,try OoLLIER'S.—Advt. BRUNSWICK BAND OF Hoes, RUNCORN. The monthly meeting of the above Baud of Hope was held on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Daniel 13isbrown. An excellent prcgramme was given, consisting of songs, duets, recitations and glees, by the following—Miss Alice Taylor. song ; duet by Miss Lizzie Leadstene and Miss Lizzie Leath wood, and recitation by Agnes Jeffreys, Nellie Green, Maggie Hildidge, Polly Dodd, Edith Sefton, and Peter Faulkner. Selections were given by the glee party in a creditable manner, under the charge of Miss Carrie Littler. Miss Norman ably acted as accompanist. Mr. Alfred Norman gave a very interesting temperance add rose. He expressed the interest he felt in the work, and urged the children to make Brunswick Band of Hope a still greater success. I • sf you want your WITCH RAPAIRED by skilled workmen take it to PRITCHARD'S.- Advt. FREE SCHOLARSHIPS AT FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL, The Governors of this ancient foundation have again shown their interest in the well being of Widnes youths by giving two free scholarships, tenable for three years, at the Grammar School. The success of Farnworth Grammar School boys is shown by their gaining scholar- ships and exhibitions to the value of £95, not counting entrance scholarships, this year, which is a brilliant record for a school of 40 boys. The entrance scholar- ships this year have been awarded from a list of 18 candidates to John Herbert Pile, 95, Halton-view ; and Ivan Baldwin, 8, Chester-street, both from Warrington. road Board School. In connection with the scholarships the grant of £lO per annum to each free scholar pre- vided by the munificence of Mr. Timmis, one of tho governors of the school, is awarded under certain con- ditions upon aMlication to the Widnes School Board. PURE IRISH B TER. Is. per lb., at COLLIER'S.—Adrt.

NON-PAYMENT OE WATER RATES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday,ninety two per- sons were summoned by the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners for not paying the water rates. —Mr. Lake the Law Clerk, explained that the unusual number Of cases was due to the rates being payable in advance in accordance with the Act of Parliament. In the past, the Water Company had allowed people to pay two or three quarters tagether, but now that the works were under the Commissioners it was incumbent that they should be paid as they became due in order that the accounts' might be properly kept. There was evidently a little misunderstanding among the public as to payment. Each defaulter had had a circular drawing attention to the Act of Parliament an 4 urging payment of the rate.— It appeared that in the majority of cases, the rates had been paid since the summonses were taken out and ilk the others the magistrates made orders for payment, ja accordance with the request of the collector (Mr. J. Jones). J.OSEPII PRITCHARD, 51, Righ-street. Runcorn, keeps iiitsarsc.LEs to Butt all eights, from a shilling a palr.—Adat. SHOCKING BRUTALITY TO A WIFS AT WIDNES.. At the Widnes Police Court on Monday before Mr. H. W.-Deacon and Councillor Gossage, Patrick Muldoon, 1, Bryn-st., was brought up on remand charged with un- lawfully wounding his wife, Annie Muldoon, on the 25tli , ult., be fracturing one of her ribs. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. The prosecutrix stated that the prisoner came home ic drink about nine o'clock on the night of the Saturday in question. She was standing in the doore; way, and her husband without any provocation kicked her on the shin, and then took her by the shoulders and dashed her down on the stairs. She was assisted to Dr. Allen'ssurgery,and was afterwards confined to her bed for a forenight,as the result of the injuries she had received. Dr. Allen said he found that the woman's tenth rib had been broken Close to the spine. Symptoms of pleurisy iritervened, and the woman's life was at one time in danger.. Pelice-cohstable Dickinson proved apprehend- ing prisoner, who in reply to the charge said his wife struck him throe or four times, and he gave her a shove, and she fell against the stairs. The prisoner was com- mitted for trial at the county quarter sessions. ROBBERY FROM A RUNCORN TRADESMAN. On Monday afternoon, at Frodsham Police Court, be- fore Mr. A. Thomas, a young man named Benjamin Wathers, 22, Canal-wharf, Chester, was charged with larcerw by finding and converting to his own use, two boxes, containing 29 pairs of sample goods, value £3 124., and one boy's serge suit, value 53. 11d., at Alvanley, on the 7th December, the property of Jalapa lins worth, of Runcorn.—Mr. Unsworth said he carried on business in High-street, Runcorn. On 7th December he was travelling from Runcorn to Ince in a trap, and had two boxes with him, containina 29 pairs of glovell and aserge suit in a parcel, addressed to Mr. Profit; Post Office; Ince. The goods produced were a portiOtt of these missed by him.--Sophia Lord, wife of Edward Lord, of the Whitl Lion, Alvanley, spoke to the prisoner coming to her house on December 7th. Ile asked if she . wanted any salt, and then said he had some gloves whi might suit her. Ile showed her those in boxes, and promised to dispose of them at low prices. He also said she could have a suit marked Si. Ild. for 23. 11d. 9he . declined to purchase anything. When asked how he could sell thetn so cheaply, he replied that he purchased ' them the previous night by auction for a sovereign.— Other evidence was given, and the prisoner when 11 charged, said "I found them between Ince and Raps- ford, an a man minding my horse must have stolen • them out of the cart, for I missed them out of the cart, , for I missed them on leaving Taryin."--The prisoner was committed to the sessions at Chester for trial.

At the conclusion of the business, the members aatdown to an excellent repast, prepared by the worthy host, Mr. Henry Darlington and full justice was done to the excel- lent viands provided. After tho removal of the cloth, the evening was spent in convi% songs being ably rendered by Messrs.Veale. Lambert, Bennison aud others. Mr. E. Newton presided. The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon. Present tit- Revs. /bean Finegan, Father Clarke, Messrs. B, Brown, It. Shaw C. Flynn, Lewis, S. Quinn, C. Barlow, and G. H. Danby (clerk). The District Education Committee reported that 42 free places had been granted. On the recommend ation of the School Management Committee, tie salaries of teachera were increased according to sea le ma,tinting to £52 at Simms Cross Schdol, £lB, at Werrineton-road, and £42 at West Bank School. The Finance Committee reported receipts £1,196 84. and payments £B6l 12s. 4d. The proposal of Mr. Shaw seconded by Mr. Brown,that Major Wareing be appointed a member of the Finance Committee, was rejected, the rest of the 8..z.,:rd voting against. The proposal to form an ambulance brigade for Run- corn has been entered heartily into by the committee of the above association, and at a meeting held on Monday evening it was unanimously decided to purchase an ambulance litter, to be placed at the disposal of the inhabitants of Runcern in cases of need, under the • direction of some members of the brigade. This will require an outlay of something like £2O, towards which Mr. Epps, secretary, has already received two guineas, Irons Me,srs. Peter Walker and Son, Liverpool, and one guinea from Messrs. Greene.% Whitley and Co., of War- rington. At the same meeting the Secretary announced that Dr. McDougall had been elected a honorary life member of the St. John Ambulance Association, Lon- don, in recognition of his able and valuable services as gratuitous lecturer to the classes at Runcorn, and for which the London Committee desired to tender its grate- ful thanks. _

Mellor, formerly a theatre proprietor and manager in the town, applied for a dancing and music license for the wooden Structure in Ditton-road, recently occupied by Mr.Ohmy as a circus. 'Mr. .1. W.Knowles opposed the application on behalf of the proprietors of the Alexandra Theatre— Messrs. T. Gerrard, W. Bray,,and J. Kiddie. In answer. to Mr. Knowles, Mr. Mellor admitted that the building was entirely of wood, and capable of holding 1,400 or 1,500 persons. There was no iron curtain. Mr. Timmis said from his personal knowledge of the place, he should advise the applicant to withdraw his application for the present,and give proper notice so that the matter might come before a full bench of magistrates. In Ma mean- time he (Mr. Timmis) would inspect the place. Mr. Mellor thereupon withdrew his application and gave notice.

The quarterly meeting of this circuit was held on Monday evening, in Brunswick-st. vestry, under the pre- , ardency of the Rev. T. Wilkes. The accounts presented showed an expenditure slightly in excess of the income, which was considered due in a great measure to the re- duction in the offertories, consequent upon the disloca- tion of trade through the coal strike. The Rev. T. Wilkes gave a return of membership considered very satisfactory, showing the total to be 634, or a net in- crease of nine during the three months. A discussion, with reference to special efforts being made to raise the moral condition of the masses was initiated bY Mr. Kniveton, but no definite resolution was arrived at. Mr. Pope, after three years' service as circuit steward, re- tired, and Mr. E. Taylor was elected as senior steward,' with. Mr. It. Ilawlinson as junior steward for the ensuing year. Mr. J. M. Frith accepted office as secretary to the quarterly meeting. Messrs. C. H. R. Harrison arid W. Sowerby were appointed auditors for the foreign mis- sionary accounts. On the motion of Mr. Beckett, a com- mittee was appointed to consider the desirability or otherwise of making an alteration in the location of the third minister.

On Wednesday evening an interesting egremony took place at the Devonshire Hotel, Ashbridge-street, Run- corn, where the annual meeting of the Loy al William the Fourth Ledge, No. 1085, Independent order ot Odd. fellows, Manchester Unity, was held in the lodge room. During the evenieg a beautifully framed past officer's em- blem of the Order was presentrd to Bro. Herbert Pendle- bury, G.M.. RS a tribute of respect, and in recognition 01 his services whilst filling the respective offices of Elective Secretary, Vice Grand, Noble Grand, and Grand Master of the Lodge. The presentation *as suitably made with a few well chosen words by Bro. William Chringhall, P.P.G.M., on behalf of the lodge. Past Grand Pendlebury in briefly thanking the members for the gilt, said that it had been a pleasure to him to assist in the working of the Lodge, and that he was grati- fied by the expression of good will made by the members. Jossvit PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- it., Runcorn.—Advt.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. At the fortnightly meeting of the above order on Saturday night, under the presidency of Mr. James Johnson, a paper was read by Mr. Edward Key, on " Tobacco, its use." The writer spoke of the nature and properties of tobacco, and its medicinal qualities. He strongly defended its use. The effect of it was to sooth and tranquilize the nervous system. He spoke of brilliant writers and ministers of eminence, who used the weed. After the paper there was a discussion, in which :he following officers took part :—Messrs. Thomas Cooke, Thomas J. Holt, Samuel Henderson, Daniel 131s- brown, John K. Little, George S. Sutton, David Smith, and Thomas Clarke. The speakers were pretty evenly divided in their opinion on the question. The habitual use of tobacco was strongly depricatcd, as it deranged the nervous system, and there were few who did not suffer from it more or less. It affected the few who did ,not suffer from it more or less. It affected the healthy appetite for food, and interfered with the organs not fully developed. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Key for his paper. MAYORAL AT Eloam AT WIDNIFS. Alderman Gossage, Mayor of Widnes has ever taken a keen and pratical interest in education. His benefac- tions to educational institutions have been frequent and generous. It was not surprising therefore, that when he heard of the success of the continuation schools com- menced by the School Board, that he should decide to receive the teachers and pupils " at home " in order to encourage them in their studies. The function took place in the Drill Hall on Thursday evening. There were about 90 persons present. Unfortunately the Mayor was unable to be present through a severe attack of lumbago, but Mr. T. S. Tim- mls who was for about twelve years chairman of the school Board acted in his stead. Mr. TiMMiS was sup- ported by the Mayoress, Mrs. Timmis, Miss Gossage, Miss Hilda Deacon, Mr. Councillor Gossage, Mr. H. Wade Deacon, j.P., C.C. During the evening a mis- cellaneous entertainment was given. WIDNES DISTRESS FUND. The final meeting ef the distress commitee was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, C.C. The financial statement showed that the contributions amounted to £3,154 ha. 81., and during the sixteen weeks the relief distributed was £2,793 13s. Bd. A balance of £353 18. remained, and the committee recommended that £l5O be left in the hands of the treasurer and the remainder spent in pro- viding clothing for the children and beddinr. in deserv llg - cases.—Mr. C.Hemingway moved, and Mr.T.Gerrard seconded that £5O be devoted towards the fund for the annual treat to the old folks in January, and this was agreed to. The remainder (£154 18s.) it was resolved should ha left in the hands of the Finance Committee for distribution. Votes of thanks were passed to all those who had assisted in the distribution of relief, and to Messrs. W. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

It was with unfeigned regret that all parties heard of the untimely death of Mr. Torn Cotting- ham Moss, on Saturday last. He was held in esteem not only by his political friends, but also by his opponents for his manly and straightforward con- duct. He was the first member for the Widnes divi- sion which was carved out of SotithWest Lancashire at the redistribution of seats. to 1885 and 1886 he respectively defeated Mr. E. K. Muspratt and Mr. Augustine Bruen, and at the end of the latter Parliament he retired owing to ill-health. Leaving politics out of consideration, no constituency bad a more hardworking membermor one more anxious to please his constituents. Ile ga7e prompt and effective attention to any request made to him, no matter how humble the applicant. It was chiefly through his exertions in London, that Widnes was granted a County Court sitting once a raonth and a local office six years ago. Prior to that time suitors had the inconvenience and expense of visit- ing St. Helens, in order to transact court business, and the change was received wi,..11 great pleasure by the tradesmen, who now recall with gratitude the service Mr. Moss rendered in the matter. In the Parliamentary work of the defunct Local Board Mr. Moss, jun., willingly lent his assistance, and he was the means of securing a postal telegraph office 'at Farnwort h. Not a rich man, yet no appeal did Mr. Moss leave wholly unanswered and he took con- ideraole interest in the local institutions. de took a prominent part in the establishment of the gym- nasium, and as an athlete aided the institution all in his power, but it is now defunct. He had also acted as president of the Athletic Club. No one would deny to the deceased gentleman the title of an honourable Englishman.

The Widnes Distress Fund Committee brought their labours to a conclusion with the satisfactory Iresult that full justice has been done all round,aud that there is lett in the hands of the treasurer, a sum of £l5O for use, should any need arise in the future. Besides this bUM £5O is to be given to the aged persons treat fund, and £l5O spent on purchas- ing clothing an 4 bedding in cases ot necessity at the present time. Let us hope the treasurer will be enabled to hold that £l5O for many years to come.

At length the bye-laws controversy is settled in Runcorn. The result of the new regulations if they are strictly and conscientiously carried out should be increased comfort in the dwellings and a con- siderable diminution in sickness, and consequent reduction in the number of deaths from what are known as preventable diseases. One great cause for congratulation is the fact that the new bye-laws will make the water carriage of excreta cheaper than any other mode of removal.Tbe present system is no doubt utterly bad, and the number of times the nightsoil is deposited before it is removed from the district is a fruitful source of nuisance. Thanks are due to Mr. Humphreys and Mr. Imison for the boldness and thoroughness they have displayed in the matter. Anent the builders deputation to the Commissioners on the subject, I had a conversation with one this week, and he stated that so far from being treated discourteously, the grea.test kindness I and courtesy and attention was displayed towards the deputation. As Mr.Meadowcroft would not have made the statement without cause, someone must have been leading him astray.

Before the "Examiner" will have been published again. Chriettnas will have come and gone, and I take this opportunity of wishing all readers " A Meriy Christmas." The coal dispute has played sad havoc with the trade of both Runcorn and Widnes, and since the settlement, so short a time has elapsed, that very many families will not have re- covered themselves, and the fe-tive season, as a con- sequence, will be robbed of 80111 e Ot tIB brightness and joyousness. In Runcorn, too, the completion of the canal has taken 80 many men out of the district that the tradesmen are complaining with cause, of slackness of trade. They console themselves with the belief that the canal when in complete working order will bring additional trade to the port, and indications strongly point to such a conclusion. May the New Year not have far advanced before the highest expectations of all are realised, and that in both Widnes and Runcorn every indnatry aid trade, may be flourishing.

Runcorn Tonic Sol--Fa Choir are giving their annual performance of the" Messiah" in the Public Hall, on the evening of Christmas Day, with the aid of an efficient orchestra, and well-known prin- ciples. Previous performances of this grand work by the choir, have been of the highest merit, and there is every reason to believe that on the present occasion they will be equalled if not eclipsed. The work is very appropriate to the season, and to those -bo take advantage of the opportunity of hearing It cannot but be elavating and enjoyable.

WEEKLY REPOBT ON THE HEALTH 01 WARRINGTON. During the week, which was the 50th of the current year, the following births and deaths werF registered :—Births ; Warrington, 44 ; Latchford 8 : t0ta1,52. Deaths: Warrington,24 : Latchford, 3 ; total 27. The excess ol` births over deaths was 25. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 254 per 1.000, against 22.3 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 24.06 the eorresponding week of last year. The death-rate from the seven chief zyrnotic diseases was equal to 1.8 per 1.000, against 3 the average rate of the four previous weeks, and against 5.8 the corresponding week of 1892. , The ages of mortality were :-0 to 1, 8 ; 1 to 5,6; sto 15. 0;15 to 25, 1 25 to 60, 9 ; 60 up 3; total, 27. The 'deaths included 1 from enteric lever ; 1 from measles ; 1 from scarlet, fever 1 from int uenza : 1 from cancer ; 2 from rilithisis; 1 from old age ; 6 from lung disease ; 1 from kidney disease; 1 from liver disease. The 'follow- ing cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week:—scarlet fever, 0; enteric fever 2. II ETEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was 41'1 Fah., and therefore 1.0 colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 55 F., was recorded on the 16th inst.,and the minimum temperature 31 F., on the 12th inst. The rainfall measured 1.19 inch. The general direction was S.W.. the reading of the Anemometer denoting 1160 tailes.—JoHN 11. GOIINALL, Medical Officer of Health.

. RITXCORN BOAItIY3CHOOLS. ANNUAL DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. SPEECH BY MRS. TOMKINSON. The second annual entertainment and distribu- tion.of prizes in connection with Greenway-road Board Schools, took place in Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening. Mr. Thomas Handley occu- pied the chair, and Mrs. Tomkineon, of Wit hington Tarporley, was present to perform the cere- shorty of presentation of the prizes. The Hall was well filled with an interested and appreciative audience, and the fare provided was enjoyed to the full. The first part consisted of the operetta Lazylaud," which is written by Louis B. Tisdale and composed by A. L. Vingoe. The characters re- presented were :—King, Joseph Savage Queen Ger- trude Atherton ; Waiting Maids, Elizbeth Livica:lf and Edith Wright ; Herald, Samuel Lane • Merry Boy, James Banner. Tne operetta is a very 'bright and en- tertaining .composition, and the music is well within the range of the youthful performers, while the subject in- culates a very suitable lesson. The scene is laid in the Zing's Palace, for which the necessary stage property had been kindly lent by Mr. Caddick of the Theatre Royal. The performers were attired in costumes suit- awe to their respective characters, and they acted, and sang their respective parts with an amount of confid- ence and ,effcct, which was highly complimentary to their capabilities, and to the complete and efficient in- structions they had received. The duet "We are aw- fully sad "by the King and Herald, followed by a dance was encored, and a similar result was achieved by Merry Boy and Herald in the duet and dance" You don't mean to say so." The chorus " The spell is broken " was received with much applause. The dialogue was also efficiently given. It shopld be men- tioned that a suitable prologue was spoken by Ben Cooper, who had donned the costume of a butcher boy. The second part of the programme was of a Iniscellaneol character, and was equally well rendered and enjoyable. ,It was as tollows :—" Language song," boys and girls ; recitation, " A grievous complaint,"ohn E. Tweedall ; Japanese fan drill, thirteen girls ; song and chorus, the game of football," Joseph Savage; recitation, "The dead dolly," Amite Stairway ; crying song, boys and girls ; comic sketch," The Irish schoolmaster," W. Mc. Quinn and others, song, " The land of the Leal," girls. The fan drill was a very pretty and graceful perform- ance, for which the girls had been trained by Miss Acton. The comic sketch and the Irish schoolmaster were encored. The arrangements for the entertainment Sze., had been ably carried out byte head teachers, Mr. J. F. Moulton, and Miss Kilburn, and had been chiefly assisted by Messrs. W. Keunan, A. W. R. Owen and Miss Acton. I he Chairman said it must be very encouraging to the teachers to see so many present that night, and com- pensate them to seine extent for the trouble they had taken. He might say that the prizes were not paid for out of the rates. They were obtained through the energies cf the teachers who arranged entertainments throughout the year,, and thus raised the required sum of money. The Government Inspector, Mr. Kytnersley, had very kindly given two lectures by which a nice sum had been 'realised towards the fund. He need not say how the -prizes stimulated the children to attend the school punc- tually and regularly and how much it facilitated the Work of the teachers. Ho saw trem the newspapers that on Saturday a deputation waited upon Mr. Acland, the minister of Education, and meted upon him to im- press upon the School Boards of the country that they should insist upon the punctual and regular attendance of children. The average attendance throughout the country was put down at 78 per cent., whereas in Run. corn it was 83 per cent., which was highly satisfactory. ' Mrs. Totnkinson, upon ascending the platform to dis- tribute the prizes, was presented with a bouquet of flowers by Miss Edith M'Laren, who requested her to ac- cept the gilt as a slight token of the thanks of the teachers and scholars for her presence that evening. Mrs Tomkinson suitably acknowledged the gift, and after- wards in the course of a long speech, expressed the plea- sure she had experienced in being able to accept their In- vitation to be present. In Tarporley they brad entertain- /Rents of a similar character, and she had often express- ed much enjoyment there, and her anticipations in re- gard to Runcorn had been more than fulfilled that even- ing by the manner in which the children had acted and sung the operetta. They had shown signs of genius,and she was sure that they were thoroughly and efficiently taught. Had she not seen this for herself she would have known it by the reports she had had of the schools which had been BO successful in attracting pupils that tke building was to be enlarged to accommodate 84 more girls and there was a prospect that this extension would not be sufficient. All this showed that the school was in a highly satisfactory state, and the inhabitants ef the town ought tu he proud of such an ins.itution. (Applause.) Sire expressed her satisfaction at the fact that the prizes were lor regularity arid punctuality as well as proficiency ; the two former were very import- ant points in school work, and also trained the children up in 'mbar; of self control, and self denial and obedieece, which would be useful to them in after life. But these desirable habits could not be formed without earnest endeavour on the part of the parents, and she urged those parents present to act the needful part for the sake of their children and for the sake of their own characters. She was sure that in the coming year tire children would remember the lesson of the operetta,and would determine that they would live not in "Lazyland" but in" busyland," and that they would have for their motto " Something attempted something done." (Ap- plause.) Mrs. Tomkinson spoke to parents of the great responsibility that rested upon parents in their respec- tive stations of seeing that their children had the very best education they possibly could have. She was glad to think that they in Runcorn had such a good chance of getting their children well placed on the lower rungs of the ladder of education. She hoped that in the near future they would find more intermediate schools,which the south of our towns could use as stepping stones to the ui iversity. She pointed out that unless parents took mu interest itt the school work of their children, they eyelet not expect teachers to do their work with the de- sired efficiency. Mrs.T.inikinson described the progress that had been made in the treatment of children and their education. Children were no longer permitted to work in factories and in mines from dawn to dusk. Now children of all classes from the highest to the lowest had an opportunity of acquiring and education which would stand them in good stead wheo grown up. Mrs. Tomkinson concluded by giving a recitation suitable to the occasion. Mrs. Tomkinson then distributed the prizes, which Mr. Moulton explained were given lor regularity and punctuality, and also for success in school work. Many of the prize winners had not bnm absent from school once during the whole year. and others had only been absent through sickness. The following boys who had not been absent once from school for the past two or three years deserved special mention :—Thoinas Poole, Joseph Harper, Percy Littler, J. Bentley, W. Andrews, Leslie Hitchmough, and J. A. Hughes. , The list of prize winners is as follows BOYS. • Standirde VI. and VII.—T. Prince, S. Lane F. Gresty, J. Banner, W. Ball, J. Hill, J. Harding, T. Cowap, M. Hollord, L. Brown, M. Corker, A. Stanway, E. Dolt. E. Streets, E. Carroll, E. Ashley, E. Sweetinan, A. Parker, M. Draper. Mr. Pritchard moved and Mr. Imison seconded a vote ef thanks to Mrs. Tornkinson, for having undertaken the duty at great self-aacrifiee. The latter gentleman remarked that it was often thought that the same kind interest was not taken in the children attending Board Schools as in other institutions, but such a gathering as that proved that the members of the School Hoard were desirous of the welfare of the children, equally as much : as the managers of other schools. (Applause.) The motion was carried.—Mrs. Tomkinson announced that she would have pleasure in giving two copies of Sir Robert Ball's hook" Starland ' for next year—one as a prize for the girls and the other for the boys. (Applause.) She wished the prize to be given for any special subject the master or mistress might select. On the proposition of Mr. Moss. a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and the proceedings terminated.—The schools 1" broke up" for the Christmas holidays on Thursday and each scholar was presented with an orange.

div.head: TO MANCHPSPEtc ALONG THE SHIP CANAL. A PRESS VOYAGE.
div.p: TO MANCHPSPEtc ALONG THE SHIP CANAL. A PRESS VOYAGE.

[BY OUFt OWN REPORTER.] About half-past nine OM Saturday morning, there was quite a flutter of excitement at the far end of/ the Princes Landing Stage, Liverpool. A cluster of spectators—of the peculiar character that is always to be found in the locality—were dividing their at- tention between the difficult task of propping themselves up against lounge posts, and eying the embarkation of certain parties on board the " Snow- drop." The certain parties in question were, indeed worthy of some inspection. They were represent- atives of " that mighty engine." the Press of Great Britain, and were assembled from all parts of the Kingdom. The occasion of their gathering was to join in an excursion along the Snip Canal to Man- chester, at the invitation of the Directors of the Company. An" Examiner" reporter had the honour of being one of the invited guests. At about a quarter to ten the moorings were castoff, end the ! " Snowdrop," with more than 100" Knights of the pen" on board, steamed up the stream towards Eastham. There was a mild breeze blowing, and the elements appeared to have decided upon being favourable to the auspicious occasion. There were fleeting clouds overhead, intermingled with " bite " of blue sky. Ever and anon the sun burst from be- hind. a cloud and sent dancing scintillations across w;wraotaauhtdleedernest,ll;oef ewatit lithoeoarretmi! shaft aoeotorti nidki , like ea, ta c reachinghi lengthn g hoef stillget han sel golden eastern anenigrnk, for the first time, the pretty 'scenery skirting the Mersey between Garston and hale Head. It was almost like an April scene and many a "word artist" retained in his mental lens, a picture of Mersey scenery. Passing through the Easthana channel, which the company have dredged eci as to be navigable to any vessel, the party reached the famous Eastham locks. This would be about half past ten. In about ten minutes the •• Snowdrop " had passed through the Eastbain docks-800fc. by 801 t., 3501 t. by 50ft. and lbOft. by 301 t. The Mersey is left behind and this is actually the Ship Canal ! Mr. Leader Williams is on Board and he now becotnes the centre of an interested group to whom he describes how, in the tidal of the waterway between Eastitain and Latchford, twelve miles are inland, and nine miles on the foreshore or the bed of the tideway. On this portian embank- ment); have had to be formed. The eminent engineer says a good deal more, and pencils are soon busy. But presently, Mr. Leader Williams, who is fond of his joke, mildly observes, " But gentlemen, you will find all the information set out in the published hand- book !" The busy" brainworkers " drop their pencils and smile, except a few, perhaps, who are not quite so appreciative. There is not much to be seen as Eastham is left, and Ellesmere Port approached. On the left is a huge bank of soil—s veritadle mountain, but a mountain that has not come there by the ordinary forces of nature. The steam navvy and the human navvy have dug it out of the ground, and it has been reared up to make way for the canal. it is called Mount Manisty, after an engineer connected with the scheme, who is a sun of Mr. Justice Manisty. Ellesmere Port, where there is a gantry con- structed on a foundation of 12,000 piles, is not a very lively place as viewed from the "Soowdrop." The vil- lage itself is out of sight. It is the terminus of the Shropshire Union Canal, the navigations of which extend to Chester and through Shropshire into North Stafford- shire. This Company have constructed a long length of wharfage fronting the canal. The most interesting ob- ject hereabouts at present is the pontaor, dry dock. It is 300 rt.. long and 70ft. wide, and two vessels are on it ready for repairs and" doing up." It is a place of recent origin, having only been created in July of last year to meet the requirements of the canal, but it now has a very respectable air of business about it. There are a number of craft about, some flying bunting in honour of the visit of the "Snowdrop" and the Press. The pos- sibilities of the canal become more and more appreciated as more is seen of tbe waterway. Saltport it is well to explain, is near the junction of the Ship Canal with the river Weaver, the Weston Canal, and the Runcorn and Weston Canal. It is the nearest shipping place for the Cheshire salt trade, and wharves,. and jetties have been constructed for transhipiment ot salt. Pending the opening of the canal all tine way through, regular lines of steamers have for some time now been running from Saltport to London, Glasgow, and Treport. To particularise, other materials of the traffic dealt with herr viz : timber, minerals, pitch, pig- iron, pottery, nitrate, rosin, farina, sugar, and saccha- rine. The Weston Marsh Lock which is 2.291 t. by 421 t. Bin., is at the mouth of the Weaver, forming the entrance to the Weaver navigation. There hag been a lot of very trying work hereabouts and at Runcorn, just a step further on. The river work that had to be under- taken was productive of continuous and serious difficulty, which taxed the utmost skill and ingenuity of the en- gineering staff. The Weaver slucies took a long time to build, but they are a fine specimen of such work now that they are completed. Ten in number, they are each 30ft. wide, rise 13ft., and weigh 50 tons. They were finished in 1890, and are intended to allow of the passage of the Weaver water. They will also be used for the tidal flow. It is said that they are capable of passing 50,000 cubic feet per second. In this neighbourhood also there is the Runcorn lay-by 1,5001 t. long, and the Bridgewater Luck 400 ft. by 451 t. This lock forms the river entrance to the Runcorn Docks which belong to the Ship Canal Company and cover an area of 147 acres. Runcorn by the way, is quite a busy place, and along with its more inland . neighbour, Warrington, is looking forward to much prosperity by reason of the making ofi the canat.

As the " Snowdrop " neared Acton Grange, the first sitting to a very sumptuous dinner was announced. Needless to say, there was no diffieulty in finding candi- dates for the vacant seats. Passing under the gigantic railway viaduct here, the "Snowdrop " Steams quickly along to Stockton Heath. And here a right royal wel- come is accorded the excursionists. At each of the various swing bridges, and along the banks, there were gathered hundreds of spectators, whose enthusiastic cheers filled the air as the veseel made her way now more slowly to the Latchford locks. Like Manchester, Warrington is prepared to swear by the canal. It held promotion meetings when the scheme first came an the carpet, it is likely to hold a demon- stration now the scheme is completed ; it subscribed promotion money, sent witnesses to London, and gene- rally interested itself. Warrington was promised docks at Arpley. but they have not yet made their appear- ance. In their last Act it is intimated by the company that they will make these docks within three years of the opening of the canal from Eistham to Latchford, that is to say, the tidal portion. The company have also entered into an undertaking with the Warrington Corporation to complete the dredging ef the Mersey at Warrington within six months from the opening of the canal under a penalty of LW a day. During this six months the manufacturers and traders of Warrington who have already barges and boats running on the river are to have access to the Ship Canal free of toll. Other traders will pi v 3d.per ton, as mentioned in the original Canal Act of 1585. The old bend of the river,whlch has been cut off, will tititnately be used tor dock purposes. Traffic ills for some time now balk running on the de- viated railways here, the grass-covei•ed embankments ot which are solid looking and massive. Some fine speci- mens of bridge building are also to be seen. The bridge that carries the deviated London and North-Western railway over the canal at Latchford is a case in point, and may be taken as typical of the rent. It weighs 1220 tens, and when being built attracted a good deal of at- tention. The piers which support it are, up to. water level, composed of large blocks of Alanley sandstone. Above water level they are composed of red bricks faced with blue bricks, and it will be of interest to learn that a single layer of one pier absorbs from 4,000 to 6,000 bricks, while each pier has required the trifliug figure of one and a half million bricks. The company made their own bricks at Statham. Before the water WAS let into the canal the view from the top of this bridge was a striking one. ID was likely to make a person giddy to look down into the depths, but the prospect ahead, where were being built the lonics that the Wallasey steamer is entering, was one of great animation and stir. These locks, the handbook tells us, are 600 ft. by 65f t. and 350 ft. by 4.5 ft., with a rise of 16ift. They are 21 miles from Eastliam. The gates. like those of the other locks, are constructed of greenheart, a very hard wood imported from Demerara, which is exceedinely durable. It is said, however, to he poisonous, so that care has to.telaken of splinters in working it. Once through Latchford lock S the " Snowdrop "soon reaches Barton locks, which are 30i miles from Eastham. Here is to be seen one of the most wondercus pieces of engineering work,connected with the undertak- ing The Bridgewater Canal is carried over the Ship Canal by means of a steel aqueduct 2351 t. long, 61t. deep and Oft. wide. During the passage of vessels through this part of the Ship Canal, the aqueduct is pivot by hydraulic power, this weight being 1400 tons and the span lXi•feet. At " tswiwile'lletnniignsowc'n a tinifei'n'g Snowdrop " passed through, there was a flat "on the squduct, which remained there while the structure was swung. All along from here to Manchester the banks were thronged by hundreds of people, who cheered the party enthusiastically as it sailed by. At , Manchester the reception simply-amounted to an ovation. Thsusands of people linetl the docks arid warehouses, ' and, as one of the party facetiously pot it. the" Snow- drop "simply rocked on the waves of wild enthusiasm which for sometime prevailed.. Whatever may have been the opinion Termed by the visitors of the financial prospects of the undertaking there was an unmistakable feeling that the company had achieved one of the most wonderful engineering undertakings on record.

Considerable Interest is already being centred on the I forthcoming procession of vessels along the Ship Canal, which will take place on New Years Day. Several large vessels which are being unloaded at Saltport, will be included in the procession, whilst many Manchester
1 I rr 4..e.avwverld.

:It merchants will have their first freight of rcerchand,se conveyed along the Canal in vessels which wlll'arrive ia time for the procession, The Warrington Slate Company have chartered the Steamship Dinorwic (owner, Bon. W. W, Vivian) to bring a cargo •of state from the Velinheli quarries for Manchester. The vessel will carry 300 tons valued at £l,OOO. Messrs. Monks Hall and Co.. are also intending to place one 6f their steam boats in he'proeession. The same company, it might be men. honed, are about to have built still another steamboat for conveying their goods to Liverpool.

I The "hangers on" at the Central Station are hav- ing a bad time of it at present, for during the past fortaight or three weeks, a good number of them have had an interview with their Worships at the Police Court, and the result has not been very plea- sant fcrr the interviewers, for they have either bad to pay a fine or been consigned to one one her of Majesty's houses of correction. The police are to be commended for their work in this direction, tar these persons are thorough pests to railway passengers. At times it is a most difficult task to get oat of the station,owing to the crowd of fellows shouting out" carry your parcel, sir," and not al- ways being content with an answer in the negative. They are so pertinacious sometimes, that the pass- enger gives in and lets his parcel be carried, even if he is not at first so inclined. The railway officials have had loud complaints from the passengers about this matter.

But it i& not only the passengers who have a griev- ance against these tiarcel carrier, but the cabmen are equally annoyed with them for a very different and substantial reason. They complain that they lose a large number of fares, owing to the class of persons referred to running, off With their custom- ers, although they have not any license to pay, Now that the °Meets of the law are .stepping in. , however, it is to be hoped that we shall see the station steps less frequent,-!d. then hitherto.

IThe state of the Warrington County C!ntrt !luring the cold weather is of a character which is any- thing but plea4ant to those who have-to i be in it a whole day long. The influenza. epidemic s very rampant at present, and to have to sit down for sever alhours in the chilly temperature, and the depressing surroundings of the court is almost equal to courting an attack of that epidemic. But the County Court is, I am afraid, a kind of peren- nial grievance. In a conversation the other day with an.offlcial who very rare 4 attends the court, I learn-that 30 years or more since,he yuent with the , Judge of that time to view a plot of ground which was to-be the site of a new County Court. This is a tolerably long time ago, but the County Court is still held. in the same place, and there is not very much probability of its speedy removal. The site was either unsuitable, or the price was too high, but whatever was the reason, the old Wes- leyan chapel has continued to be the place for the settlement of civil disputes unto this day.

How comes it to pass that two lawyers in pass- ing opinions upon the same circumstances will so often come to huch tliameticrally opposite conclu- sions with regard to these circumstances? Is the . law so elastic that it can be twisted and stretched any way the learned fraternity wish to pull it ?Mr. Mulholland answers, "No !" Ina. case at the County Court last week, he observed that it was generally stated that 'give a lawyer a guinea, and you can get an opinion any way you like." He however. contradicts this assertion. He maintains that 1,1 person's colluring of the circumstancss.may be such that the lawyer. cannot be acquaintetl with the whole truth, and be has to give his opinion accord- . ingly.. Detractors of lawyers please ncts,this.

Many Warringtonians will be glad to hear that. Mr. 11. T. Spencer, 8.A., M.Sc., son of Mr. H. Spencer, who was for some years stationed in War- rington Inland Revenue Office, and resided. in , Museum-street, has accepted the unanimous call to the pastorate sent to him •by the Congregational Church at Wavertree. Mr. Spenc.,r is at present a student at Mansfield College, Oxford, and wilt not commence his pastoral duties until June next...year. %Viten in Warrington he was a member ef Wycliffe Congregational Church, and an active Sunday school worker.

I have at hand a copy of the Christmas r_umber of the" Angler." The paper itself, which cizezulat,es ' both in the United Kingdom and Americr.,Appar- , ently possesses a conaiderable amount of intarest to the 300 or more anglers of Warrington. The number I contains the continuation of a story. A water, Frolic on the Norfolk Broads ''—by "K Q.," who, it •is whispered, is a gentleman residing in the neigh- bourhood of Warrington. Whether this be true or not I cannot say. I only know that, I rditerate the general wish expressed among local ang!ors,-when I express the hope that the story will fl.tul its way into book form. I am one of those unfort?nate men who have not yet read "Three Men in a lloat," but, for genuine, healthy humour and fun, I am ,quite content with the four men in the boat of Mie "Water - Frolic," From beginning to end the.story is brim- ful of a good norm.. d j ,Ility, and is embellished with many flashes of merry wit. There are not wanting, either, many indications of the deeper and . more ob,ervant side of the writer. The story will , become a popular book for an idle hour. I think I . am safe in predicting.

I notice too, that this particular number of ,the Angler" gives a prominent place to the amusing article on the " Delights of Angling " by Luke . Blunt, which appeared in the " ,Examiner " aume months ago. Respecting this writer, I have received from a well-known Warrington tradesman the fol- lowing extract from a letter which was sent to hint from an old Warringtonian in Ainterioa:—"Wo have your batch ot papers to hand. There is an article in the "Examiner" by Luke Blunt, Can you tell. toe me who the writer is ; I believe.his name i 3 only a nom de plume. lam very much ini crested i2,A Antll=, . her of his articles, especially the one on the, llth November on the distrtisq. It was a most llowerful plea on behalf of the suffering poor,and in response to it I have plessuro in sending you a moaay order for one dollar, which I leave to you to make use of.. My regret is that the sum iS not greater, but I have, not drawn any salary myself for three muia,ths."

At the Borough Court on Thursday, John Malley, stationed at rford Barracks, was charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous night, in Winwick- street, and also with assaulting Charles Sddlow, at the same time .and place.—Mr. Sudlow, boot and shoe dealer, Wiawick-street, said that on Wednesday night ke was in the house when a daughter came rushing in stating that a soldier was in the yard. He (witness) went to le4na and ordered him out, whereupon the pris- oner began to remonstrate and used very bad language. He pushed the prisoner out of the yard, and the latter attempted tet-strike him with his belt. Witness fol- lowed prisoner to report him, but when near the Central Station, the priscner turned round, and struck him on the head with his stick, cutting the ear. A crowd assembled and the prisoner was given in charge. P.C. Roper said he found the prisoner near the Central Stat- ion very drunk and acting like a madman. Mr. Sudlow was bleeding very much. He brought the prisoner to the police station. Sergeant Chantler also gave evid- MICA. The prisoner was committed to gaol for one Month hard labour. A FBROCIIIIS DOG AT LARGE. John Ashley. farmer.
