Delahay stated that he was called to the " Rein:ley " in consequence of a disturba nee. He there saw the prisoner in a drunken state outsid, and was obliged to lock him up.—John Marsh said thar prisoner was a netorictua character at that part of th;. towa, awl be had giro

• orders not to. serve him with drink at any time. • On Saturday night, prisoner commenced to make a disturb - mice because he was refused and he was ejected. He thereupon picked up a large stone and deliberately flung it into the bar; the stone just " scraping " his (witness's) face. He was ebliged to call in the assistance of the police.—The magistrates iranosed zepenalty ef 10s. and , costs or 14 days' imprisonment. TUESDaY,—Before Mr. E. J. Guest (chairman), Dr. Starkey Smith, and Mr. R. Garnett. THEFT OF A DRFSS.—Phcebe Ryan, a married woman, residing at 25, Lord Nelson-street, was charged with stealing from the shop of Isaac Houghton, pawnbroker, Mersey-street, the previous morning, a black dress, value 185. 6d., his property. Prisoner pleaded guilty. The Chief Constables statement allowed that the prisoner went to the complainant's shop the previous morning to pledge some clothing, and soon after her de- parture. Mr. Houghton missed a black dress valued at 18s. or 20s. Information was given to the police, and D.S. Monaghan visited the various pawnshops, giving a description of the missing dress. Later in the day the prisoner gave a woman the dress to pledge for her, at Mr. Greaves' pawnshop, Church-street,. The dress was detained, and the police communicated with, and when charged, the prisoner pleaded guilty. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for fourteen days hard labour. WERNESDILL—Before Mr, John Fairclough (chairman), Mr. John Geddes, and Mr. J. H. Fleming. FALSE ATTESTATION.—jOhn Kemp was charged with wilfully making a false attestation when enlisting in Her Majesty's South Lancashire Regiment on the 10thl July, by stating that he did not belong to the Reserve. ' An officer from the barracks, who appeared at the court, said that the prisoner's conduct had been good.—Defend- ant said that he was reduced to absolute poverty and want, or he would not have done such a thing,—Mr. Fairclough said that he thought it was a hard thing that the man could not join the army again if he wished. There was a good deal of excuse for him, but the law must be carried out and defendant would be sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour. Tiinesese.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman) and Major Ridgway. A DESERTER.—Bernard Callig,han, was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's East Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Burnley, since the 18th inst. P.C. Barlow said he was in Sankey-street when he met the defendant. He noticed his clothing, stepped him, and afterwards took him to the police station. The defen- dant then admitted being a deserter. He was remanded to Strangeways gaol to await an escort. P.C. Barlow. applied for, and received, the usual reward. Franee.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Mr. W. Pierpoint, Dr. Gornall, and Councillor Roberts. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF a House AND CART.--Jatßeg Byrne, a stranger to the town, was charged with being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart on Thursday morning.—The magistrates fined prisoner ss. and costs or seven days. Constable Roper proved the case. DRUNK AND DISORDEULY.—Martin Dolan, 8, Berry's Yard, Tanners-lane, was fined ss. and costs for this offence. Famous DRIVING.—John Baguley, Mill-street, was fined 10s. and,costs, for furiously driving a horse and cart in Bridge-street on the 18th e inst.—Constables Cooper and Clough proved the case. CRUELTY TO:A Hoasm—Edward Cotterall, Hatton, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state on the 13th inst. Inspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A.' said that he saw the defendant on. the above date, driving a bay gelding attached to a cart on which were the defendant and his wife. The horse was very lame, and on exam- ination it was ascertained to have a spavin on its hock which was very much inflamed and tender. Although warned by the inspector, the defendant persisted in the horse going along with him.—P.C. Arnaon corroborated, and the magistrates fined the defendant in the costs. FEMININE ARENITIES.—kIary Coyne, 8, Rose-yacd, was charged by Catheriae Ellison, 2, Pillings-court, with assaulting her on the 16th inst. Complainant said that on that date she was standing in Dial-street when the defendant came up and called her a foul name, and because this was•resented, she commenced pulling her hair, and otherwise abused her.—The defendant who appeared in the court with a black eye, said that all the hair pulling was on the other side, and also showed the black eye as evidence of the complainant's ill-usage.— The magistrates considered that one was as bad as the other, and dismissed the case.

div.head: WARRINGTON. COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON. COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAL—Before Major •Pickmere (chairman) and Mr. W. Mortimer.

POACHING.—EdW—HI-13 io.oili-,w—a-s-eharged with commit- ting trespass on December, 4th, in Great Sankey, by entering upon land belonging to Lord Lilford in search of conies without having license to do so. Mr. J. White who prosecuted said that James Fairclough, a tenant of Lord Lilford met defendant in a field tenanted by Albert Kilshaw. ,Defendant was accompanied by a lurcher dog and had some nets in his hand, and had also a rabbit. Fairclough warned him to go off the land, but he imme- diately afterwards went into another plantation. The most important feature in this case was that the defend- ant, although warned off the land, defied Fal.lough by gem., into the other plantation. This would ha.te been an going offerioe had ,Paircleugh. asked his name and address, although it amounted to the same thing.— James Fairclough was called and corroborated Mr. White's statement.—The defendant was further charged with trespassing on land in the occupation of Thomas Perks, Burtonwood, in search of conies, on Dec.lth.-1 ; Mr. White said that defendant was seen by Thomas Perks near a rabbit burrawin his field, in company with ; I another man unknown- Perks went to him and told I him that he would have him summoned, to which he I replied that if that was so he would turn his ferret all along the ditch. He, however, did not put his throat into execution. He (Mr. White) was instructed topressi ' the case.—Perks who was called, corroborated the soiici- tor's statement and the magietrateainflicted a fine of .Qs. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. THEFY OF A. LIVE ,Grainger, Sankey', Bridges, was charged with stealing from Green Bank,:, Penketh, on December 15, a hen, valued 23. 6d., the pro- perty of John Newcomb. The complainant's son said that he met the defendant coming out of the gate of Green Bank at about 10 10 p.m. on the...l:sth inst.. with a bag on his back. Witness asked him what he had, but he simply replied "Good night," and went away. Later on in the night, he was brought back by the police, and a live hen in his possession was identified asi belonging to his Ovitness's) father.—P.C. Slingsby said that he met defendant in Penketh at 10 450 n the same night carrying a hag on his back. When asked what he had, he replied that he bad some potatoes which Mrs. Newcomb had given him. He was taken to New- comWs house, and it was then discovered that he had stolen the hen.—Defendant was fined 103. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. BICYCLE ON THE FOOTPATH—Peter Hill was fined 28. 6d. for riding his bicycle on the footpath in Orford, on the 7th inst.
bisnaMAPTB

RUNCORN PE ITT SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. James Handley. Doas.--For keeping a dog without a license, Thomas Baker, of King-st.' was fined 6d. and costs 9s. Bd.— Richard Abel, was fined 6d. and costs Bs. Bd. for having a dog at Halton wearing a collar without a name in- scribed upon it. CHARGE AGAINST A GREENGROCER.—Peter Gregory, greengrocer, 31, Ellesmere-t., was summoned for hav- ing in his possession at Runcorn Market, on the 2nd December, unjust weights. Inspector .lf. Timmins, found a lib. weight ten drachms light and a 21b. weight fifteen drachms light.—The defence was that the weights were never used, but had not mixed by the children.--:-A gne oflOs. and costs was imposed. DISCHACGED.—Jno. Worthington, of Mason-st., Run- corn, was charged with stealing 561bs. of coal, value 5d., at the Big Field, Norton,the property of John Jack- son, contractor. As the prosecutor did not press the case, the prisoner was discharged. , Row P. 4 THE TIIEATRIL KilgrassJl, Chancer-at. was bound over to be of good behaviour for six months, for fighting in the Theatre Royal on Saturday night. VAUB.ANCY.—Thos. Kenhaw was sentenced to seven days hard labour for begging in Regent-st., on Saturday night. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence fines were imposed upon Peter Carter, Wm. Shaw, Patrick Howarth, and .fotin Moores.

ACCIDENT AT A T. HELENS CHKINrCAL WORKS. On Wednesday, a youth named William Bellamy, of Chapel-st., St. Helens, employed in the laboratory at Messrs. M'Brido's chemical work. was severely crushed against the wall by one of ,the waggons in the siding c the works. He was removed to the Providence Hos. tal in an ambulance, where it was found one of his' was fractured in addition to oner injuries. TIM GAMBLE INSTITIITE.—APPOINTMENT OF ARCHITECTS. At the meeting of the Gamble Institute Committee, held at St. Helens, on Wednesday, it was docided to en- gage Messrs. Brig,cs ana Wolstenholme, of Blackburn, to whom the assessor for the premiums awarded the second prize for the designs of the new technical schools and free library, as the architects to carry out the execution of the new buildings. It is not anticipated that any decision respecting definite plans will be arrived at for some months.
t ospi- legs

ACCIDENT IN ST. HELENS STATION. Thomas Roughley, a middle-aged man employed by Mr, Waywell, butcher, Peter-st , St. Helens, met with a serious accident in St. Helens Station on Monday. The passenger train from Wigan had arrived at wenty minutes to three, and was about to leave for Liverpool, when Roughley hurriedly entered the station, and made as though he would throw a parcel to some persons who were looking out for him from the near window. To get to the carriage he had to jump down and cross one set of metals, and in jumping he fell, and his leg was broken, A goods train was coming on the line, hut it was stopped, the driver having noticed the occurrence, and Roughley was lifted out of danger, and carried by the company's servants to the hospital.

div.p: THE i,gIAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1893.

OLD BOYS v. Rut:coml.—Played at Wavertree, before a good attendance. The Runcornians were not strongly represented, and the team included several aspirants from the second string. Davies opened the play for Runcorn, and following the usual exchanges, play settled down in the Boys' half. The Runcornians carried the pack, but Harrison gathered the ball smartly and sent on be Watt, who ire turn parted to Taylor. The last named played raced on and ,on reaching Butterworth parted to Renshaw, who had no difficulty in scoring. Taylor took the place and landed a fine goal. Central play followed until a free kick against Runcorn placed the Boys in :nod position. Taylor and Bullen made further headway. Faulkner and Myers recovered the ground, and, by a pass forward, Robinson lost a 'good chance of scoring. Exchanges between Taylor and Butterworth brought central play , again. Wilsen and Bullen came nicely threugh the pack, but kicked into Butterworth's hands, with the result that the home 25 was reached. Loose forward play benefited the home players. Goold got away from a line out, but missed his final kick, arid Butterworth was enabled to save, but was injured in the attempt and was compelled to retire. Immediately on restarting the ball was placed for Taylor, but the attempt was charged down, and from the pack the Runcorn forwards raced off to within a few yards of the home line, Watt saved nicely, and Harrison cleared the danger with a kick and follow up. Taylor, who took up Butterworth's position kicked strongly down, and a long pressure was main- tained on the home defence. Prompt tackling robbed J. V. Taylor of a good opportunity to get off, and imme- diately afterwards J. Faulkner secured from the scrim- ' mega and ran in a clever try,Richardson'i attempt being a °spited one, the ball striking the upright and rebound- ing into play. Following the drop out, the Runcornians were again busy in attack. Morris essayed a run through but, unfortunately, handed forward, though a moment later packs were formed on the Boys' line. Taylor cleared with a lofty punt, and following up Bullen reached the Runcorn 25, where some keen forward play was witnessed. Harrison replied well to a free kick, and P. D. Wood further supplemented with a punt to touch near the Runcorn line. Half-time arrived without any further scoring, the Boys leading by points. Re- suming, Butterworth took his place in the team. The Boys bad the better of the opening exchanges, and Watt raced to within a yard of the line, where I he lost • possession, and the visiting forwards took the ball on their feet to midfield. By steady stages the visiting scrimmagers plodded on, and the Old Boys' de-1 fenders had a busy time. Off-side tackling, howevefr, lost their ground. After a brief visit to the Runcorn half, play located in front of the Boys' posts,where Bar. rigors and Ilinshaw pat in plenty of work in stemming strong rushes. Bell eventually got the ball away, and Butterworth in replying sent into touch at midfield. Roger Wilson got off strongly from the pack and reached, the opposing 25, where a collision with Butterworth again brought play to a standstill. Resuming, Renshaw was given a good chance, but failed to hold the ball. For a long time the Boys pressed their opponents, but at length Faulkner raced off and was not pulled down until well on the line, a touch down accruing shortly afterwards. Goold got away from the kick out and ran three parts of the field, but was overhauled, and Morris recovered the ground from he ensuing pack, when Armour tackled hire splendidly, which brought the game to a close. Result—Old Boys, 1 goal (5 points) ; Runcorn, 1 try (3 paints). Teams : Old Boys—A. C. Armour, back ;A. H. Renshaw, J. V. Taylor, and J. Bell, three-quarter backs ;A. R. Harrison, and H. C. Watt, half backs; R. P. la ilson, J. C. Goold, R. D. Wood. W. Smellie, R. M'Turk, R. S. Armour, E. W. Bullen, F. Graham, and A. H. Simpson, forwards. Run- corn—Butterworth, back ; Morris, Myers, and Richards, three-quarter backs; Robinson and Faulkner,half-backs ; Clark, J. Moore, Davies,Wiliiams,G. Moore, H. Thomas, R. Reece, J. Stubbs, and A. Taylor, forwards. RUNCORN VICTORIA Y. DITTON RECREATION FIRST.— 'The Vies journeyed to Ditton on Saturday with a very , weak team, being short of Shaw, Nichols, Johnson, INevitt, Simpson, Burton. and Coleshill. The Rees were 1, strongly represented. From a scrimmage Murray got hold, gave a kick and Nickson ran, awl picking up scored an easy try, the Some player converting. Shortly after Ditton scored another easy try, the place kick fail- ing. Murray in endeavouring to pick up knocked the ball on, and carried it over the line. The referee allowed the point, the place kick failing. This seemed to rouse the Vies, and the forwards taking the ball at their toes, attacked strongly, having hard luck several times. The Rocs scored all their points in the first quarter of an hour. After the change of ends the Vies again attacking their opponents strongly, forcing Bates to concede a minor. This brought no relief, Molyneux, Bettley, and Carruthers played a grand game. Carruthers getting the ball from Poole, ran well, passed to Johnson, who scored a meritorious try, Hammersley kicking a goal. At the finish of the game the Vies were in proximity to the Recs line. Result :—Ditton Rees, one goal two tries Runcorn Victoria, one goal four minors. RUNCORN VICTORIA " A "v. AprLETON.—At Runcorn. The Vies had a poor team owing to the heavy call being made upon them by the first team. Conliffe was very prominent at half back, Whitley scoring a try, Marsh , failed at goal. Whitley, Tatlock' and Derbyshire were , very prominent. A hard fought game resulted in a draw.—Runcorn Vice" A" one try, Appleton one try. ASSOCIATION.

WARRINSTON V. ALLHETON PAR.—This fixture was brought off on the Cricket ground at Arpley, the home team being minus the services of Mather, Linaker, Anthony, and Norman. The visitors started play, and Clarke relieved a rush ef the Park forwards and lb id put in a good run, and centering to Connor that player put his side ahead with an excellent shot. The homesters pressed almost continuously after this, but did not further augment the score, which at half time was War- rington 1 goal, Allerton Park nil. The homesters olayed hard during the second half, but this did not prevent the visitors from equalizing, the ball going through, off Clarke's foot. Warrington pressed towards the latter part of the game, but darkness prevented accurate shoot- ing and the final score was Warrington, 1 goal; Allerton Park, 1 goal. With four men off the homesters placed a good sound game, and were on the attack for the greater portion of the game. Warrington have not been tee`en on their own ground this season except by the doughty Evertonians, and this fact speaks for itself. WARRINGTON UNITED V. WARRINGTON ALEION.—This match was played or the ground of the latter before a goodly muster of spectators. Edwards kicked off forth.. United who at once began to take up the running but Griffiths spoiled their efforts by returning the b %II to midfield. Here give and take play followed, neither side being able to score. The United soon after pressed again and forced a corner which, however, nothing re- sulted,the play on both sides being very even. Half time Was shortly afterwards called, with the score United nil, Albion nil. On the restart the homesters made a good attack, but could not break through the defence of Houghton and Costello, both playing a wood full back game. The United, however, not to be denied, tried bard to force the game and succeeded in their efforts. taking the ball down the field. Dakin releiving the ball registered a neatly shot goal, the Albion goal-keeper having no chance with it. This reverse seemed to waken the homesters up, who tried hard to score, their efforts being, however, frustrated by the visitors' backs. Play was in midfield when time was called with the score unaltered, the final reading—Warrington United, 1 goal; Warrington Albion, 0.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON T. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

The return match between these teams was played on Saturday, on the Wilderspool-road ground. There was but a moderate attendance, to which the poor record of the visiting team was no doubt due. The only change in the Warrineton team from that which gave the Swin- tonians such a fright on the previous Saturday, was, that Potts went to the centre, and Carey to the outside left. The Rangers who were assisted by P. R. Lawless of Warrington, kicked off towards the pavilion goaLand the opening was of a very slow character until Lawless by a punt transferred play to the •Warrington -.25. The Bates and Potts, however, quickly recovered the lost ground and the Rangers' lines were threatened time after time. Lightfoot relieved, but Jolley again secured and was within a yard off the line when Smith kicked dead. From the drop out, over eagerness lost Warrington a splendid chance of scoring. For the first time in the ' match the local three-quarters now had a chance cf ! distinguishing themselves, and after the Bates had passed, Pdtts, DMUS, and Massey took up the running, the last-named being well cared for by Walker. Par- lane saved his side brilliantls,and although Carey mulled at half-way he soon recovered and the Rangers were hard defending once more. At length after a drop-out, "Smack" Bate cleverly dodged Parlane, and scored near the corner. Nevins failed to augment. Parlane dribbled well mother drop-out, but Berry soon had the ball back at its original end, and Heesom was then called upon for the first time in replying to Hargreaves. Touch was found close to the line, but Lawless upset a movement of the home team by intercepting a pass. However. the Rangers could not keep the locals back; and the Bates again had the ball on the goal line, and from another scrimmage here John Bate dodged prett- ily over for the second try, Fair. Turner this time failing to utilize a difficult place. From the drop-out, Carey made a brilliant run through his opponents, and Dono- hue also made some short sprints. At this point John Bate was hurt, and retired for the remainder of the game. Evans went to half back, and amid great laugh- ter, Turner was placed three-quarter. He, however, con- trary to all expectations proved that he was not wanting in the requirements of this position,and in the first scrim- mage formed he accepted a pass from Evans in fine style but Carey failed to take advantage of the opening and tall time arrived with the score of Warrington two tries to nil. Atter the interval the visitors rarely got out of their own 25. Turner was loudly applauded for some clever play, passing judiciously, and helping to maintain the defence in first-class style. The eccentricities of the locals caused endless amusement, and the match was looked upon at this juncture as representing a burlesque of Rugby football. The Rangers took advantage of Warrington's relaxation and crossed the centre line, but they had barely time to get an insight of the strange territory before Potts effected a brilliant rue, but he was pulled up on the line. However, the effort led up to good results, for passim, by the half-backs saw Turner accepting a pass in grand style and scoring a meritorious try at the corner, a point which he failed to augment. Heesom was twice applauded for some clever play, but a penalty kick against the visitors was bacliy utilized. More threatened, but this was an expiring, effort. The light was too bad to allow of the players being dis- tinguished, but from what could be gleaned the last few minutes saw Massey effecting a fine run and passing to Bailey, for that capital forward to score. Final :—War- rington, four tries ; Manchester Rangers. nil. Warring- ton : F. Heesom, back; C. Potts, P. Carey, J. W. Evans, and .1. T, Massey, three-quarter backs ; John T. Bate and James Bate, half-backs; Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, J. Berry, T. Donohue, W. Nevins, J. Taylor, J. Buckley, and E. Bailey, forwards. Manchester Rangers : Smith, back ; ,Lightfoot, Lawless, Morris, and Walker, three- quarters ; W. Hargreaves and Parlane, half-backs ; J. and A. Hargreaves, Connor, Birk.s, Crossdale, McLachlan, Emery, and Wood, forwards. STOCKTON HEITZ T. WARRINGTON RANIIIRRS.—PIayed I at Stockton Heath on Saturday. Stockton Heath kicked !off, and immediately pressed, and from a pass by Smith, Baldwin nearly scored, Hamblett saving in the nick of time. Stockton Heath secured a free kick, and, follow- ing up, rushed the ball over the Rangers' line Smith grounding the leather. Glover, as usual, landed the goal. From the kick-out the Rangers played up better, Monks especialiy, but Longmore was very safe, and returned well. Play settled in the Rangers' 25, when the Rangers were penalized, and Broady taking the kick dropped a splendid goal. Half time score was, Stockton Heath, two goals ; Renews, nil. On restarting the Ran.

to score, but the defence was too secure, and they were forced to beat a retreat. Shortly before the call of time, Broady, securing the ball, dropped his second goal. Stockton Heath proved winners by three goals to nil. - -

WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S V. HELSIM—Played On the latter's ground. The hemesters won the toss. The Saints started the ball, play settling at centre, the home team having slightly the best of the game. The Saints' forwards, however, improved and completely outplayed their opponents, giving Woods and Bennett every oppor- tunity of showing their smartness behind the pack. The score at half-time was 3-2-0 to nil. On turning the Saints attaoked, Woods starting some splendid passing, the ball travelling across the field on several occasions and the home lines being crossed frequently. Final score :—St. Mary's, 8-2-0; Flelsby, nil. WIDNES T. STOCKPORT.—PIayed at Widnes 1-efore 2,000 spectators. Stockport had several men away, but Widnes had a strong team. Haslain kicked off for Stockport, Drummond returned well, and Widnes were soon in Cher opponents' quarters. Clarke rushed over, but the ball was brought bark for offside. Several scrimmages ensued on the Stockport line, but their for- wards at length transferred play by a grand dribble. Cazke broke up the rush. Stockport were several times penalized for informalities in the ecritumage,but Widnes , could not get rid of thevisitors' attack. Barber made a fine run, but Peters failed to take his pass, and a good chance was lost. The home team's combination was excellent, but the Stockport defence was very safe in their tackling, and prevented any score. Drummond put in some grand work at half back, and was the instig- ator of all the Widnes attacks. Some gra-ad passing be- tweealroehey, Alforde, and Clarke ended in the last- named scoring a fine try. Barber kicked a goal from the place. From the centre kick Stockport attacked strongly. Toohey brought relief, and by a series of scrim- mages Stockport would not play an open gome. Widnes took the play to the other end, hut they could not and an opening_ Half-time score ;—Widnes one goal, Stock- port nil. The 4ay during the second half as very smart, and the home team had the best of the cause throughout Final result ;.Widnes 2 goals 2 tries,Stock- port nothing,

PIQUE/STU A. F. C. v. LTllll.—The return match be- tween these two clubs came off at Penketh on Saturday. The visitors kicked off against a strong wind with the hill in their favour. The play was of a fast and exciting nature and evenly contnted, each goal being visited in turn. The home right got away and from a long pass by Boswell, W. Parson scored the first goal. The visi- tors made several good rushes down the field only to be driven back by Bowyer's huge kicks, the home forwards again got to work and by splendid combined play reached the visitors goal when from a centre by Bowyer, %V. Parson again scored. The interval arrived with the home team two goals in their favour. On resuming, the home forwards soon put the visitors on the defence,play was carried into midfield where Highain kicked to the visitors' back who failed to return and Dunbill taking advantage scored a third goal. The visitors play was getting weak and the home forwards playing splendid combination worked their way again down the field where Bowyer shot, and the ball resting between the custodians'a feet, W. Parson rushed it through thus putt- ing on No 4. The visitors began to play rough and fouls became pretty frequent and on many occasions they had to be cautioned by the referee. A strong rush enabled the visitors to score their only goal. The rest of the game was anything but pleasant, and from a scrimmage in front of the visitors goal N. Parson scored. Shortly afterwards the whistle blew for the call of time when the score stood. Penketh five goals, bymm one goal.

POST OFFICN T. BANK-STRINIT MISSION A.F.C.—The above teams met on tho Post Office ground on Saturday. The P.O. started and alter five minutes play Bank-street scored from a serimmage near the goal. The P.O. now worked harder and as a result of their efforts, Hallows equalized with a splendid shot. Even play followed, and then the visitors pressed. Another goal eventually falling to their credit. The P.O. started off with a dash and almost immediately forced a corner, from which Cox once more made the scores even. Half time: Post Office, 2; Bank-street, 2. The Post Office pressed the greater part of the sec md half, and, adding another coal by Cox, won a pleasint game. Final : Post Office. 3; Bank-street, 2.

div.head: NEW IND-aTRY FOR, WARRINGTON.
div.p: A NEW IND-aTRY FOR, WARRINGTON.

still another has been added to the multifarious industries of Warrington, which earn for the town the title of " Little London." • The latest addition to the manufactures of the place has been made by Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., and takes the form of an iron and brass bedstead manufactory. The premises occupied by the Company are those lately in the tenancy of Messrs.Murgatroyd.and Company, School Brow. The industry is the only one of its cdaracter in the locality, and, indeed, there are few places out of Birmingham in which the manufactur- ing of iron and brass bedsteads is carried on. However, as the demand for this class of bed- stead is increasing, both at home and abroad, we may expect to see similar enterprises spring up in many new places. Messrs. Monks, Hall aiad Co., hat had their places fitted up with all the latest mechanical requisites, and have engaged a staff of experienced artisans. Probably with a further idea of seeing to tile quality of the articles they turn out, the,companv manufacture their own rods, an almost unheard of thing with other manufacturers. This has created widit may almost be described as another new industry, which finds employment for a large numoer of men. The bedsteads, in addition to cots and chairs' are constructed of iron reds, and are fitted up in the im- , proved " dovetail" fitting style. The rods are manufactured from pig iron, at the forge, at tithertons Quay, and subsequently the articles pass through four departments before they reach the stage of completion. From what we can gather tile industry is likely to grow to a considerable extent in Warrington. The company have already commenced to supply merchants in most of the leading towns of the north, and expect shortly to commence an export trade. The establishment is already capable of turning out 600 bedsteads per week.
MR. S. S. WOODS, M.P., AT HAYDOCK.

div.head: ALLEGED VIOLATION ON ME ROSEBERY
div.p: ALLEGED VIOLATION ON ME ROSEBERY
The Prizes will be awarded every month during 1894, in each of the 8 Districts, as under:—
AGREEMENT. THE EMPLOYER,' LIABILITY BILL.

A largely attended meeting of Haydock miners was held on Wednesday night, at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, to consider certain griev- ances alleged to exist at the collieries belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Limited. The miners state that the management are breaking the agreement come to at the Rosebery conference by inter- fering with Lhe field prices and the old rate of wages. It is alleged that private reductions have been taken off the yardage allowances, and that the firm are overstock- ing the collieries, thereby making it impossible for the men working to get a living wage. Mr. S. Woods, M.P., I and Mr. E. Walkden addressed the meeting. Mr. Woods referred at great length to the alleged disputes. He said that at the Wood Pit he was informed that there were over 140 sets of tallies, meaning that double that number of men were working. The pit could only wind suffici- ent coal to give wages to the men on ninety sets of ttllies. He also dealt with the wages question and the Empliyers' Liability Bill, and thanked the Government ir the determined efforts they were making to pass a bill to give due and proper protection to life and limb. Th?. Lancashire miners had decided to inform Mr. . Asquith and Lord Salisbury of the true opinion and views they held on the question as expressed in the terrible strike of 1880, and in hundreds of meetings since that they were opposed to any contracting out. They pee- ferred the safety which the provision of the Act' gave to any monetary considerations which might be got from an outside association or insurance company. In con- clusion, Mr. Woods urged the miners not to stand still, as there were great things that had yet to be accom- plished for the working man. The following resolution was unanimously carried :—" That this meeting of Haydock miners desires to express unbounded gratitude in respect of the settlement of the recent coal strike, especially as it has prominently brought before the pub- IL; of this country the question of a minimum wage,and that the policy of the Miners' Federation has triumphed in the face of the strongest opposition. We also desire to thank the Government and its loyal supporters for the determioed manner in which they have championed ti e Employers' Liability Bill through the House of Corn- moos, and hereby pledge eurselves to give them every assistance in our power until they carry this measure through Parliament into law." At the close of the meeting Mr. Woods announced the decision of the House of Commons on the Lords' amend- ments to the Liability Bill. The greatest satisfaction was expressed when it was known that the Commons hal condemned the Lords' amendments by the large majority of 62.
--fiegar-ding the disputes at Haydock Collieries, we understand that Mr. Woods will communicate with the owners, and it is hoped that a satisfactory settlement will be arrived at.

div.p: EA.RLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
PRIMITIVE METHODIST M lITITA.L IMPROVEMENT

CLASS. The weekly meeting of the above class was held on Monday evening. The Rev. E. R. Davies pre- sided, ana there was a fair attendance of members. A paper was read by Mr. R. Dring on "Poverty, and some of its causes." Mr. Dring dealt with the question at some length, giving as some of the causes, early marriage, gambling and drunkenness. The discussion on the paper was opened by Mr. J. Taylor, and continued by Messrs. George, Clarke, Oilman, Holleyock and Traverse.

ST. JOHN'S CHURCH. A congregational tea party and concert in con- nection with St. John's Church, Earlestown, vvis held in the Parochial Mission Hall on Saturd.,y evening. There was a fair number present at tea which sas presided over by lady members of the congregation. After tea a concert was given, the ' Rev. E. W. W. Kaye presiding in the unavoidable absence of the Vicar. A good programme of songs, glees, &c., was given by the following: Misses M. Conway, Mayhew, Phillips, Barcroft, Messrs. Ban- ton, W. Mayhew, and J. Banton. Mr. G. Weeks efficiently accompanied throughout.

GOOD TBMPLART. The usual weekly session of the Mope of Earles- town Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the Co- operative Hell, Earlestown on Monday evening. Bro. A. Morris C.T. presided and there was a good attendance of members. Bro. O. Clarke L.D. read a ' circular from the Temperance Orphanage soliciting donations, and Bros. Clarke and Ratcliffe were ap- pointed to collect on behalf of same. An interest- ing paper, entitled " A trip to Mona" was read by Bro. Clarke, and a discussion followed. A vote of thanks to the essayist concluded an enjoyable even- ing.

THE HOLIDAYS AT EARLBSTOWIC For Christmastide the London and North-Western Company's Wagon Works will close on Saturday at noon until nine o'clock on Thursday morning. The Vulcan Foundry Company will close on Friilay evening, until Wednesday January 3rd, and Messrs. T. and T. Vicars, will close on Fliday might until Wednesday morning next. All the tradesmen in the town having posted notices that their establish- ments will close on Boxing day. The Railway Company have made arrangements for cheap trains to the principal centres, and there is no doubt full 'advantage will be taken of the opportunity.

EARLESTOWN TONTINE SOCIETY. The annual general meeting of the members of the Pride of Earleitown Tontine Society, was held on Saturday evening in the club room, Viaduct Hotel. There was a good attendance, Mr. A. Great- ( holder, presiding. In the absence, through indis- position, of Mr. C. Audley the secretary,Mr. H. Parr ; ! read the statement of accounts for the pest year. The total receipts amounted to £94 Is. 7d. and the expenditure to £6O 5-., of this amount £4l 13s. 41., had been paid t) the sick members, the balance in hand being £33 164. 711. It would be disposed of by dividing £3O 12s. 7d. amongst 58 members at 108. 7d. each, the remainder £34s. being carried to the reserve fund. The balance sheet was unani- mously adopted. The election of officers resulted in Mr. A. Greatholder being elected chairman,Messrs J. Farragher and T. Walton stewards, Messrs. J. Bolton and J. Muscroft, auditors, Mr. C.Audley,sec. and Mr. Sharp, treasurer. The retiring committee were re-appointed. MASONIC INSTALLATION AT ASHTON. On Tuesday last, at the Gerard Arms Hotel, Ashton, the members of Faith Lodge, 484, of Free- masons, celebrated the festival of st. John, when Bro. F. Harwood, P.M., was again installed W.M., by Bro. A. Skeen, 1.P.M., assisted by Bro. P. Aspinall, P.M. The newly appointed W.M., after- wards investO his officers for the ensuing year, as follows :—Bro. Skeen, A. Jackson. S.W., W. Gilbert, 1. W., Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, chap., J. Simp- kin, P.M. 13; ov. O.P. treasurer, J. N. Paterson, P.M. P.P.D.G. D.C. secretary, T. Nevitt, P.M. D.C. W. ' Leather. 0., T. Richie, S.D., T. Howard, J.D., J. Watson, 1.G., R. J. Berry, C. G. Guinness, C. H. Astle and T. A. Frost, stewards, W. Storror, Tyler. At the conclusion of the masonic business, the brethren sat down to a sumptuous banquet, catered for by the host, Bro. Armstrong, at which the usual loyal and masonic toasts were heartily drunk by the brethren. The W.M. in the name of the lodge had the pleasing duty of presenting Bro. Skeen, LP j . M., with a handsome P.M. eWel. Many brethren, and invited guests were prevented from being present through influenza.

div.p: SONS OF TBMPIZRANCE,..

- The usual fortnightly meeting of Samuel Morley Sect ion of Cadets was held in the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening, at 7 o'clock, Bro. F. Parr, W.A.. presiding. Two new members were proposed for membership. This flourishing society has, dur- ing the year, doubled its membership, which now numbers nearly 70 members. The following mem- bers have gained prizes for proposing the most new members : For the year, Olive Clare; for the last half year, John Birkenhead, first prize; Hannah Pickett, second prize; Charles Earlarn, third prize. This society is the best and most economical society in the district. The Britians Need Division met at 7.30, Bro. S. Marsh, W.A., presiding. One new member was proposed. After the opening ceremony the following officers were elected for the next half- year: W.P. S. Foden, W.A. J. French, R.S. E. Wolfe, F.S. J. Prenot, A.F.S. H. Jenkins, Con. R. Yorke, Con. J. Crompton, I.S. W. Kennings, O.S. S. Heaton, Treas. J. Judson, Chap. 0. Pickett, Patron of Cadets, J. Judson, assistant Patrons, 0. Pickett, William Wheatley, Division Reporter. 0. Pickett, Auditors, W. Pearson, W. Wheatley. The meeting was closed at 9.30.

THE WISE THOUGHT.
SKETCHES OF IRISH CHARACTER. BY Mrs. S. C. HALL

She was sitting under the shadow of a fragrant lime tree that overhung a very ancient well ; and, as owni ltyh its wo fh oehr N"Jew'sorali harp, chry "hthe the water fell into her pitcher, she was minglin instrument the nes learned to play. She was a merry maiden of sweet seventeen; a rustic belle, as well as a rustic beauty, and a "terrible coquette ;" and as she had what in Scotland they call a " toeher, " in England a "dowry, " and in Ireland a "pretty penny o' money," it is scarcely necessary to s ate, in addition, that she had—a bachelor. Whether the tune— which was certainly given in alto—was or was not designed as a summons to her lover, I cannot take upon myself to say; hut her lips and fingers had not been long occupied, before her lover was at her side. "We may as well give it up., Morris Donovan," she said somewhat abruptly; look, 'twould be as easy to twist the top off the great hill of llowth, as make father and mother agree about any one thing. They've been playing the rule of contrary these twenty years, and it's not likely they'll take a turn now." "It's mighty hard, so it is," replied handsome Morris, that married people can't draw together. Norah, darlint ! that wouldn't be the way with us. It'd one we'd be in heart and sowl, and an example of love and " "Folly, " interrupted the maiden laughing. Morris, Morris, we've quarrelled a score o' times already; and a bit of a breeze makes life all the pleasanter. Shalt talk about the merry jig I danced with Phil Kennedy, or repeat what Mark Doolen said of me to Mary Grey ?—eh, Morris ?" "Leave joking, now, Norry; God only knows how I love you'" he said, in a voice broken by emotion: I'm yer equal as far as money goes ; and no young farmer in the country can tell a better stock to his share than mine; yet I don't pretend to deserve you for all that; only, I can't help say- ing that, vhen we love each other (now don't go to contradict me, Norry, because ye've as good as owned it over and over again), and yer father agreeable, and all, to think that yer mother, just out of divilinent, should be putting betwixt as for no reason upon earth, only to "spite" her lawful husband, is what sets me mad entirely, and shows her to be a good-for—" "Stop, Mister Morris," exclaimed Norah, laying her hand upon his mouth, so as to effectually pre- vent a sound escaping; it's my mother ye're talk- ing of, and it would be ill-blood, as well as ill-bred, to hear a word said against an own parent. Is that the pattern of yer manners, sir ; or did ye ever hear me turn my tongue against one belonging to you?" "I ask yer pardon, my own Norah," he replied meekly, as in duty bound; for the sake of the lamb, we spare the sheep. Why not? and I'm not going to gainsay, but your mother--" " The least attid's the soonest mended l" again in- terrupted the impatient girl. 'Good even, Morris, and God bless you; they'll be after missing me within, and it's little mother thinks where I am." "Norah, above all the girls at wake or pattern, I've been true to you. We have grown together, and since ye were the height of a rose-bush, ye have been dearer to me than anything else on earth. Do, Norah, for the sake of our young hearts' love, do think if there's no way to win your mother over. If ye'd take me without her leave, sure it's nothing I'd care for the lois 9f thousands, let alone what ye've got. Dearest Norah. think; since you'll do nothing withoutther consent, do think—for once be serious, and don't laugh." "I'm not going to laugh, Morris," replied the little maid at last, after a very long pause ; I've got a wise thought in my head for once. His reve- rence, your uncle, you say, spoke to father—to speak to mother about it? I wonder (and he a priest) that he hadn't more sense ! Sure, mother was the man ; but I've got a wise thought. Good night, dear Morris; good night." The lass sprang lightly over the fence into her own garden, leaving her lover perdu at the other side, without possessing an idea of what her wise thought' might be. When she entered the kitchen, matters were going on as usual—her mother bustling in style, and as cross "as a bag of weasels." "Jack Clary," said she, addressing herself to her husband, who sat quietly in the chimney-corner smoking his doodeen, it's well ye've got a wife who knows what's what I God help me! I've little good of a husband, barring the name I Are ye sure Black Dien's in the stable?' The sposo nodded. "The cow and the calf, had they fresh straw ?" Another nod. "Bad cess to ye, 'can't ye use your tongue, and answer a civil question ?" continued the lady. "fly dear,'' he replied, sure one like you has enough talk for ten. ' This very just observation was, like most truths, so disagreeable, that a severe storm would have followed, had not Norah stepped up to her father and whispered in his ear, "I don't think the stable door is fastened." Mrs. Clary caught the sound, and in no gentle terms ordered her husband to attend to the comforts of Black Nell. "I'll go with father myself and see," eta Norah. "That's like my own child, always careful," observed the mother, as the father and daughter closed the door. "Dear father," began Norah, 'it isn't altogether about the stable I wanted ye, but--but—the priest said something to you to-day about--Morris Dono- van." " ITcs, darling, and about yerself, my sweet Norry." "Did ye speak to mother about it ?" "No, darling, she's been so cross all day. Sure Ago through a dale for peace and quietness. If I was like other men, and got drunk, and wasted, it might be in rason ; but— As to Morris, she was very fond of the boy till she found that / liked him; and then, my jewel, she turned like sour milk all in a minute. I'm afraid even the priest 'll get no good of her." "Father, dear father," said Norah, suppose ye were to say nothing, about it, good or had, and just retend to take a sudden dislike to Morris, and let the o her himself, she'd come round." p "Oriest speak tut of opposition to me, eh 1" yes.., "And let her gain the day then 7—that would be cowardly, replied the farmer, drawing himself up. ,No, I won't. "Father, dear, you don't understand," said the cunning lass; sure ye're for Morris; and when we are—that is, if—l mean—suppose—father, you know what I mean,' she continued, and luckily the twilight concealed her blushes—' if that took place, it's you that would have yer own way." "True for ye, Norry, my girl, true for ye ; I never thought of that before !" and, pleased with the idea of tricking' his wife, the old man fairly capered for joy. 13nt stay a while—stay; aisy, aisy he recommenced ; bow am I to manage? Sure the priest himself will be here to-morrow moniing early; and lie's out upon a station now, so there's no speaking with him; he's no way quick either : we'll be bothered entirely if he comes in on a suddent." "Leave it to me, dear father—leave it all to inc I" exclaimed the animated girl ; only pluck up a spirit, aril whenever Morris's name is mentioned, abuse him—but not with all yer heart, father—only from the teeth out." When they re-entered, the fresh-boiled potatoes sent a warm curling steam to the rafters of the lofty kitchen; they were poured out into a large wicker kish, and on the top of the pile rested a plate of coarse white salt; noggins of buttermilk were filled on he dresser; and on a small round table a cloth 14sziar.fada-al4-auLle-draLail.ll,9-aZAALCUllgaanzo

delicale repast which the farmer's wife was herself preparing. "What's for supper, mother?" inquired Norah, as she drew her wheel towards her, and employed her fairy foot in whirling it round. "Plaguy snipeens, " she replied; bits o' bog chickens, that you've always such a fancy for; Barney Learey kilt them himself," "So I did," said Barney, grinning ;• and that stick wid a hook, of Morris Donovan's, is the finest thing in the world for knocking 'em down." "If Morris Donovan's stick touched them, they shan't come here," said the farmer, striking the poor little table such a blow with his clenched hand, as made not only it, but Mrs. Clary jump. "And why so, pray ?" asked the dame. "Because nothing belonging to Morris, let alone Morris himself, shall come into this house," replied ' Clary • he's not to my liking anyhow, and there's no good in his bothering here after what he won't; pt. ' " Excellent !" thought Norah. ^ Lord save us I" ejaculated Mrs. Clary, placed the grilled snipe on the table, what's °erne to the man?' Without heeding his resolution she was proceeding to distribute the savoury 'birdeene when, to her astonishment, her usually tame hus- band threw the dish and its contents into the flsmes; the good woman absolutely stood for a moment aghast. The calm, however, was not of long dura- tion. She soon rallied, and commenced hostilities.: "How dare you, ye spalpeen, throw away aiNy of Cod's mate after that fashion, and I to the fore? What do you mane, I say ?" " I mane, that nothing touched by Morels Donovan shall come under this roof ; and if I catch that girl of mine looking at the same side o' the road he walks on, I'll tear the eyes out of her head, and send her to a nunnery I" "You will! And dare you to say that to my face, to a child o' mine I You will, will ye ?—we'll see, my boy! I'll tell ye what, if I like, Morris Donovan shalt come into this house, and what's more, be master of this house; and that's what you never had the heart to be yet, ye poor ould snail !" So saying, Mrs. Clary endeavoured to rescue from the fire the hissing remains of the burning snipe. Norah attempted to assist her mother; but Clary, lifting her up, somewhat after the fashion of an eagle rais- ing a golden wren with its claw, fairly put her out of the kitchen. This was the signal for fresh hostili- ties. Mrs. Clary stormed and stamped ; and Mr. Clary persisted in abusing not only Morris, but Morris's uncle, Father Donovan, until at last the farmer's helpmate swore, ay, and roundly too, by cross and saint, that, before the next sunset, Norah Clary should be Norah Donovan. I wish you could have seen Norry's eye, dancing with joy and exultation, as it peeped through the latch-hole; it sparkled more brightly than the richest diamond in our monarch's crown, for it was filled with hope and love.

The next morning, before the sun was fully up, he was throwing hi early beams over the glowing cheek of Novell Clary ; for her " wise thought" had prospered; and she was hastening to the trysting tree, where, "by chance," either morning or even- ing. she generally met Morris Donovan. I don't know how it is, hut the moment the course of true love " runs smooth," it becomes very uninteresting., except to the parties concerned. So it is now left for me only to say; that the Maiden, after a due and proper time consumed in teasing and tantalising her intended, told him her saucy plan, and its result. And the lover hastened, upon the wings of love (which I beg my readers clearly to understand, are swifter and stronger in Ireland than in any other country), to apprise the priest of the arrangement, well knowing that his reverence loved his nephew, and niece that was to be (to say nothing of the wed- ding supper, and the profits arising therefrom), toe well, not to aid their merry jest. - What bustle, what preparation, what feasting, 1 what dancing, gave the country folk enough to talk about during the happy Christmas holidays, I cau. not now describe. The bride of course looked Lively, and "sheepish ;" and the bridegroom—but bridegrooms are always uninteresting. One fact, hOwever, is worth recording. When Father Dono- van concluded the ceremony, before the bridal kiss had passed, Farmer Clary, without any reason that his wife oould discover, most indecorously sprana up, seized a shilelah of stout oak, and, whirling it rapidly over his head, shouted, "Carry me out I by the powers she's beat! we've won the day I—ould Ireland for ever Success, boys ! she's beat, she's beat !" The priest, too, seemed vastly to enjoy this extemporaneous effusion, and even the bride laughed outright. Whether the good wife discovered the plot or not, I never heard; but of this I am certain, that the joyous Norah never had reason to repent her "wise thought."
TIIE TALE OF A LOST WEDDING RING.

"Well, my dears," said Uncle George, looking round on the group of young people gathered round the fire on Christmas Eve, "talking of the way things are lost and found, I'll tell you a story of the strange way your Aunt Emily's wedding. ring was lost just after we were married. "I had been gazetted captain to my regiment, which was then stationed in India, and as I had to join at once, I wasn't going to leave Emily behind ; so we just got married, and started off by P. and 0. to join the regiment. Well, on the day we got to Aden we were both standing at the port- hole of our cabin looking down into the water, and I was holding Emily's hand, when suddenly there was a splash in the sea, and a shriek from your Aunt Emily, 'Oh, my wedding-ring !' and there, sure enough, if it' hadn't slipped off and gone to the bottom. "She was inconsolable. It was 80 unlucky: no other ring would ever be the same, &c. ; but at last she was pacified, and I promised to buy her the best in Bombay when we got there, and so I "Well, after we had been in India a few months, Emily's health broke down, and she was ordered home, and I was ordered to a distant station in the hills, where I couldn't take her, so, after a great deal of worry, the only thing I could decide en to do was to accompamy her as far as Aden, and let her go to England alone to wait until I got my long leave. The night we got there we went and had an oyster supper, and when I opened the fourth oyster, what do you think I found?" "Not the ring ? " broke from all the group round the fire, in various accents of astonishment and incredulity. "No—an oyster!"
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23,x1893.

div.head: CHRISTMAS WEEK IN DENMARK.
div.p: CHRISTMAS WEEK IN DENMARK.

Nowhere are good old Christmas customs more pleasantly observed than in Jutland. Even the little birds of the air are no forgotten. A small wheatsheaf, saved on purpose from the preceding harvest, is laid in the garden overnight on Christ- mas Eve, in order that they also may eat and rejoice. The farming folks believe that at midnight on Christmas Eve the cattle all rest together and stand upright ; and on the following day they and the hors, and in particular the watch-dog, are fed with the best of everything by these reverent, simple-minded, tradition-loving people. From the 25th of December to the new year no one works, and all the young people dance. And the new year is not only danced in, but—at least, in certain places—it is doe in, every one who can get hold of firearms discharging them at Ids neigh- bour's window by way of wishing- him a happy new year.

How TO " KEEP " CHRISTMAS. —Don't spend it anywhere. div.head: PROVIDING FOR A" RAINY DAY": A SUGGESTION.
div.p: PROVIDING FOR A" RAINY DAY": A SUGGESTION.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me a space in your valu- able paper to express my humble opinion on the late coal strike and the lesson to be learned. No doubt you will agree with me that such a deplorable state as then ex- isted in the town of Warrington ought to impress upon us the necessity of seeking remedial measures in oader to prevent such a calamity falling upon us in the future. And now, Sir, with a little indulgence I will suggest a way by which to cope with the distress which might again be so prevalent in .our midst. Let us as Warringtonians adopt a policy of helping ourselves, and not depend too much upon other people to help us. Let there be a fund established in our town; each per- son, male or female, to contribute one penny per week towards that fund, and let the monies remaining from the late distress fund go for the purpose of establishing this fund, and by that means we shall be in a position to defend .ourselves in times of emergency.--Yours,
JOHN WM. MUSKETT.

Sir,—Mr. J. C. Dalton, in yours of Saturday last, has the audacity ,to still doubt my plain, straightforward proofs, copies of the correspondence being,in my posses- sion, and which several people in Warrington have seen. The persecuting clause was found by the three gentlemen I named, viz,, ,Dr. Cumming, Admiral Jia.rcourt, Sir John Maxwell. They saw it and read it, unrnutilated in the Cardinal's own Pontifical, as submitted to them at the episcopel 'residence, Golden-square. St. Liguori, whose writings Manning and Wiseman appi used and so did the Papacy by _making him into a saint, says However, letoaths be ever so valid, they CALI be re- laxed by the church." Loyola wrote:o That we may in all things attain the truth, that we may not grr in anything, we ought ever to hold it a fixed ,principle that what I see white I be- lieve to be blaek,if the Hierarchical Church defineaso to be." Wiseman prefixed a preface to such trash ascthis, yet Mr. D.advises me to read other books besides Jewel, Blakeney, &c. The,autie of Norfolk, on November 28, 1850, wrote F should think that many must led as we do, that ultramontane opinions are totally incompa- tible with allegiance to our sovereign (Queen Victoria) and with our constitution." Pope Gregory XVI.on Auenst 15, 1632, wrote We cannot hold in toolmuch ho'rrer liberty of opinion and the Press, and particularly this maxim, that every elan ought to enjoy liberty of eori- science." Mr. D. does this , look like tolerance, and re- member these are the words ()fa see:tailed infallible Pope, supreme Pontiff, sometimes called Lord God the Pope Pope Pius IX. in September, 1E54 declared that Ito- manism, with all its rights (?) ought to be exclusively , dominant, in such sort that every other worship shall be: banished and interdicted. Mr. •D. does this not look like persecution? Cardinal Manning said that if Pro- testantism could be destroyed in England, " tne whole world lies open to the church's will" (August 6, 1859). That Protestants should be punished bylaw, thst they should be fined, imprisoned, hanged, for Christ does not forbid heretics (i.e., Protestants) to be ten away and put to death, and therefore, heretics in common with all 'other malefactors, may and ought. by public authority, either spiritual or t-mporal, to be chastised or executed. , for proof for these teachings of Popery, see • " Madern Avernus," published by Hatahards in .1874.. Page 65. The author is still living, and well able to defend his book. Are heretics justly punished with death-? Thomas Aquinas, a so-called canonized saint, says Yes, be- cause forgers of money or other disturbers of the State are justly punished with death, theretore. also, Leretics (not heresies) who are forgers of the faith (?) and,_as ex- perience testifies, grievously disturb the State." The same is proved from the c-aidemnation of the 14-ch Article of John Huss, in the Council of Constance--Dens,vol. 2, pp. 83-89. Now, Mr.D. this is a class book in Maynooth , College. Daniel French,barrister,the greatest controye.r- sialist the Papacy has had this century, on the .--4.ltith evening's discussion with Dr. Cumming said ;—" I ask of my antagonist (Dr. Cumming) where, in what book, is to be found one word relative to the 'baptism of in- fants ? Now, I ask, unless tradition come to the rescue of my learned friend, by what refining ingenuity will he call upon the Bible to protect him in baptizing-infants, that cannot give the answer, that cannot exclaim, ' I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.'" Net Mr.D tells us Christ instituted Popery. Christ never instituted infant sprinkling or dipping.—Yours truly, R. FOULKES. frodsharn, December 19, 1893.

div.head: LIFE IN SOUTH AFRIC4.-AN INTERESTING
div.p: LIFE IN SOUTH AFRIC4.-AN INTERESTING

LETTER. Sir,—Perhaps it would be of interest tp...a few of your readers to learn that recently I succeeded in capturing a large snake named "Cobra di Capella" at " Camps Bay " where I had been rusticating. This is a suburb of Capetown, situated between Table Mountain, and the Lions Head, a picturesque, well wooded seaside summer resort, which is a place well patronised during the sum- mer months by people who are anxious to get away Irani business to the peace and quiet of the country. There have been as many as sixty tents erected in the vicinity, and people who reside in Capetewn look forward to the summer so that they may enjoy a well earned holiday in the cool bracing atmosphere and indulge in sea bathing, which is much appreciated after the oppressive heat experienced in town. Some people make a practice of camping out merely to sleep at Camps Bay after the toil of the day, the train and tram running from Capetown to Seapoint, making it an easy journey to the camp. Others again camp out for a month or two and all speak highly of the benefits they derive from the change. Not having been well and thinking a rest would prove bene- ficial, I decided to join with two old friends of mine, Messrs. C. C. H. Brown and F. M. S. Pennell, late of the Derby Post Office, and now holding appointments in the postal service here. They very kindly offered to put me up in their tent as long as! wished to stay (I may men- tion they purpose camping out for three or four months). Taking advantage of their kind offer, I transferred onself to the camp and feel like a giant refreshed after taking things very easy and indulging in sea bathing to a considerable extent. Now to relate my adventure. During a stroll through I a part of the forest for the purpose of gathering fir cdnes and dried sticks, as was my custom for the purpose of making a fire. I was startled, and may add horrified, to see a large snake suddenly rise up a few yards from me and make ready to spring. The day was exceedingly hot and no doubt the snake had come further than it anticipated so as to bask in the sun. However, what was I to do? I had nothing whatever to defend myself with, so I hastened to the tent for a stick. In the mean- time the venomous brute had disappeared, but I knew he could not have gone far and standing on a little eleva- tion between two tents, I was amply, rewarded, after waiting for a quarter of an hour, to see the snake emerge from the tent on my left, a well directed stone brought ' the beautiful specimen low, it, however, quickly recov- ered itself and disappeared into the tent again. Not daring to approach too near for fear he should spring upon me unawares, I waited for over an hour for him. At last! summoned up courage to unfasten the ropes in front of the tent so that I might get a better view cf the enemy. Having done this, peered carefully inside but failed to discover his whereabouts. This, of course, put me in a dilemma. He might have escaped through another part of the tent whilst I was so intently watch- ing the front at which he had shewn himself, and I was beginning to fear I had lost it. Taking up my stick again I went round the outside of the tent and com- menced probing at the canvas and matting that lay inside hoping to dislodge him, I ran to the front, gazed in, and there to my great joy I saw him slide into a piece of canvas that lay partially overlapped, now was my chance and with a few ini,.htv strokes across the head I had the satisfaction of seeing the snake lying dead before me. I carried it to my tent and laid it at full length on the ground. Messrs. Brown and Pennell, who arrived from town shortly after my capture, expressed their surprise at such a monster being found there, and they proceeded to measure and found it was five feet, three and a half, inches from tip to tip. Luckily I have not disfigured the snake in any way and as the skin is so beautifully marked, I decided to preserve it, I obtained a large glass jar and having half filled it with spirits the snake was arranged inside. We had numerous visitors at the camp to see the Cobra, and one and all expressed their sur- prise at the size of it, at the same time braising me for coolness in attacking such a deadly snake. This speci- men of snake is very fond of taking possession of the bed, especially those erected in tents, and have been repeatedly found coiled up either under the bed clothes or around the pillow, therefore it behoves everyone camping out to carefully examine their bed before retir- ing to rest. Of course, such events as these tend to make pleasure seekers uneasy, especially as this kind of snake generally go about in pairs. On parting from my friends to return to town.! gave them both strict injunc- tions to keep a good look-out for the companion snake. Up to the present, however, nothing has been seen of it.—Yours truly,
JOSEPH SMITH. Government Telegraphs, Capetown, S.A., Nov. 28 1893.
