BOARD OF GUARDIANS: "AN IMPERTINENT LETTER." Sir,—ln reading your report of the last meeting of the Board of Guardians, my attention was called to the confirmation of the minutes of the Committee of Pad- gate schools, re purchase of Musgraves' stoves. It was stated that a letter from a tradesman had been received, which by some of the committee had been called an "im- pertinent letter," and by one, I am told, an insulting one. I shall he obliged, if, in justice to myself, as the writer, you will kindly insert in your next Saturday's paper the letters referred to, copies of which I en- close. I cannot understand, sir, for what reason the commit- tee should go to Manchester in preference to Messrs. Musgraves' agent in Warrington, who, had he been ap- plied to, would have been willing to contract for the work, and,. having competent workmen on the spot, would have been able to have supplied and fixed the stoves quite 48 cheaply. Mr.J.C. Sutton tells the Board that if these stoves had been made byWarrington work- men it would have been a different thing, but, Sir, E fail to see what the difference is between a workman and a tradesman; both have to pay rates and taxes,which fall heavier on the ,tradesman than the workman. Since I have been in business in Warrington I have paid nearly one thousand pounds on rates and taxes, and yet if there is an order to be given out the committee prefer to spend thezatepayers' money out ef town. It does not matter to the Clerk or the committee how the tradesman makes his profits to pay the rates, and Mr. A. J. Jolley does not seem to think that tradesmen are worth con- sideration. Mr. J. C. Sutton, who for many years car- ried on an ironmonger's business ia the town, must know very well,that it is possible for a tradesman to eel( his goods at less than the manufacturer. He can, if he so desires, give the public, and often does, a share of his profit, but it -is scarcely likely that a manufactorer who knows his goods are wanted would be willing to do so; and yetilr.•Sutton says they went to Manchester because they could buy the stoves cheaper. I consider, Sir, I have been badly treated. I was at some considerable trouble and expense last February, at the ref:pest of the. Committee, preparing a plan and estimating for heating the schools with hot water. I have reason to know that my tender for this work was the lowest received; but the work was not carried out, and stoves are now used instead. I am much onliged to Mr. Shaw and, likewise Mr. A. Jolley for supporting him, as it gives me the opportunity of letting the public judge ii either of, nay letters bear the name given them by the committee.—Apole.gizing, Mr. Editor, for taking up so much of your valuable space.—l am, yours faith- fully, 51, Bridge-at., Warrington.
JOSEPH S. GARLAND.

The following are .capies of the letters described as " impertinent " and -" insulting " : November 14, 1893. To the Committee of Padgate Industrial Schools. Gentlemen.—Re, Heating of wards with Musgraves' stoves. .As sole agent for Musgraves' stoves in Warrington and-district, lam prepared to under take the supplying and lxing of above upon the same terms as their Manchester • house. Some time ago I offered through Mr. Minesto provide and fix a stove of Mr. Musgraves for the approval of the Committee, and I am sorry to find that you have gone to a Manchester house to do so.' If you have not definitely ordered, I trust you will do so through their responsible agent, and a large ratepayer.—l have the honour to be, gentlemen, yours truly, fosEpg S. GAar.,41,11). I also sent another letter to the Chairmau,of which the following is a copy : November 21, 1893. Dear find that the sub- committee of Padgate schools, have ordered crow Messrs Musgraves of Manchester, four stoves supplied and fixed at a cost of £4l 4s. Bd. For several years I .have been Agent for Musgraves' Stoves, and am sorry tk find that the order has gone to Manchester. I offered through Mr. Mines some time ago to provide and fix one of these stoves on approbation. I write now to say if your Com- mittee feel satisfied with these four stoves and decide to put:them in the other wards,l shall be willing to execute the•order on the same terms as their Manchester eouse. I hope therefore, at no dist.int date to be favoured with the Committee's orders which shall have my best atten- tioa--I am, dear sir, yours truly, JOSZPH S. GARLAND.

We are nowhere told that any special reverence is due to 1 the mother of Christ, as such; let alone the constant erection of her effigy in wood, or stone, or on canvas. As I to the veneration of relics, I never could see any sense in worshipping crumbling wood, decaying hones, rusty nails or rotting-rags, even if they belonged to " good ' men. One of any ancestors was a good man, and he left a relic. It was in the shape of an old-fashioned beaver hat, but so far from venerating it, I rather fancy it served as a football; and I always feel in a similar frame -of mind when I see deluded beings paying homage to such." relics "as I have described . "B. L." also says that humanists" wish to persevere with one mind in prayer with Mary the mother ofJesus and with His brethren,' as set forth in Acts, i, 14. But, in admitting this, "13. L. acknowledges the practice of a Romanist doctrine which I omitted in my previous letter—prayers for the dead. No such doctrine is sanctioned by the pas- sage alluded to. .Ncthing could be more natural than the prayers on that occasion, for when the Apostles returned from Mount Olivet to their abode, they held a prayer meeting for everybody in the house. "8.L." is also unfortunate in his reference as to" indulgences." Mat. xviii, 18, says -nothing about "power to remit sins" being given to the Church, but it does allude to a power to bind and to loose, a power which was not con- ferred on the Church. but upon all the disciples. Then, as to" confession "there is no-power of judgment given to the Church on this subject. We are exhorted in Luke xii. 8, to confess Christ "-before men," but nowhere are we directed to confess our sins to a priest or any man. Our fellowship is with - the Father, and with His Son Jesus Christ ? (John i, .3) As to the clergy being a " separate" class, we do not find that the Apostles were; andi just as Barnabas and Saul were separated for their work, so are all true disciples who have also to "come out from among them and be ye separate, saith the Lord." " ILL." goes on to state that St. Peter was cer- tainly distinguished frona all the.other Apostles. I admit that Peter was. He was distinguished for what would be described in these days as cheek, and for the severe ;rebukes he suffered at the hands of Christ and Paul. What could bomore Scathing than the words of the Master as he "turned and said unto Peter, Get thee behind me Satan-; thou art an offence unto me; for thou savourest not the things that tool God, but those that be of men." Truly this sentence-is the only fitting one for the Romish Church of to-day.; for it is un- aoubtedly more Satanic than Christlike, and so far from the Bible witnessing ," the truth and propriety " of the doctrines of the Catholic Church, it to my mind does the every reverse. bit'. Alfred T. J. Hilton is anxious as to the Bible, and I am sorry he has had to go so far afield for the informa- tion he de*/ 9 respecting it. Brixton is not so very far from Paternoster Row, and if he will visit the Oxford University Depot there,and purchase a little book called "-Helps to the studs' of the Bible," he will get all the knowledge he requires. I may, however, inform Mr. Hilton that I am certain that my own interpretation is the right one ; but as.l am, a somewhat busy individual anttherfditor's space is limited, I regret that I cannot stay to explain " how I arrived at this interesting state ' of mind." As to Mr. J. C. Dalton, he is amazed that J should say Christ did not make the Catholic Church (Roman Catho- • lic, 1 mean here Mr. Dalton), and I have still to say that I adhere to the statement I made, notwithstanding Mr. Dalton s incorrect quotations frotn the Bible, alooek that he needs to become a little more familiar with. The churches mentioned in that book certainly do not include the Remish Church, for it could not be one of the Churches of Asia, or the Church that was in the house of Aquila and Priscilla,. Mr. Dalton makes the most of the passage" Thou art Peter,aeul upon this rock I will build' my church." but is most obvious that the " rock ' meant was not that of Peter, but the rock of faith:- for we are told elsewhere (Ephesians V) that the church is" built upon the foundation of the Apostles and pro- phets. Jesus Christ being the chief corner stone "(not the pope) " in whom all the building fitly framed to- gether groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord " &c. My contention was, and is, that the Romish church is not the church that Christ founded, and but for the fear, Mr. Editor that I have already trespassed too much upon your space t could go on to show :Ant the homish religion is no more like the religion of Jesus Christ than • Mr. Dalton is like .

thee things which Mr. Peers has ignored, and assuming the navvies did descend the pit(which I do not think under the circumstances they would have done tot a moment) he asks if the masters would have been justi- fied. Yes,John in the eyes of the law,and made chiefly by landed proprietors and capitaliats,and under your peculiar system of ethics they would have been justified, and I have not the least doubt in the world, the law would have defended this course even to the shedding of blood. It all depends upon the ethics, John. Time was when I the holding of sl.ives was legal, and if some poor "hardly entreated brother," burning to be free left his master for freedom, the bloodhound would soon be on his trail. Would not the slave owner have been justified John, and would not the country have defended him? Under the law, and under the code of peculiar morals that then prevailed, lie would have been justified. It all depends , upon the ethics John, and we are having no more ethics of that kind if you please. I can quite understand Mr. Peers' hostile attitude against the wealttimroducara and silent acquiescence in the doings of the wealth appropriators. It is the fault of his training and we must make die allowance. He seems hurt that so ''level headed " a man as Mr. Whitham could not see that he was contending in favour of ill-paid labour. Mr. Whitham could see at a glance as everyone else must, that he was contending valiantly on behalf of the strong against the weak, that the logi- cal effect of his.doctrines is to bring down wages to the lowest point, to widen the gulf between the rich and the poor, to compel the poor man to produce wealth for the idle rich to-consume ; that such doctrines breed a sense of humiliation in some workers and a feeling of hatred in others en the Otle hand, and.a spirit of haughtiness and insolerree.on the other. " Man requires something more than work in this old world " says Mr. Price, to which Mr. Peers gives his gracious assent. Yet Mr. Peers upholds a competitive system under which the life of the average worker is as monotonous as the life of a Warrington 'bus horse. There is however, hope for the future ;a time will come when the worker will enjoy the advantages of culture, which his labour now enables only the rich to enjoy,; when he will have courage enough to hold up his herd In the presence of any man, when he will have time to live a man's life ; and com- mune with the dead whose spirit lives in literature, and to smile upon the face of nature and be glad. I feel that Mr. Peers on serious reflection must come round to the same view of life as I now take. It cannot all be done in a moment ; there was a time when I took much the same view as he, and I can quite appreciate the mental obstacles in his path. It is those bad old ethical principles that are playing the mischief. We must wait and work.—Yours

div.head: "POLEMICAL AMENITIES.
div.p: "POLEMICAL AMENITIES.

Sir,--Ln imitation of your erudite correspondent Mr. Peers,' will commence my answer to his letter published in your issue on the 9th instant with a quotation. Mr. Lecky " Rationalism in Europe " (vol. i. p.sl,ed. 1870), thus contrasts Catholic and Protestant intolerance. " Catholicism was an ancient Church. She had gained a great part cf her influence by vast services to 'man- kind." " She rested avowedly on the principle of authority. She was defending herself against aggression and innovation. She might point to the priceless blessings she had bestowed upon humanity, to the slavery she had destroyed, to the civilisation she had founded, to the many generations she had led with hon- our to the grave. ,She might show how completely her doc;rines were interwoven with the whole social system how fearful would be the convulsion if they were dea- -1 troved. and bow absolutely incompatible they,were With

the acknowledgment of private judgment. These con- siderations would not make her blameless, but they would at least palliate her guilt. But what shall we say of a church that was but a thing of yesterday, a church that had as yet no services to show, no claims upon the gratitude of mankind, a church that was by profession the creature of private judgment, and was in reality generated by the intrigues of a corrupt court, which nevertheless suppressed by force a. worship that multi- tudes deemed necessary to their salvation, and by all her organs, and with all her energies persecuted those who clung to the religion of their fathers? What shall we say of a religion which comprised at most but a fourth part of the whole Chris- tian world, and which the first explosion of private judg- ment had shivered into countless sects, which was nevertheless so pervaded by the spirit of dogmatism that each of those sects asserted its distinctive doctrines with the same confidence, arid persecuted with the same unhesitating violence, as a church which was venerable with the homage of twelve centuries ? So strong and so general was its intolerance that for some time it may, I believe be truly said,that there were more instances of partial toleration being advocated by Roman Catholics than by orthodox Protestants." So far so good, Mr. Lecky. Mr. Peers complains.that I should have to go so far back as the Revolution for "a home thrust." Not so, my dear sir. What about the dings of the Commune? What about the murder of the venerable Archbishop of Paris, Monsignor Dart What about the expelling of the religious orders from France? The suppression of religious education in the colleges and public schools? What about the open pat- ronage of infidelity by those in authority in the French Republic ; the expelling of Christian Brothers from the schools ; the expunging of even the name of God and: our Blessed Saviour Jesus, His Holy Mother, and all holy references from the instruction books in the schools and colleges? What, my friend, of the doings of your Ger- man Rationalistic gentry ? What of the Kulturcamp ? Why even now the religious orders of the Catholic Church are forbidden to live in Germany. But,says Mr. Peers, in answer to my charge against the Rationalists: "This was not the Rationalism of Hume,Lecky,lluxley, or Spenser." Oh, no ; it was not your smug, respect- able English Rationalism, but it was Rationalism as op- posed to authority, which authority Mr. Peers is pleased to call" a galling bondage,"" a quarrel among Catho- lics " (nice Catholics). Alas, their fathers were Catho- lics; this, then, was what Rationalism mads of them. Mr. Peers ventures the opinion that "bout these gentlemen were born in the faith they so zealously., de- fend. Like cabbages (very complimentary) where they are planted there they stay." Well, my dear friend, you are wrong, so far as lam concerned. I was reared in a low church atmosphere, and am a Catholic, by God's grace,from conviction. Butt would rather be a cabbage were I was planted in the Protestant Church of Eng- land retaining the belief in the Divinity of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, than to trust my eternal salvation to poor finite reason, as do your egotistical Rationalists. Faith to them is a bubble burst. The truth of a divine teacher to expousid the mysteries of revelation to all na- tions is by them set at defiance and made void. It would be a sad and bitter day for Eneland were these Rationalists to get hold of our little ones,the lambs of the flock. They would rob them of tho priceless gift, of holy faith, and what would they give in return? What are the results of their work in the world? Simply negation, as far as belief is concerned. But what are the visible results of their reasonings? Infidelity, an- archy, and bloodshed. Thank God there is one plank on which Mr. Foulkes and myself, the Protestants and Catholics,can stand shoulder to shoulder, and it is on the plank of religious education, resisting Rationalism and , all the other works of darkness which go by the name of liberty. In conclusion, let me say that Mr. Peers does not ob- ject to throwing a little mud himself, notwithstanding his outcry against such proceedings when he first penned ' his title " Polemical Amenities."—l am, Sir, yours &c., J. C. DALTON.

CIIRIST AND THE ROMANISTS. Sir,—My previous letter seems to have fallen amongst your readers with as terrifyirut an effect as the h Anarchist hcmh which was recently thrown in the midst of the French senators. Like the bomb, too, my epistle fell somewhat imperfectly ; but all the imperfections were not due to me. I little dreamed when I wrote the phrase "Stations of the Cross," the word " stations " would turn up in print as •• statims" ; nor did I think that my caligraphy, had as it was, was in so chaotic a condition, as to cause your printer to omit a line in the attempt to make sense of my remarks! However, I am not the first individual who has suffered at the hands Of the printer, and Mr. J. C. Dalton is welcome to all the Nix he can find in that fact. Mr. Dalton makes merry over the circumstance that I referred to the " Catholic." church ; but, in order that he may be no longer in doubt as to the church I had in my mind, I have altered the heading of this letter, and I trOst it will tie more to his ta.,te. But, as several cor- respondents have flown to Mr. Dalton's rescue, it will perhaps be better if I deal with them in order. Your correspondent "B. L." says that "The worship of the mother of Christ, and the veneration of the relics of good men, are the result of the ordinary feelings of humanity."

div.head: "COMMON JUSTICE."
div.p: "COMMON JUSTICE."

SOCIALISM. Sir,—Having been too busy for the last three weeks to have an oppertunity to write, it seems eur friend, Mr. John Peers, is delighted in the thought that (like the bantam cocks) he has had the last crow. Shakespere says " When igu3rance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise," and I would let Mr. John Peers " stew in his own juice" —.to quote the language of a well-known politician—if it were not that duty compels me to dispel the cloud of harmful ignorance concerning the party I am proud to claim as my party, and that is, the Secialist party. That party, is the party of the future. It has come to Eng- land like all foreigners, to stay here, and don't you for- get it. A gentleman in a high position in Warrington, a leading light of the Liberal party, and one whom I blame as much as anyone for destroying the party he be- longs to (as far as Warrington is concerned), with his cranks, said to me once that he thought Socialism arose from disappointment. For once he was right. To quote the words ot the immortal Victor Hugo :

Au banquet de la vie, Infortune convives. Most people have come too late to this life's feast, and have to put alp with the crumbs, as did Lazarus. My Liberal magnate's inference was not that however. He meant that 'Socialist leaders were so because they were not allowed to lead any where &se, and therefore tried to form a party of their own to acquire power, thus imputing to them a sordid selfish motive. It is not so. The first Socialist of the Christian era was Christ Him- oelf,and He was mot selfish. Would that all Christians and professed Christians followed His dictates 1 But when Christ was crucified, Christianity died with Him—if not With Him, with the last of His Apostles.. A pretty 'specimen are those Christians of to day. Take " Holy Russia "on one side, and Christian England on the other; pioes William of Germany, who wants all his soldiers to say the Lord's prayer every morning, and yet to know no will only his(the Emperor's) will. Roman Catholic, Spain, Italy, Portugal and the rest, what are they doing ? Keeping their millions of soldiers armed to the teeth, res.dy at a moment's notice to butcher each other, for a cause they would not know of. Now all these nations' leaders are professed Christians. and make a great show of their religious belief. Presi- dent Carraot, the head of the French Bourgeois Republic, is en very good terms with his Holiness the Pope of Rome, and the Italians are so much afraid of the Pope being reinstated on his temporal throne that they have joined in an alliance with the enemies of France for fear France would reinstate him. There you are ! The blessings or religion, piummged France into war in 1870, because Bismarck had plagued the Jesuits, and the Empress Eugenie used her influence with her husband, Napoleon the Little, and urged him to try and put Roman Catholic Austria at the head of German Unity as it used to be previuus to the battle of Sadowa. The result was instead of France" slugging" Germany, she got all the " slugging " herself, and the Jesuits remained where they are up to date, exiled from the empire of William of Germany. France fought for Italy in 1859, and made that country what she is, and if it were not for the quarrels got up by the Jesuits on one side and the Protestants on the other, the two countries would be good friends. So much for the blessings of religion.. In all these things remember the poor people pay for all, work for all, suffer for all. I would not say fer that, that Christianity is played out. Atheists do say so, but it ie a mistake. Christianity never had a fair try yet. Christ, when He was walking about with His disciples, had everything in common. One of the dieciplee carried the purse and paid all dues and demands,ancl onus when money was scarce in Capernaum that disciple was inclined to keep the only coin they had,and " slope" the market toll collector, but was told by Christ Himself to give to Cresar what belonged to Cresar. My Liberal leader met me the day after Sir A. B. Walker's will was published in the Papers and he said to me : " What do you think of Walker's four millions ?" Said he "If I had my way I would take it from the heirs and distribute it to different good institutions." " Well," said I, " I would do no such thine. and I am surprised at you, a magistrate, who should know and uphold the law. lam a Socialist and have much differ- ent ideas about the matter." He asked me what I would do, and this is what I said : " Whatever a man has got, we Socialists would let him possess it in peace a-,d enjoy the fullness of his goods, and we would proteet every man and his property. But we would take good care no man could possihly get more of the goods of this world than was good for him or the safety and the happiness of his neighbours. That may be done in. various ways. To begin with the brewers, we would municipalise the drink trade, and pull down all your rickety old dens of Infamy in the slums, and make the " pubs" comfort- able club houses, where honest and peaceable citizens could congregate without fear of being robbed or insulted, cheated or poisoned with bad drink." " Ohl" said he, "we would not agree with that ; it would make the • pubs ' too respectable." "My dear sir," said I, " you are a bigot and past praying for ; therefore I would not waste my time longer with you." • Now, you see the difference between a Liberal leader and a magistrate and the Socialist. Our Liberal leaders are now making a fuss—and well they may—about the rates of the town being 63. 4d. in thee. with a prospect of turning up next year to the tune of 7s: in the L. Let Warrington borrow £lOO,OOO, or, if need be, £200,000.1 and build her own " pubs." Out of the profits, after paying interest on capital,- the rates might be reduced to a minimum of is. in the 2. And that could be done without robbing anyone of one penny piece, let alone four million pounds, as our magistra.e friend would have us do. The Socialists do not want to take any- thing fro:n anyone ; they want to stop lawfully licensed thieves—he tfiey lawyers, clergymen, brewers, land- owners, or master bakers—from robbing the poor. As things are, I consider a poor publican has a great deal to contend with. It is almost, if not totally, impossible for a publican to pay his way and keep within the law. I pity him. I know places in different towns which are really not tit to exist, but they belong to some big brewery and are tolerated, and the keepers of them have to encourage gambling and prostitution to make money for a brewer who builds, or helps to build, churches and presents the livings to needy relatives. leurther,the brewers wax rich and buy land and property to no enc Land become omnipotent beings in the districts in which they live. They may dispise to sit in the Council Chamber of the borough where their interest is, but they put up puhlicane as puppets to do the work in the Council for them.. Now the Socialists look at these things and are,disappointed to lied the people so silly as to work their own ruin. The State is governed by three powers, or otherwise three powerful pieces of machinery--lst, the clergy ; 2nd, the police ; 3rd, the army. In what condition are these three machines ? In a very bad condition, and we Socialists intend to do some repairs and alrerations Ito them, and if they are past repairing, set them on one side and put up some fresh machines in their places. ' Let us bein with the Church. That machine is in a very bad condition indeed. The wheels are so clogged , with rust that they la ill not move. The Church does everything contrary to the purpose it was established forl It takes sides with the rich, oppressors of the poor. Jesus Christ denounced those oppressors. The Church , Should lead the people instead of which it misleads them. A good percentage of time clergy of the Church of Eng- land are unfitted for the posts they occupy, but as advancement in the Church goes by purchase, a clever curate may linger on in life with a wife and family on £BO per year. and less than that sometimes, to keep and educate six children and appear respectable, while a numbskull may be a rector with £l.OOO or £2,000 a year over a parish of five or six hundred inhabitants, not one quartertof wham avail themselves of his services. Yet Jesus Christ said the labourer is worthy of his hire.

The other Sunday at the Warrington Parish Church,ll the Mayor and Alderman and Councillors, and a good many leading members of society, sat to listen to a ser- mon, The Rector advised the publican element who had got into full power on the Ist of November to be good and keep their" pubs "in good order. In so many words he advised them to keep respectable. He must have an idea that there is a screw loose somewhere, and he is not far wrong. It the Rector would consent to come with me I would show him the beauties and sights of Warrington. lam at his service at any time in any I weather, night or day, and if Ido not open his eyes with what I can show him lam not a Frenchman but a Dutchman. You may ask what can the Rector do to alter things. There you are. Read the Church prayer. book. The clergy officiating at the Church can lawfully refuse the Holy Communion to any member of the con- gregation whona he knows to have done something wrong until he mends his ways, repents ,and becomes as good as he ought to be to approach the Holy Communion Table. And if the Rector came with me there are a few big nobs that I know of,who would get the "chuck out" of congregation, or alter their ways anyhow. There was another sermon preached in Warrington in a Nonconformist place of worship, and the tone was quite different ;it pleased me well. The Rev.A. Mursell told his hearers that it was wrong for shareholders to live on dividends in luxury when poor fellow creatures had to slave 18 hours a day for a bite of bread and eat it in the cold on the splash board of the cab they drove night and day in all sorts of weather. That is the way a clergyman should speak ; but you cannot expect it to be done in the Church of England', until that Church stands on its own bottom, and is self supporting. The aristocracy have a vested interest in the church, and thosewho are not with us are against us. So Christ said, and therefore the Church must work for the rich and help to oppress the poor, and she _does it.

Having said so much I feel lam encroaching on your space and on the patience of your readers. So I will conclude until next week, when, with your kind permis- sion,l will deal further with socialism, versus the present system of government.—Yours, &c.,_
A.' BR OUCHEMITE.

div.head: DISLENTE R.
div.p: A DISLENTE R.

WORK, WAGES, AND ETHICAL PRINCIPLES. Sir,—l could scarcely repress a smile when I read Mr. Peers' reference about the " amount of abuse" he said be was receiving in these columns. Really, I thought it was the other way about, but as this is not argument,l think we might let it pass. Mr. Peers believes he might achieve greater popularity if he cared for it, by advoca- ting " the abrogation cf ethical principles, &c." The inference is, that Mr. Henry Whithatn, Mr. Brouchemite, myself and others who have defended the colliers in their resistance against the cutting down of wages in- stead of profits, desire to revise the decalogue, in order that it may fit in with our progaganda. I would not advise Mr. Peers to advocate the abrogation of any such thing : but he might preach a stricter adherence to true 1 principles, for which he professes so much solicitude. Let us review the beautiful "ethical principles" which underlie the system which Mr. John Peers de- fends. A number of men whom we have very foolishly 11 permitted to become the owners of a natural cunurio- dity which they have never seen,and whose assumption ! of ownership Mr. Peers himself declares is al-surd, enter without consulting their men into contracts involving either a loss of the masters' profit or the men's wages. They desire to recoup themselves and ask for 25 per cent, reduction, which the men will not agree to. Now, one would think that Mr. Peers' " ethical principles" ' would allow of the men having a voice in a matter of so much vital importance,and without whom no coal could be obtained at all. But you are mistaken, they do no such thing. The " ethical principles" of Mr. Peers,are, in fact, very peculiar ; formulated so that the rich may get richer, and the poor may get poorer—or steal. He would maintain a system under which a starving man may go to a coalowner and offer to take the bread out of the motith of a struggling miner by consenting to work for lower wages. Thus one unemployed man would obtain work, the worker would be thrown upon public charity, and Who would reap the benefit ? Mr. Peers' protege, the man who is starving on £lOB a week. Ethical principles! Fudge! These are the principles of the devil hitnself. rhey may find defenders in Mr. John Peers, in interested capitalists, and in bishops who associate with them ; and in ecclesiastics of lesser rank Who would not like to offend the austere prelate, and in many a Nonconformist pulpit, I doubt not, but such ethics are no les' false for all that. Of course Mr. Peers says every mtn has a right to sell his labour in the best marke,t at the best possible price. He exclaims "have I not repeatedly said so ?" Yes,John, you have, and straightway gone and denied him the right. Did I not show you in my last letter ? What is the use holding that a workman has such a right in theory, if you deny him the right to practice it ? The miners were exercising this right when Mr. Peers dis- covered that some chemical workers were thrown out of work because there was no coal to be obtained. "oh," says John, "this won't do ; you are justified in rigor- ously enforcing and upholding, your right, but you must- not ti. it,because other people will suffer." Not that the_ coalowner must not make the demand for a reduction, but that the miners must not resist, because ft causes so much inconvedience and expense to other people, you know." Well, we are not having any ethics of that' kind ts-day, Rim, thank you. Mr. Peers thinks it is a pity men should lose sight or the iniquitous means they employ in their endeavour to arrive at the goal they have in view, and mentions the " fanatic "who advises them to do this. lam just a little in doubt as to whether I ant the particular " fana- tic" referred to, but I think I may fairly assume that I am. Personally I hate lock outs and strikes ; I desire a much more peaceful method of re-adjusting industrial disputes, but under our competitive system lean quite conceive that there are times when a resort to these bar- barous instruments is inevitable. But as every man has a right to sell his labour in the best possible market at the highest price, I don't quite see under this particular standard which we have set up, where the" iniquity of the means employed "comes in, the chemical workers notwithstanding. In my last letter. reeked Mr. Peers to explain how the miners were to uphold their right to the highest price, except by throwing the chemical labourers idle. His silence upon this point establishes the impreg- nability of ivy position. I notice further that he attempts to build up an argument on the basis that a workman is not justified in refusing to let others work in his stead. A workman possesses no such legal right, nor has he the power to do it, but he has both a legal and moral right to exercise peaceful influences to prevent him stepping in and, by accepting work, reducing the standard of wages, and as a consequence the standard of living. During the salt Union strike in September, 1893, non- union men were employed ; but through the mediation of the Bishop of Chester they were brought out again, and the old hands were reinstated. I mention this to show that there is something higher even than musty legal parchments ; that there is A code of ethics which recog- nises something distinctly unfair and mean in one man stepping in at a crucial stage, and inflicting an injury upon the weaker party to a dispute. Heaven knows that men are but human, and that they are often com- pelled to do mean things, not from choice, but stern necessity. But what has this got to do with Mr. Peers' attitude en the coal lock out. Have I not shown in my previous letter that the members of the Miners' Federa- tion were not guilty of violence and intimidation ? Have I not before pointed out the absurdity of describing the miners as "tyrants " because some few that you could count upon your fingers and toes have been guilty of violence? When will this champion of the coal owners be able to perceive that because one man in a family commits murder, it does not follow that thu whole of the other members of the family are murderers as well ? I am not concerned about Mr. Peers suppositious case as to whether navvies on strike would be justified in taking the colliers' places in the pit. I was defending the colliers against the attacks of Mr. Peers, and believe I have succeeded. But I may say that the wages of col- liers and navvies very nearly approximated so that there would he no advantage, and therefore no necessity for the navvies, to take the miners pick. Besides, had they done so, navvies' wages would' have gone up with a bound, so that their stay in the coat hole would have been short and the case would have been, so far as the miners were concerned in statu quo. But overlooking

RUGBY FOOTBALL.

Again did our home eleven write victory over their engagement, with the Manchester Rangers. But it was not difficult to perform this task ; it was compartively an easy matter for a team which have been practicing writing that gratifying word. The Manchester Rangers do not make any boast of their claims for first rank hon Airs, and as a team they are not an impressive corn- bination. Considering the many reverses they are en- countering it is a wander they do not put up the shutters and clpse business. However, one must not be hard on them. They served to provide Warrington with a canter for 'twere a pity for us to make a brag of the local win of four tries.

Heesom was at back again and played a sound game, but the performances of the three quarters were rather erratic. Indeed, one did not require the assistance of a hydraulic engine to work up a smile of amusement, when witnessing the behaviour of these erstwhile energe- tic individuals. At one time a halo of brilliance was the thing to be hung above their performances, whilst at others a jester's cap would have been a more appropri- ate, though more modest crest. However, they were no doubt only seeking amusement, and, besides, is not that thrice-glorious period at hand, the time of wassail and gaslamps, and moving pavements? Another thing, it is ' the time for goodwill and generosity, of which, by the way, I would remind that promising player, Carey. I'm sure he was not in any way too generous with his corn- peers when he had the ball in his possession. But prob- ably he had a weakness for leather ; in that case I know where he can get good durable steaks very cheap. By the way Fair Turner was placed at three-quarters. Some people were inclined to treat this as a joke. But it wasn't. When Fairfield scored a try from that posi- tion it was voted to be an instance of his versatility.

The two Bates showed their clever combination against the weak opposition, but unfortunately John Bate re- ceived another injury which caused him to leave the field. By the way, I see that the two Bates—known in the football world now as the " brothers "—are again in for county honours.

Mr. E. A. Connor, the centre forward of Warrington Association P.C., was playing for the Preston North End team against Bolton Wanderers last Wednesday. The famous Preston team won by four goals to three, and out of the four Connor scored one.

div.head: _ ALLEGED BREACH OF WARRANTY.
div.p: _ ALLEGED BREACH OF WARRANTY.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, Jo9hua Boydell, Bowdon, sued James Daley, 37, Scotland- road,Warrington, for £33 for breach of warranty for a chestnut horse,and there was also a counter claim for £ll 15s. for the keep of the horse. Mr. H. J. Longton represented Boydell, and Mr. A. Browne represented Daley. Mr. Longton said that the plaintiff resided in Bowdon, and was a tailor,carry- ing on business in Warrington, Manchester, and other places. The claim was for £33 paid by plain- tiff in respect of a horse which was purchased by the plaintiff for the defendant. The history of the case was as follows :—ln April the plaintiff bought a black mare from the defendant for £25. It was agreed that the mare was to be suitable for the plaintiff's use, but after trial of the mare, it was found to he unsuitable, and his client informed Daley of the fact. The two parties came together on May 29, and a second horse was chosen, It was in respect of this horse that the present case arose. It was agreed that an additional .£8 in exchange with the black mare for the chestnut horse. On May 28, the bargain was made on the express warranty that it was to be suitable. The horse was taken to plaintiff's residence next morning, and in a few days a witness named Benstock examined the horse and discovered it as unsound, and had a curb:in its hocks. Mr. Boyden thereupon wrote to the defendant informing him of the state of the horse. The horse was taken to Daley and taken in without any protest. Boydell subsequently came once to Warrington to examine some other horses belonging to Daley,but none of them were suitable. Daley had not sent the money back,and the present proceedings were instituted.—Joshua Boydell, the plaintiff, and Mr. Jesse Boydell gave corroborative evidence.— Amos Henstock gave evidence to the effect that the horse had a curbed hock.—Frederick Buswell said that he was groom to Mr. Boydell at the time the horse was brought to Bowdon. He took the chestnut back from Altrincham to Warrington, and although it was all right at the commencement of the journey it was rather lame when he arrived at Warrington. Ile left the horse with Mrs. Daley. —Wm. Wilkinson said that he saw Daley's son rubbing something on the horse's leg.—After evi- dence of George Pane, the manager of Messrs. Boy- dell's Warrington shop, to the effect that he paid the two sums of .£25 and £8 for the two horses and got receipts, Mr. Browne, for the defence contended that there was no warranty given in he present transaction,which was simply an exchange.—Arthur Shawcross, veterinary surgeon, Sankey-et., said that he saw the horse at the time Mr. Boydell bought it. He had intended to have bought it himself, but it was not stylish enough. It had no curb then, but at the present time it had one.—Peter Daley,the son of the defendant, denied that there was any curb on the horse's hock before it was sold.—Jas. Daley, the defendant, was then called, and said that the transaction was simply an exchange, and no war- ranty whatever was given.—His Honour, in sum- ming up, said that he did not consider that there had been any warranty given, or if there had been, he did not believe that there was any breach, be- cause the defendant and his brother had plenty of time to examine the horse. He would, therefore, give judgment for the defendant in the claim, and in the counter claim he would give judgment for the plaintiff.
